rows.q: What is the originary hypothesis?
rows.a:
The originary hypothesis is the starting point of everything in Center Study. It is Eric Gans's answer to a question that sounds simple: how did language begin? It turns out to be the same question as how the human began, and how the sacred began.

## The short version

Gans proposed it in *The Origin of Language* (1981). Katz summarizes it this way: it "posits a singular event within which language, or the sign, originates" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-1)). Katz stresses how little it needs: "The originary hypothesis is easily summed up in a couple of paragraphs, at most, and all it really assumes is that human beings are mimetic creatures" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)).

## The scene, step by step

**1. Mimesis leads to rivalry.** We learn everything by imitating others, and that includes learning what to want. If I imitate your desire, sooner or later I want the very thing you are reaching for, and my model becomes my obstacle. Katz puts the dilemma plainly: such a conflict "can only be resolved in one of two ways: one defeats the other; the two share the desired object." The first outcome is what every other species does. Only the second "could [produce] something like a 'community'" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2), [p-3](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-3)).

**2. The animal order breaks down.** Picture a group of late hominids around a kill. "Normally, feeding would proceed in accord with the pecking order—the alpha animal eats to satiation, then the beta, and so on. On our hypothetical occasion, the intensification of mimetic desire overrides the pecking order as all rush to the meal at the center" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-41)). Each wants the object more because the others want it. This is the **mimetic crisis**.

**3. The aborted gesture.** "One member of the group hesitates in the face of this emergent disorder—his reaching for the central object is aborted; this action that has not been completed becomes a sign, and can be imitated. It is a sign of deferral" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-42)). A grab turns into a point. The same capacity for imitation that drove everyone toward the object now spreads the gesture that holds them back. That gesture is the first sign.

**4. The center becomes sacred.** No one on the scene can say "I decided to stop." They have no language for that, and in any case each of them is only copying the others. So the power that holds them back seems to come from the object itself. "The creation of the human is mediated by the creation of the sacred center as the creator of the human" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)). This is why Center Study begins from **the center**, the thing everyone attends to and is held back from, and not from individual subjects.

**5. Sharing, then ritual.** The group then divides and eats the object (Gans calls this the *sparagmos*). Afterward the gesture is repeated over the remains, and that repetition is the first ritual: a re-enactment so that the community does not have to stumble on the gesture again in the next crisis ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-8)).

Out of this comes a definition of the human: "the human is that being who is a greater danger to himself than is posed by any external danger" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-2)). Out of it also comes the formula that underlies most of Center Study: representation is the **deferral** of violence.

## Why an *event*, and not a gradual evolution?

Human signs are conventional. A word means what it means because we treat it as meaning the same thing every time. But conventions seem to require some prior way of agreeing on conventions. Katz calls this "the properly paradoxical question of how conventions could have been formed without the means of forming conventions," and argues that only a scene can resolve it ([Addressing an Objection](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-26)). His shorthand for what language is: being able to say **"this is the same"** ([p-27](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-27)). No animal signal does that. Hence the rhetorical question: "How could language have emerged other than in an event?" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-6)).

## Gans's departure from Girard

Rene Girard, Gans's teacher, put a collective murder at the origin: the group's violence converges on one scapegoat, who is then revered as a god. Gans's objection is that a killing alone would not be memorable. "There needs to be some formal acknowledgment of the event—there needs to be a sign." And once the sign is what matters, "if the real point is the pointing, the killing itself is superfluous" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38), [p-39](/post/event-origin-center#p-39)). The originary scene is nonviolent at its core: violence is deferred, not discharged.

## What Katz adds

Two of Katz's emphases shape how Center Study uses the hypothesis.

**Firstness.** Gans tends to describe everyone signing at once. Katz objects that "It would simply be too miraculous for all on the scene to simultaneously emit and recognize the sign." On his account someone hesitates first, unevenly, and most such scenes would have failed. "All we need to imagine is one time where the hesitation is marked a bit more precisely" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-11), [p-13](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-13)). This asymmetry at the origin becomes the root of Katz's thinking on hierarchy, leadership and pedagogy.

**The scene never closed.** No one could ever certify that the originary scene was over, because any such certification would itself take place on a new scene. So "we have never left and will never leave the originary scene" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-12)). Every utterance either continues the gesture of deferral or risks a "premature attempt at appropriation that will collapse the scene" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-8)).

## Its status

It is a hypothesis, and it is unfalsifiable: no dig will ever turn up the scene. Gans himself concedes that "Any such hypothesis must be in some sense a just-so story. But its heuristic value is undiminished" ([The Origin of Language](/post/the-origin-of-language#p-128)). Its claim rests on minimality, on being the simplest scene that accounts for the conventional sign, and on how much it lets you explain.

## Trying it out

Katz offers a compact translation of what the scene accomplished: "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)).

Take a meeting where two colleagues are about to start talking over each other for the floor. Someone says, "Let's go around the table." The "rush" toward the center (here, the floor) is converted into a shared sign everyone repeats, a procedure, and the procedure creates an order where there was about to be a melee. Center Study reads every institution, from etiquette to courts of law, as an elaborated version of that gesture.

## Where to read next

- [Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin), then [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence): short talks on why we can't avoid thinking about origins, and on what "deferral" means and why it is the key word.
- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself): Katz on why so few people take the hypothesis seriously, and what it asks of those who do.

A question to carry forward: if the first sign was a *refusal* to grab, what would it mean to treat each thing you say today as either continuing that refusal or quietly reaching for the center yourself?

rows.q: What does Katz mean by imperative exchange?
rows.a:
## The short answer

An imperative exchange is a relation with the center that runs on commands in both directions. You obey what the center tells you to do, and in return you tell the center what you need from it. The center might be a god, a king, an institution, or just "reality." Katz's clearest formulation:

"Ritual is an exchange with the center: the participant fulfills some command of the center while making a request of the center. It is an asymmetrical imperative exchange." ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2))

The textbook case is sacrifice. The worshipper brings his goat to the altar because the deity has ordered it, "while, in exchange, the sacrifice represents a request, on the part of the one offering the sacrifice, that the deity continue providing these benefits (more goats)" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-1)).

The exchange is asymmetrical because the center gave first. The goat, the herd and the community itself are already its gifts.

## Where it comes from in originary grammar

"Imperative" here is meant in the grammatical sense: a command, demand, request or plea, as opposed to an *ostensive* (pointing at something present) or a *declarative* (a statement about something that need not be present).

On the originary scene the central object holds the group back. In effect it issues a command: stay your hand. Once that object has been consumed, the center lives on beyond any particular object. Katz says it now "receives imperatives along with issuing them, and is therefore increasingly defined by this dialogue with the community" ([The Discourse of the Center](/post/the-discourse-of-the-center#p-3)).

Imperative exchange therefore starts when bare pointing is no longer enough. Katz writes: "Imperative exchange with the center results from ostensive failure, and aims at restoring an ostensive relation to the center. The people consume together the meal they have been granted by the center in accord with the rituals derived, which is to say, commanded by, the center, and in return request from the center that the next meal be made available" ([Ostensive-Imperative Generativity and Scenic Design Practices](/post/ostensive-imperative-generativity-and-scenic-design-practices#p-3)).

## Why it matters: failure produces thought

The concept earns its place because exchanges fail. Sometimes the rains don't come and the hunt fails. In that case either the ritual was performed badly and must be tightened, or a new command has to be heard ([same essay](/post/ostensive-imperative-generativity-and-scenic-design-practices#p-4)).

The declarative arises in exactly this gap. Its first job is to explain why the exchange broke down, which is the origin of myth, with its stories of the god's anger, a rival deity, or a hidden fault in the community ([Programming, Power and Declarative Culture](/post/programming-power-and-declarative-culture#p-3)). Katz pushes the point down to thinking itself:

"Thinking begins with the failure of some imperative exchange—I did this, but reality didn't supply that, and why in the world should I have expected it to... The declarative sentence, then, is best understood as the conversion of a failed imperative exchange into a constraint" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)).

The structure also never goes away. It "cannot be eliminated—it is embedded in our habits... if I do this, reality will supply that" ([same](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)). Katz calls it "our most fundamental orientation to the world" ([Sovereign Commands, Anarchistic Demands](/post/sovereign-commands-anarchistic-demands-gablog#p-14)). Even stripping away our hidden imperatives is something we do in obedience to another imperative ([#p-15](/post/sovereign-commands-anarchistic-demands-gablog#p-15)).

## The escalation and the break

Left to itself, imperative exchange escalates. The more the center is held to have given, the more it must be paid: "in the end, the most treasured possession, i.e., your first born." The God of the burning bush, whose name is a declarative sentence, breaks the cycle "not by demanding less of His devotees but by demanding more: by demanding all of you, all the time" ([The Sovereign Remembering of Names](/post/the-sovereign-remembering-of-names#p-8)). If the center has given everything, "there is no more commensurability and therefore no more exchange" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-24)).

Katz calls what replaces it **interrogative imperativity** ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-14)). The question shifts from "how do we get what we're owed" to "what makes you think obligations can be calculated?" ([#p-15](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-15)). Prayer is the model throughout, and refined prayer turns its request into a request for further command: "tell me how to serve you," and finally "help me to know how to donate to you" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-40)). This is also why Katz can say that "desire is the unfulfilled imperative," and that prayer defers that imperative rather than insisting on it ([Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-3)).

In the recent essays the concept is put to new uses. Technology is "perfecting the imperative," and our relation to it has the shape of "petition meeting command": "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-19), [#p-20](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)). Imperative exchange then branches into perfecting the imperative on one side and "soliciting the nomos" on the other, meaning credit, property and assets ([Originary FinTech](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-18)).

## Applying it

Take someone who has followed every rule at work, made the long hours and the extra reports, in the tacit expectation of promotion. That is an imperative exchange. When the promotion goes to someone else, Katz's definition of resentment fits exactly: "your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)).

The person now has the same options the ritual community had:
- **Tighten the ritual**: work even harder by the same rules.
- **Myth**: build a story of a saboteur or favoritism.
- **Declarative constraint**: conclude "promotion here doesn't track compliance," which is a rule learned from failure.
- **The post-sacrificial move**: stop haggling over what is owed and ask what the institution actually commands, as in "tell me how to do what you are telling me to do." Katz would add that the gap the person stumbled on is where useful feedback to the center comes from.

## Where to read next

- [Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial) is the clearest single treatment of the move from imperative exchange to interrogative imperativity.
- [Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory) shows how failed exchanges generate the declarative and thinking itself.
- [Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange: Originary FinTech](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech) carries the concept into technology, credit and the nomos.

A question to try: pick an institution you rely on, such as a university, an employer or the state. What are you tacitly commanding it to do in return for your compliance? And what would it mean to turn that demand into a request for clearer commands instead?

rows.q: What is the difference between the signifying center and the occupied center?
rows.a:
The short answer: the **occupied center** is whoever actually holds the center, the ruler or head of whatever body is in question. The **signifying center** is the center as the source of meaning and order, which that occupant can embody, betray, or fail to live up to. They began as one center, and the question of how they relate is, for Katz, the central political problem of the post-sacral world.

## Where the distinction comes from

Start with the originary scene, the hypothetical event in which the first humans, converging on a shared object, convert their grabbing into a gesture of deferral. Something is in the middle, but something more than that thing is "there." In the lecture on the center Katz puts it this way:

"This means there’s a subsistent center beyond the center at which any particular thing sits—so, there’s the center, and there’s centrality, or, as I’ve called it, the occupied center and the signifying center." ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-6))

The animal gets eaten. The centrality that held everyone back and then let them share in order outlasts it. In another essay he describes this as "the different between the slain deer at the center of the originary scene and the divine utterance calling upon the newly human group to cease and desist and then approach in an orderly way" ([Writing as the Programming of Scenes](/post/writing-as-the-programming-of-scenes-the-affordances-of-god#p-19)).

For a long time no human occupied the center. That changes with the Big Man, who seizes the ritual center and controls distribution. Since then, as Katz explains in a Q&A, "The \"occupied center\" is the state, or the head of government," "But the center is also the source of meaning, coherence and consistency--it's what makes an order an order" ([Bouvard on Center, Collective Intentionality, and Power](/post/adam-katz-how-do-you-define-the-concept-of-the-center#p-10)). More compactly: "the \"signifying center\" is the meaning with which we imbue the occupied center and all its branches" ([same](/post/adam-katz-how-do-you-define-the-concept-of-the-center#p-11)).

## Fused, then split

Under sacral kingship the two are held together in one person. The same passage says the difference between deer and divine utterance is "the difference between the 'God' and 'Emperor' components of the God Emperor" ([Writing as the Programming of Scenes](/post/writing-as-the-programming-of-scenes-the-affordances-of-god#p-19)). A later essay glosses them as "the 'signifying center' (the sacred) and the occupied center (the imperial)" ([Hyperstitching](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative#p-1)).

Once a human occupies the center, though, there is a question that never arises when a deer or an ancestor-god is there: "the problem becomes determining, or knowing, that the center as occupied is the same center as the center as signifying" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-155)). The Axial Age revelations, especially the God whose name is a declarative sentence, pull the two apart, because no man can now be God. Katz states the result bluntly: "if no human can be a god, then why should anyone be at the center; and yet someone must be and, in fact, is" ([Writing as the Programming of Scenes](/post/writing-as-the-programming-of-scenes-the-affordances-of-god#p-20)). With the collapse of sacral kingship, "the problem of the relationship between the signifying and the occupied center opened up and became the central, still unsolved problem of social order" ([Debits and Credits](/post/debits-and-credits#p-13)).

## The wrong way to relate them

The modern solution has been to set up a rival, purer version of the signifying center and judge the occupant against it: "The ruler must himself be ruled by God’s law, and then by “Reason,” and then as a “servant of the people,” and so on—all concepts controlled by the disciplines" ([Talk of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-talk-of-the-center#p-2)). Katz calls these "super-sovereignties." Whoever claims to interpret them becomes a hidden competitor for the center, which leaves power permanently contested. He asks instead that we "resist opposing antagonistically the two centers" with appeals to "God-given rights, some open-ended horizon of equalization, resistance to 'tyranny'" ([Writing as the Programming of Scenes](/post/writing-as-the-programming-of-scenes-the-affordances-of-god#p-20)).

He does not deny the tension. Imperatives from the central authority "are only worthy of being followed if the central authority is in accord with the signifying center" ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-1)). The question is where the signifying center makes itself heard, if not in a court of appeal above the ruler.

## Where you actually meet it: the imperative gap

His answer is the **imperative gap**, "a difference between the imperative uttered and the imperative obeyed (or, for that matter, defied)" ([The Center, its Affordances and Issuances, and Time](/post/the-center-its-affordances-and-issuances-and-time#p-3)). No command specifies everything its execution requires. The person carrying it out has to supply the rest, and that is where the signifying center speaks: "The voice we hear from the center in that case is the signifying center’s, as it tells us how to fill the imperative gap in our asymmetrical exchanges with the occupied center" ([Generating Idiomatic Intelligences](/post/generating-idiomatic-intelligences-and-translation-practices#p-4)).

So the signifying center "can inform the practices of individuals in ways that are irreducible to commands given by the center’s occupant. This doesn’t loosen the bond between individual and center, though" ([Scale](/post/scale#p-11)). It makes you a more active participant in the center, not a judge standing outside it.

The *Anthropomorphics* chapter on the topic uses the example of people escaping a burning building. Whoever knows the way out takes the lead and hands out tasks, and the center of that scene, getting everyone out, is clear. Trouble starts when the person in charge comes to depend on keeping a majority rather than on the task, so the occupied center drifts away from what the scene is for ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-10)). Holding to the signifying center then does not mean overthrowing the leader. It "shifts the focus of the question from “this man” to the specific command" ([same](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-18)).

## Applying it

Suppose a hospital director orders a ward to cut the time spent on each patient. One response treats the order as illegitimate in the name of "patients' rights" and fights the director. That uses the signifying center as a weapon against the occupied one. Katz's alternative is to ask what this command, from this office, at this point in the hospital's history, is trying to keep going, and to carry it out so that its fulfilment shows that purpose. Where that turns out to be impossible, the failure itself becomes information returned up the chain. The occupant is still obeyed. The signifying center comes in through *how* the order is obeyed.

In his more recent work he tries to bring the two together through succession. The occupant selects "not just the next occupant, but the next occupant to select the next occupant" ([Hyperstitching](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative#p-1)), so that the continuity of the order is built into how it is held. He also suggests that in a healthy order the signifying center is barely noticed: "The occupied/signifying center, then, is more powerful and all-encompassing the more it goes unnoticed" ([The Holding and the Held Center](/post/the-holding-and-the-held-center-beyond-disagreement#p-3)).

## Where to go next

- [Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center): the chapter of *Anthropomorphics* that develops the distinction through the burning-building team and the question of selecting a successor.
- [The Holding and the Held Center](/post/the-holding-and-the-held-center-beyond-disagreement): a short later essay on how the social center "holds" you while you attend to some local center of your own.

An exercise: think of a command you recently received at work or elsewhere that could not be followed exactly as stated. What did you add to carry it out? Did that addition serve the person who gave the order, the institution's ongoing purpose, or something you held against both?

rows.q: Explain the ostensive, the imperative and the declarative, and why the order matters.
rows.a:
Center Study starts from a claim about language: speech forms are not interchangeable tools. Each came into being at a particular moment, to solve a particular crisis, and each still carries that origin inside it. The sequence goes ostensive, then imperative, then interrogative, then declarative. It comes from Eric Gans's *The Origin of Language*. Katz takes it over and builds an "originary grammar" on it. Once you see how each form grows out of the one before, you can see why reversing the order, treating the statement as the basic form of language, is the error he spends much of his work taking apart.

## The ostensive: pointing at the center

The ostensive is the sign of pointing or naming: "This!" It is the first sign. On the originary scene, a group converges on a desired object. Mimetic rivalry overrides the animal pecking order, and someone's grasp hesitates and becomes a gesture that others imitate. That gesture of aborted appropriation designates the object instead of seizing it. Katz:

> "The first sign is an ostensive sign—that is, it is inextricable from the event in which it is issued and therefore constitutes the object it refers to." ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6))

Notice "constitutes." The ostensive does not label something already there. It makes the object into a shared center by holding everyone back from it. The ostensive only works in presence: the thing is here, we are all looking at it.

## The imperative: a mistake that gets rescued

How do you get from pointing to commanding without assuming that someone already *wanted* to command? A command is exactly the form that doesn't yet exist. Gans's answer, which Katz adopts:

> "The imperative is a result of an “inappropriate ostensive.” One member of the community issues the ostensive sign in the absence of the object, and another member of the community then supplies the object." ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-1))

Someone points or names when the thing isn't there. Perhaps it is a child imitating a gesture without understanding it. Someone else redeems the sign by fetching the object. Neither person intended to invent the command, but now there is a repeatable form. What drives the rescue is the key concept of **linguistic presence**: "What participants in a sign community desire above all is the maintenance of linguistic presence" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-4)). A sign that fails to land opens a crack in the scene, and the community closes it.

This shows a method that runs all through Center Study. New forms are born at the margins, from mistakes that get retrieved, and are only later taken up by those in authority.

The ostensive and imperative also form a pair. A command is complete only when it is fulfilled and confirmed, as when the nurse hands over the scalpel and says "scalpel." Looking backward, the imperative also "makes more explicit the “command” implicit in any ostensive" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-10)). Every pointing already carried an implicit order: let this be, don't grab it.

## The interrogative and the declarative: telling someone their demand can't be met

Next comes the harder case: an imperative that *can't* be fulfilled. The demander presses, then softens, and "the imperative becomes an interrogative" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-14)). A question is a prolonged command. It is a demand that has started to concede it might not be met.

The answer to that question is the first declarative. It repeats the name of the object and attaches an "operator of negation," a "don't." That gives us, roughly, "the thing—not." This is Gans's negative ostensive. Katz adds something of his own here. The "don't" faces two ways. It tells the asker to stop demanding, and it records a command, ultimately from the center, that the object be absent:

> "The originary structure of the declarative, then, contains a double imperative" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-22))

This is the birth of "reality," "a world that exists over and beyond our desires and demands, and that can therefore refuse and “refute” those desires and demands" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-20)). The speaker can say, in effect, *you must give this up, because "reality," which precedes us both, has so dictated it* ([p-23](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-23)). The declarative is a deferral of an imperative that threatened to break the scene.

## Why the order matters

**1. The later forms don't replace the earlier ones; they reorganize them.** Katz's formulation is that "the higher linguistic forms do not supersede the lower ones but, rather, articulate them in new spatial and temporal configurations" ([Originary Grammar and Political Transparency](/post/originary-grammar-and-political-transparency#p-2)). The declarative is irreducible, as biology is to chemistry, but "the declarative [is] constrained by the imperative order it transcends" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-15)). Even the most abstract science "must come home to the ostensive". A physics experiment still has to give someone a meter reading to point at ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-228)).

**2. Forgetting the order is what metaphysics is.** Katz works with Gans's definition of metaphysics as "the assumption of the linguistic primacy of the declarative sentence" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-5)). Writing made sentences into objects of study. From then on it became possible to treat commands and pointings as incomplete statements, and to dream of a world fully described in declaratives, where every action is derived from propositions. Katz says the declarative "is born in terror of the imperative" ([Accessing the Ostensive within the Declarative](/post/accessing-the-ostensive-within-the-declarative#p-1)). Taken alone, it keeps trying to abolish its own parents. He calls that a "destructive fantasy" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-1)). In practice it doesn't free us from commands. It produces commands disguised as descriptions, issued by whoever controls the disciplines that write the descriptions.

**3. The order gives you an ethics and a method.** Katz states it starkly:

> "“Bad” and “evil” lie in imperatives that obscure the ostensive they issue from, in interrogatives that are actually imperatives, in declaratives that don’t situate you on a field of ostensives" ([Scenic/Event Intelligence](/post/scenic-event-intelligence#p-9))

From this follows his account of what statements are *for*. "The proper use of the declarative sentence is, first of all, to expose the ostensives and imperatives embedded in another declarative sentence" ([On the Proper Use of the Declarative Sentence](/post/on-the-proper-use-of-the-declarative-sentence#p-1)). A sentence is "the tip of an iceberg."

## An application

Katz's own example: someone says, "I just want to be able to take my kid to the emergency room without going bankrupt." It sounds like a simple declarative of desire. Run it back down the sequence, though. What is it commanding? A whole order of trained doctors, staffing levels, funding, research priorities and certification. Who would have to issue those commands, and what would that person see when the command was carried out? Katz proposes a deliberately satirical reply: "so, you want a slave class of emergency room physicians forced to work 16 hours a day for subsistence." He adds that pursuing the question leads to "the question of who could we expect to provide for the preferable alternative" ([Declarative Culture, Properly Understood](/post/declarative-culture-properly-understood-gablog#p-8), [p-9](/post/declarative-culture-properly-understood-gablog#p-9)). The point is not to mock the desire. It is to put the statement back on its scene: whose command, aimed at what shared object, confirmable by pointing at what?

## Reading next

- [A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social) walks through the whole derivation step by step and includes Katz's "double imperative" amendment. It is the best single place to start.
- [On the Proper Use of the Declarative Sentence](/post/on-the-proper-use-of-the-declarative-sentence) shows how to apply the grammar to the vocabulary of the disciplines, words like "society" and "structure," and to turn them back into commands from a center.

**An exercise:** take one sentence you read today in a news story, such as "Inflation remains stubborn." Ask what question it answers. Then ask what demand that question softened. Then ask what someone would have to point to in order to confirm it. Where the chain breaks, you have found what Katz would call the sentence's "disciplinary imperative."

rows.q: What is singularized succession in perpetuity?
rows.a:
## The phrase, word by word

**Succession** is the transfer of the center from one occupant to the next. In Center Study the center is wherever shared attention converges. Since the "Big Man" took over the ritual center, it has been occupied by a person: a chief, a king, a president, a boss.

**Singularized** means one occupant names one successor. A parliament, an electorate, a board or a priesthood does not do the naming. Katz first reached this by working through absolutism. He started "with the maxim that sovereignty is conserved, and that it always has a locus," and concluded that "the most certain test that power was in fact held was that the sovereign selected his successor. Otherwise, would it not be those who selected the successor who wielded power?" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). If someone else picks your successor, that someone else is the real sovereign.

**In perpetuity** sharpens the point. You are not picking whoever is best for the job tomorrow. In Katz's words, "it's not just a question of choosing the best person for this job right now, but the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor, seeing to all the conditions enabling that successor, who will best choose his successor, and so on" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). The chain opens onto infinity. You cannot actually pick your tenth successor, but you can build the institutions that make continuity more likely.

## Why it is originary and not just a constitutional preference

On the originary scene, the human community is the deferral of a violent rush to the center. Ritual repeats that scene so that the community is the *same* community before and after. Katz draws the consequence: "If ritual aims at ensuring that the community practicing it remains the same, then once the center has been usurped by a human figure, the most fundamental rituals are succession rituals" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-48)).

That is why he will say flatly that "there is nothing more to governance than singularized succession in perpetuity." The common good, consent and natural right are, in his view, "either dispensed with or subsumed within it" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-1)). And then: "Singularized succession in perpetuity is the umbilical cord linking us to the originary scene—hence its indispensability. Whatever 'good' or 'right' that you might have in mind means nothing if the governor of today is not handing off the reins to the governor of tomorrow" ([same essay](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-2)).

## Descriptive and normative at once

Katz insists the concept is a diagnosis as well as a program. Everyone with any authority is already trying to bias the future toward those who will carry on their work: "if you really want what you say you want, how can you just let it all go after you step off the scene? If you're serious, you must want to pass the baton" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). So it works as a measure: "a flawed society is one in which succession is not attended to and accounted for and a pathological society is one in which succession is actually subverted; meanwhile, the cure is to identify, protect and articulate those forms of succession that nevertheless survive, as they must, as no order can destroy it altogether" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-13)).

This is also why he calls it "the most anti or non-liberal concept possible" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). Liberal rotation in office keeps the outside option of replacing the ruler permanently open, and this concept is meant to close it.

## It is not a frozen line

The successor is "not made once and for all, in the form of a permanent vice-president" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-8)). "The ruler always has an officially designated successor, but it would also be the case that he could change this designation at any time" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-8)). The whole order gets organized around producing, testing and commemorating candidates, through academies, public trials and succession rituals. In Katz's later version, "in place of the sacrifice of the central figure we have the high stakes lawsuit against him" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)).

Those revisions carry information. If every authority at every level publicly ranks its successors, then "these constant fluctuations in succession replicate price change by providing information about who will be directing a particular link in the supply chain" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). This is where the concept turns economic. Capital values things by discounting against expected future earnings. Succession offers another way of valuing the present by the future, one that "broke[s] the link between futurity and discounting" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-14)).

## All the way down

The concept is not only about heads of state. Every practice has a succession problem: "you could define a practice in terms of the singularization of the one who will succeed it" ([Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics#p-27)). Katz even folds it into "selving," the work of staying the same self across scenes. You know the concept is working when it is clear "who will be enough like you to be the same under transformed conditions" ([Selving](/post/selving#p-22)).

## Applying it

Take any project you care about: a reading group, a small business, a family farm, a political movement. Ask the SSIP question. Who, specifically, would carry this forward? Is anything you do now making that person more likely to exist and be ready? Would *they* know how to choose *their* successor?

Most projects fail that test quietly. Their "values" are stated, but nothing in their practice forms the people who would inherit them. Katz's [central-imaginary test](/post/language-the-ultimate-source-and-analysis-of-data#p-6) applies the same pressure to politics. Take any political demand and ask what authority could satisfy it lastingly. You find yourself "will[ing] its continuation on its own terms," which means helping it select a successor who can select a successor ([same essay](/post/language-the-ultimate-source-and-analysis-of-data#p-7)).

Katz anticipates the obvious objection: what about a bad ruler choosing a bad heir? His answer is that a weak occupant who tried to name a successor would expose how little power he actually holds: "The successor such an occupant selects would not, in fact, succeed" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-7)).

## Where to read next

- [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity) is the clearest single statement: where the concept came from, the bad-ruler objection, and its turn against capital.
- [Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center) is the chapter in *Anthropomorphics* that sketches the institutional picture: academies, candidates, and how to live under a regime that doesn't yet do this.

An exercise: pick one institution you belong to and write three sentences describing how its succession actually works, not how it officially works. Where you find yourself unable to say who decides, Katz would say you have found where the center is leaking.

rows.q: What is the Big Man, and what changed when he appeared?
rows.a:
## The Big Man

To see what the Big Man is, start one step earlier. In the originary hypothesis, humanity begins on a scene. A group converges on a desired object, and the convergence is halted by a gesture of aborted appropriation, the first sign. The object at the **center** becomes sacred. For a long time afterward the center stays non-human: an animal, an ancestor, a ritual object around which an egalitarian community distributes what it has. Everyone gives to the center and receives from it on roughly equal terms.

The Big Man is the figure who breaks this arrangement. Katz takes the term from Gans, who took it from the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins. Katz notes that Gans "took over the concept from Marshall Sahlins ... and then—did nothing with it" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)). Much of Katz's own work is an attempt to do something with it. (Sahlins's ethnographic setting, Melanesian "big men" who win standing through feasting and gift-giving, is background from outside the archive.)

### How he emerges

The Big Man does not rise by force. He rises by out-giving everyone else inside the gift economy:

> "acting on his 'producer's desire,' or imagination ... [he] disciplines himself and accumulates sufficient goods, power and the indebtedness of any other member of the community to place himself beyond any possible reciprocal gift relation" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-5))

"Producer's desire" is Gans's term for the disposition to imagine the community as a whole and take initiative for it. It is set against "consumer's satisfaction," the insistence on getting one's equal share. Katz's shortest version is: "If one leader can throw a big enough potlatch to bankrupt his rivals and turn them all into dependents, then he has occupied the center" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-10)). In this account the Big Man's power comes from **deferral** and discipline: he produces more and consumes less than others.

### What changed

**1. A human now occupies the center.** This is the decisive point. "The Big Man occupies the center that was originally occupied by the shared object of desire, consumption, ritual and ancestry" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-6)). Katz calls it "the first revolution in human affairs," and traces from it "all the kings and emperors and prime ministers and presidents and even 'bosses'" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-16)). It also cannot be undone: "Once the center has been humanly occupied, it must remain humanly occupied" ([Sacral Kingship and After](/post/sacral-kingship-and-after-preliminary-reflections#p-2)). Katz also reads it as the first demystification, since a human taking control of ritual and distribution was "'demystifying' regarding the community's commitment to its sacralized animals and ancestors" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-8)).

**2. The center now distributes, and a person carries the debt.** On the originary scene everyone is indebted to the center. "When the Big Man seizes the center, he takes on the debt," though Katz adds that there is "never a perfect identity between the Big Man and the center" ([Debits and Credits](/post/debits-and-credits#p-7)). His one real obligation is to give: "The only real 'rule' for the Big Man is that he indeed distribute" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-9)). This is also where the distinction between the **occupied center** and the **signifying center** comes from, and much of Katz's later thought works inside that gap.

**3. Resentment changes its target.** Before, resentment was aimed at the absent sacred center for withholding itself. Now:

> "it is no longer directed towards the absent center for not presenting itself, but towards the occupant of the center precisely for occupying it and thereby denying my own centrality (which I model on his)" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-26))

This resentment is paradoxical. I model my own centrality on his, so the more securely he holds the center, the more I feel my centrality denied. Katz also says the Big Man "generates resentment, rather than just envy ... because he doesn't just have things that others want but sets the terms of communal interactions" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-5)).

**4. Hierarchy and sovereignty begin.** "Everything done in the space he governs is done, ordered, or permitted by the Big Man," which makes him "the first form of sovereignty" ([What is to be Undone?, 1](/post/what-is-to-be-undone-1#p-8)). With him come the governing problems that never go away. He has to discourage coups without crushing useful ambition. He has to decide when to settle disputes and settle them visibly well. And he has to deal with "those who want to eliminate 'Big Manness' itself (and restore the egalitarian community)" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-6)). That is why Katz can say "The Big Man is the beginning of history and of all our ethical and political dilemmas" ([What is to be Undone?, 1](/post/what-is-to-be-undone-1#p-7)).

**5. A historical sequence starts.** From the Big Man runs a line "to the chief, to the sacred king, to the divine emperor, and then to the Axial Age" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)). The sacred king is "the inheritor of the Big Man's labors, enabled and hedged in by myriad rules and expectations" ([Sacral Kingship and After](/post/sacral-kingship-and-after-preliminary-reflections#p-2)). This bears on a dispute with Girard. In Gans's and Katz's account, human sacrifice does not stand at the origin. It arrives with the human occupation of the center: "the divine becomes more human as a single human become more divine" ([Coming to a Head](/post/coming-to-a-head#p-24)).

### Katz's own stance

Gans largely treats the Big Man as a stage in history. Katz takes sides. He reads modern politics, left and right, as positioned for or against what he calls the Big Man revolution. In his account the Left is "ferociously, primordially, opposed to precisely this" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-11)). His own project of **singularized succession**, in which the occupant of the center names his successor, is an attempt to answer the problem the Big Man first posed: how a humanly occupied center can be handed on without the rivalries it provokes destroying the order.

### Applying it

Take any group that thinks of itself as leaderless, such as a collective, a reading group, or a "flat" startup. Katz's point is that someone still "takes the initiative, someone sets the tone ... and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). The Big Man question for such a group is never whether the center is occupied, because it is. The question is whether the occupation is acknowledged and made accountable, or denied, in which case the resentment it draws has nowhere legitimate to go.

### Where to read next

- [Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction) is the clearest single account of the Big Man, from his emergence through to the reactionary politics Katz draws from him.
- [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf) develops the paradox of resentment toward the occupied center and connects it to Katz's argument about succession.

A question to take with you: if resentment toward the occupant of the center is modeled on one's own wish for centrality, what would it take for someone at the margin to turn that resentment into something other than a wish to replace him?

rows.q: What is thirdness in Katz's recent essays?
rows.a:
In the recent essays (2023 onward), "Thirdness" with a capital T names a specific project Katz proposes: a company that would render judgments on disputes and run a betting market on those judgments. The name carries an older, more general idea he had been using for years, so it helps to take the two in turn.

## Where the word comes from

Katz explains the name directly: "Thirdness (a reference to Washington’s third man as well as Peirce’s concept of generality and significance created through agreement)" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-22)).

The Washington reference is to a clause in Washington's will. It provides that disputes over the estate "shall be decided by three impartial and intelligent men, known for their probity and good understanding; two to be chosen by the disputants—each having the choice of one—and the third by those two." These men were to judge "unfettered by law, or legal constructions" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-8)). So the "third" is the arbiter between two contending parties, someone whose authority comes from their judgment and probity rather than from the legal apparatus.

The Peirce reference goes back further in Katz's own writing. From outside the archive: in Peirce, firstness is quality or possibility, secondness is brute reaction between two things, and thirdness is mediation, law and habit. In a 2017 post Katz had already adapted this, writing that thirdness "is the recipient and normalization of the interplay of firstness and secondness, founding and institutionalization, but it is also the position of the witness or spectator" ([The Single Source of Moral and Intellectual Innovation](/post/the-single-source-of-moral-and-intellectual-innovation-gablog#p-11)). Elsewhere he says civilization "depends upon deferral to the judgment of the 'third person'" ([Flouting Civilization](/post/flouting-civilization#p-11)). The recent Thirdness turns that witness-position into an institution.

## The core idea: centering the juridical

The starting point is Katz's claim about the juridical, meaning the whole order of courts, cases and judgment. Thirdness is "an extension of my centering of the juridical as a minimal condition for the constitution of events: nothing “happens” that could not be framed as including potential claimants before some tribunal" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-1)).

He places the juridical between two dangers. Below it is the vendetta, the endless cycle of revenge. Above it is the "antinomic" vendetta, which puts the whole order on trial, ultimately its distribution of property and authority (the *nomos*). The juridical works by "placing a ceiling on the vendetta by introducing higher order arbitration at those points where the vendetta threatens to undo imperial order" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-1)). In Center Study terms, a judgment is a mode of deferral: it converts a rivalry heading toward violence into a framed case before a third.

## The project: from journal to prediction market

The proposal changed shape as Katz worked on it. At first it was a journal that would frame events as virtual "cases." It would then grow into an arbitration firm, which would attract parties with good-faith disputes, while "those parties interested in honing grudges for the sake of institutional blackmail would avoid the firm like the plague" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-7)). Next it became a prediction market. Ordinarily you can only bet on events that have an official closure, such as games or elections. Constituting events as juridical cases would "make it possible to bet on any event," because "you would really be betting less on the event itself than on the judgment rendered" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-13), [p-14](/post/thirdness#p-14)).

The cases are designed to be close to even. The company "would want to frame all events so as to make the odds essentially 50-50, so that the company, like any bookie, just skims the vig off the top" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-16)). This matters because the 50/50 shifts attention away from guessing the obvious outcome and toward the deliberation itself. You win by anticipating more finely how a well-trained, impartial team will reason.

## Data exchange instead of punishment

The newest and hardest part is the shape the judgments take. Thirdness aims "to transition the juridical—opposing claims lifted out of the vendetta by being adjudicated by an enforcing third party—into data exchange," with "each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)).

Katz illustrates with a confrontation between protesters and a police officer, recast as a mutual lawsuit. The protesters might be asked to supply a theory of justice and the state that would justify their actions. The officer might be asked to identify a resource from his training and experience that would have let him handle the situation better ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-19)). The settlement consists of knowledge that changes future conduct: "To settle a case is to have each side know something about the other side’s likely future actions that they didn’t before" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-23)).

The horizon is paradoxical, as with much of Katz. If judgment became perfectly reliable, people would anticipate it and stop bringing cases: "The perfection of the juridical would then be its abolition" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-4)). So in the end "you’d be betting on which decision the Thirdness team deems more likely to increase the likelihood, albeit asymptotic, that Thirdness will be abolished as it is taken up in all everyday practices" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-23)).

## Idioms, currency, and a way of thinking

Thirdness also connects to Katz's work on idioms and currency. Phrasings that come out of good settlements can circulate: "Currency can be eliminated from the settlement insofar as the settlement itself becomes currency" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-25)). This is part of what he calls idiom mining and "learncoin."

It is also a discipline of thought anyone can practise. Look for the 50/50 point in any dispute: "speak only of the 50/50, and continue your discourse by spreading the 50/50 through all the implications of the starting point of your discourse" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-2)). It reaches inward too: "Even you, yourself, are an ongoing process of settling accounts between competing claimants" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-11)). The purpose, he says, is "to use the concept of justice to systematically take the temperature of institutions and generate knowledge about them that would not have been generated otherwise" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-16)).

Katz is candid that this is a model, not a running business. He suggests Thirdness "does probably need first of all to be a more conventional online journal," and that "it’s better to be more of an academy, training the new officer class" ([Modeling Thirdness 2](/post/modeling-thirdness-2#p-16)).

## What to read next

- **[Thirdness](/post/thirdness)** is the founding essay. It sets out the journal-to-arbitration-to-market progression and the Washington clause.
- **[If… Then: The Idiom of Data Exchange](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack)** is where the self-abolishing horizon and the protester/police example are worked out.
- **[Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence)** shows how the 50/50 becomes a method of writing and thinking, not just a betting rule.

An exercise: take a dispute in today's news. Instead of asking who is right, which usually has a lean, construct a narrower question about it that a careful judge could decide either way with roughly equal likelihood. Then ask what each party would have to learn, or show, for the judgment to leave both less likely to end up there again. That is the Thirdness move in miniature.

rows.q: What does it mean to say there is no economy, only the debt to the center?
rows.a:
The phrase is the title of an essay Katz wrote with Zack Baker, and it compresses a whole argument. In plain terms: what we call "the economy" (self-interested individuals trading on markets that run by their own laws) is not a separate, self-standing domain. It is one historically specific way of representing something older and more basic, which is our obligation to the center. As the essay's abstract puts it, thinking through the center "reveals the “economy” as nothing more than an ideological representation of our more primary debt relationship with the center" ([There Is No Economy…](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-2)). Elsewhere Katz says it more bluntly: "There is no “economy.” There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)).

Here is the argument step by step.

## 1. The debt starts on the originary scene

A quick gloss for newcomers. Center Study begins from the originary hypothesis: a group converges on a desired object, comes close to violence, and the gesture of holding back becomes the first sign. The object becomes the center. It holds everyone's attention, and because it is now shared it seems to give itself to the group. So the first relation to the center is already lopsided. The center gives first, and the community is in its debt. Katz writes that "the undeniable observation that it is an asymmetrical exchange, with the center first giving and those on the periphery then responding in kind, makes talk of debt unavoidable" ([Data as Currency and the Debt to the Center](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-1)). Ritual sacrifice is the community paying on that debt: "humans have always acknowledged a debt to the center—otherwise, what were all those sacrifices about? Exchanges with the center are intrinsically asymmetrical" ([Urbanomics](/post/urbanomics#p-11)). The general formula is: "Social life is the recording, enforcement and payment of debts to the center" ([Debits and Credits](/post/debits-and-credits#p-6)).

This is why Katz pushes back against David Graeber. Graeber's critique of debt needs an originally debt-free, egalitarian community. Katz answers that "the central object always obligates the community" ([Discipline and Debt](/post/discipline-and-debt#p-7)). Even memory counts: "memory, or commemoration, is itself a recording of debt" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-3)).

## 2. Money is a record of debt to the center

If debt comes first, money has to be explained from it, not from barter. Katz draws on Christine Desan's history of English coinage: the king issues tokens to people who pay what they owe him early, and those tokens can then circulate. So "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center, and that record can in turn become a way of paying debts to the center" ([There Is No Economy…](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)). Markets, likewise, do not arise on their own: "Markets have historically been created and managed by states, for the purpose of maintaining ritual and military institutions" ([Debts and Deferences](/post/debts-and-deferences-gablog#p-3)). Money is therefore "the means through which the imperial center extends the indebtedness of its subjects by spreading this indebtedness differentially and asymmetrically among its subjects, creating a credit chain maintained through a variable combination of faith in the system and capacity for enforcement" ([p-29](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-29)).

## 3. Where Katz parts from Gans

Gans had argued that the market transaction is "no longer an extension of the originary scene but a minimal model of it": buyer and seller pay at the same moment, so the debt is settled immediately. The essay is written against this. Katz grants that the simultaneous exchange is real "on the most “everyday” level of exchange, like, say, buying a cup of coffee in a diner" ([p-9](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-9)). But even the coffee only seems instantaneous: "Instantaneity or simultaneity is a fiction, or virtual, and the interval within which an exchange can be considered instantaneous depends upon the extent to which the relation between the indebted subject and the debt imposing and money issuing institutions remains the same over time" ([p-31](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-31)). Your five dollars settles anything only because a center stands behind the currency and will keep standing there.

## 4. How the "economy" came to look autonomous

If this is so, why do we believe in an economy at all? Katz places the turn in late seventeenth-century England. The Bank of England became the state's creditor, and the two-party system turned occupancy of the center into regular rotation ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-1)). From then on the source of money appears separate from the sovereign, and Locke supplies the story of money as a commodity agreed on by convention, "in order to obscure the inherently political nature of money" ([p-40](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-40)). The result is a state that is "ultimately a debt enforcement institution" ([p-50](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-50)), and a modern twist on the old debt: "we’re all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern, but what is modern is that the value of our debt is determined by expectation of future earnings" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)). The "economy" even gets treated as a deity in its own right, a "metaperson" whose will economists try to divine ([p-43](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-43)).

Katz's quarrel is not that this huge system of credit exists. That was probably necessary. His quarrel is with the way it gets described: "what is not necessary, though, is the obfuscation of this condition by representing it as if grounded in individual exchanges" ([p-47](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-47)).

## 5. Applying it

Take a home mortgage. In the "economy" vocabulary, two parties freely agree on a price for time. In the vocabulary of debt to the center, the case looks like this. The bank's ability to lend rests on a lender of last resort. That lender's credibility rests on a state that enforces debts. The state's credibility rests on confidence that the order will still be the same order in thirty years, with the same courts and the same currency. Your house is an asset valued against expected future earnings, and that valuation is really a bet on the continuity of the center. That is why, for Katz, questions of money eventually become questions of succession. Credit "is always a bet on succession," as he puts it in the later essays, and the essay ends by imagining an order that would no longer be an "economy" but "a “tributary” order, in which our originary debt to the center is acknowledged and paid" ([p-95](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-95)).

The claim also has a personal side. It answers the question Katz asks bluntly: "Why, in the end, does anyone feel they have to do anything?" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-4)). The obligation you feel is not leftover superstition. It is the originary debt, now running through banks and courts.

## Where to go next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf): the full argument, including Drumm's "outside spread" and "outside option" and the reading of derivatives as ritual.
- [Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession): how credit, party rotation and succession are tied together, and what a different credit order might look like.

A question to work on: Katz says the "simultaneous" market exchange is a fiction that depends on the center staying the same. Choose a moment when that fiction broke, such as a hyperinflation, a bank run or a currency collapse. What did people turn to in order to settle their obligations once money stopped working, and what does that show about where the debt actually lay?

rows.q: What is scenic design?
rows.a:
# Scenic design

## Starting from the scene

Center Study holds that the human begins on a scene. A group converges on a central object everyone wants, and the crisis is deferred by a gesture that stops short of grabbing. That gesture is the first sign, and the object becomes the center. A scene is that arrangement of center and margin, held together by signs.

Scenic design starts from a simple point: scenes don't stay in place on their own. They have to be maintained, rebuilt and furnished. Katz notes that the scene is "really an undeveloped concept in Eric Gans's work" and adds that "There's no scene without some 'setting.'" ([Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics#p-4)). His shortest definition:

"Technics is the continual reinscription of the scene—scenic design practices are events within scenes that design scenes in ways that facilitate new events." ([Event Intelligence](/post/event-intelligence#p-14))

## Where it begins: ritual

The first scenic design is ritual. The originary scene ends with a ritual-like repetition of the gesture, probably around some remnant of the shared object. In later rituals that gesture comes first: memory is "'front-loaded' so as to guarantee the results of the scene in advance. This is the setting of the ritual scene, and therefore the original 'technics'" ([Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics#p-5)).

So the first tool was not a spear. It was "some ritual enhancing 'device,'" something that would "materialize the memory of the originary scene by drawing or enhancing the boundary between center and periphery" ([Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices#p-4)). Altars, masks, costumes and the skills needed to make them follow from the need to keep the center apart and the margin arranged around it. "So, technics, as I've been arguing over several posts, is scenic design" ([Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics#p-7)).

## How wide the concept reaches

Katz then folds media and technology into one category. Media are all the means of constituting scenes. Technology is the arrangement of human practices once they are no longer held inside ritual. Taken together:

"Every practice is designing a scene; or, really, redesigning a scene, or some portion of a scene" ([Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices#p-2))

This "would include all practices, large and small, carried out by the powerless as well as the powerful." Building prisons is scenic design, he writes, but so are fences, police, and "habits of scrutinizing others and reading situations which themselves get built into the scene." Surveillance, data collection and machine learning now belong to it too, so that "deferral will increasingly be referred to learning to navigate designed scenes" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-9)).

Scene and furnishing can also trade places: "A telescope developed to scope out the enemy becomes the lever of a new scene once it is pointed toward the stars," which Katz calls "the reciprocal convertibility of furnishings and scenes" ([Programming](/post/programming#p-7)).

## What makes design better or worse

If everything is scenic design, the useful question is what good design looks like. Katz gives several criteria that fit together:

- **Revelation.** "The purpose of scenic design is revelation: scenes should be designed so as to maximize information coming from the center" ([Literature as Para-Data](/post/literature-as-para-data-and-intelligence-exchange-with-the-center#p-1)). A well-designed scene lets you see what the shared center requires.
- **More scenes, not more functions.** "Scenicity itself is to be maximized, and technology should generate more scenes, upon which practices are possible, and the tendency of the technological imagination to insert individual activities as 'functions' within a 'system' must be resisted" ([Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics#p-13)). This ties scenic design to meaning, which here means being able to say something that stays the same across scenes. By contrast, he calls liberal-capitalist settings "scenes designed to scurry around on, not find a place within" ([Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics#p-11)).
- **Name and place.** "We all have some place we should be, and some name we should inhabit, and we can only find our name and place within a social order designed to produce scenes that afford such findings" ([Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices#p-18)).
- **Succession.** An imperative is a command. Design passes commands along through relays, "so that the final imperative should always be to perfect a practice predicated upon singularized succession in perpetuity" ([Fict-tech-tion; Archae-tecture](/post/fict-tech-tion-archae-tecture#p-10)). In Katz's political terms, singularized succession means the holder of the center designates who comes next, and that successor does the same. A good scene sets things up for whoever takes it over.

There is a built-in limit. Design is always deferral that is never finished: "the more mapped out implementation of scenic intervention simply produces even further reaching implications beyond those which have been 'input' to the design." We can hold mimetic violence back "more intentionally… but never in a way that will free us from continuing to do so" ([The Thing That It Is](/post/the-thing-that-it-is-toward-a-curriculum-for-the-officer-class#p-7)).

## Two applications

**A classroom assignment.** Katz says designing assignments is "as good an example of design practices as anything else I can think of" ([Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices#p-11)). A good assignment does not ask students for their "opinions." It sets their everyday vocabulary against the language of a discipline. The mixed "inter-language" that results then becomes the center of the classroom, something everyone can point to and examine together. He extends the same logic to online posting. Trolling also designs a scene, since it provokes responses you can use, but "the problem with trolling is that it locks everyone into their initial positions, whereas it is better to open up new positions" (p-16).

**A building.** In "archae-tecture," a new structure takes as its imperative to stand in relation to its surroundings "in the same way the previous structure was situated in relation to its surroundings." Working out what "the same" means here sends you back through the site's whole history: "the future of the place must be derived from its origin" ([Fict-tech-tion; Archae-tecture](/post/fict-tech-tion-archae-tecture#p-11), p-13). Katz stresses that this is "an ultimately literary model for thinking about design," not advice for architects.

## What to read next

- [Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices): the main statement. It merges media and technology into the concept and works through the pedagogy example in detail.
- [Scenic Technics](/post/scenic-technics): the history from ritual through the ancient empires to capitalism, and the criterion of meaning.
- If the center and the scene are still new to you, [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center) is the most accessible way in.

An exercise: pick a scene you are on every day, such as a meeting, a group chat or a dinner table. Ask what holds the center apart, which furnishings and habits keep people in place, and what one change would open a new position rather than lock in the old ones. If you tell me which scene you chose, we can work through it together.
