rows.q: What is the pointman?
rows.a:
The **pointman** is Katz's name, introduced in the 2025 essay *The Pointman*, for whoever occupies the center: the person at the head of a scene, institution or polity, the one whose commands everyone else is in some way carrying out. He says so directly: "I can now replace the clumsy “occupant of the center” with “pointman,” as a more resonant and less technical-sounding synonym" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)). The new word adds more than convenience, though, and to see what it adds you have to see what problem it answers.

## The double sense of "point"

Some background for newcomers. In Center Study, human community begins on a scene where everyone's desire converges on one object, the *center*, and the first sign is a gesture of deferral, a pointing that holds off the violent grab. Every later social order keeps that structure: something or someone holds everyone's attention, and attention can turn into reverence or into violence. Once a human being occupies the center (the "Big Man," the chief, the sacral king, later presidents and CEOs), that person is both the source of order and the most exposed target in the community.

"Pointman" holds both sides of this together. Katz defines him this way: "He is at the point, taking the initiative, gathering all initiatives under his banner, and at the same time the one everyone points to, out of wonder, curiosity or outrage, with the finger of accusation" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)). He also notes the etymology: "center" comes from "point," which comes from "prick," "i.e., to wound, to cause to bleed" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)). So the word builds in the danger of the position. To lead is to be pointed at.

## Why Katz needed the figure

The essay starts from the Axial Age (the era of the prophets, Socrates and Jesus). In that period a new sacred figure appears: the innocent victim whose unjust death exposes the whole order that killed him. Katz grants that this was a moral revolution, but he argues that its legacy has decayed into the *victimary*: "the centrality of the victim to Axial Age and successor models (modernity) has led to the extreme dysfunctions of the victimary" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-5)). Under that logic the most powerless figure always wins the moral contest.

His "most minimal" solution is to keep the Axial scenario but "subtract the death of the victim (who will therefore no longer be a victim)" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-8)). The pointman is a figure who draws all attention and accepts the risk of the position, but who wants to *win*, that is, to govern, rather than be vindicated by losing. Katz describes him as "someone who is indeed ready to lose, resistant to compromise that would in fact be failure, but making every effort to win, clarifying what that would mean at each point along the way" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-14)). He calls this "the latest iteration of the Big Man," and what gets commemorated is no longer a death but "the pointman’s reception, seizure and eventual transfer of power" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)).

Katz names the obvious problem himself: "how do you prove you are willing to die without actually dying?" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-10)). His answer is the succession ritual. "In place of the sacrifice of the central figure we have the high stakes lawsuit against him, which might be brought by any subject and might end in the ruin of the pointman (or the subject)" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)). The challenger has to be ready to take the position himself if he wins. Exposure is kept, but bloodshed is replaced by the juridical.

## Looking for the pointman is an activity

Katz insists this is not passive waiting: "it’s not waiting for Godot," because you are testing candidates and drawing conclusions from the events they create. He even adds that "someone so engaged in the process of pointing out the pointman might end up having been the pointman all along" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)). His own example is how he followed Trump's first term. He took Trump to mean what he said, measured events against that assumption, and kept open both the possibility of a hidden strategy and the possibility of simple failure, assigning each a shifting likelihood ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-15)). That stance is the model for how a subject relates to a would-be pointman: neither cheerleading nor opposition, but sustained inquiry into what success would look like.

## What the pointman does, in the later essays

In the essays that followed, the term does structural work.

- **Succession.** The pointman's "priority is to establish succession and a pool of eligible and loyal successors," formalized by publicly nominating and ranking candidates ([Ve/ortexicality](/post/ve-ortexicality-post-axial-age-morality#p-8)).
- **Credit.** If everyone with authority publicly names and ranks successors, those fluctuating rankings start to work like prices, and "the pointman is determining credit, thereby “counter-usurping” the central bank" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-6)).
- **Obedience as a bet.** Using Colin Drumm's term "outside option" (a possible replacement waiting in the wings), Katz writes that "the degree and quality of your fulfillment of imperatives coming from the center (the “pointman”) constitutes a bet on the likelihood of the replacement of the pointman by an outside option" ([Notes on Governance](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics#p-1)).
- **Intelligence.** At one point he identifies the role institutionally: "central intelligence does and should govern, with the director of central intelligence the pointman" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-11)).

The name itself did not settle. A few posts later Katz decided that "the perfect term already exists and has for a long time: dictator," in the old Roman sense ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1)). By 2026 he writes "the sovereign, or pointman, or dictator (but maybe I’ll stick with “sovereign”)" ([Perfecting the Imperative](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-15)). The three words name the same role. "Pointman" is the one that keeps the originary scene visible: the pointing gesture, and the wound.

## Applying it

The structure works at any scale. In a meeting that stalls, someone eventually says "here's what we'll do." That person is at the point and also now the one everyone can blame. Center Study asks: does this person own both the initiative and the exposure, and are they preparing someone to take over? Or are they pushing the risk onto a scapegoat, or doing the leading without being visible as the one who leads?

## Where to read next

- [The Pointman](/post/the-pointman) is the founding essay. Read it whole for the Axial Age argument and the succession-lawsuit ritual.
- [Notes on Governance and Center Study Politics](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics) is short. It shows how the pointman reorganizes obedience, investment and politics into one question about succession.

A question to take further: think of an institution you know well. Who is its pointman, and does that person publicly name a successor? If not, who is actually choosing the next one? By Katz's logic, that is where the power really sits.

rows.q: Apply Center Study to a company whose founder is stepping down with no successor named.
rows.a:
Center Study puts this case at the heart of its political thought. For Katz, succession is the most basic problem of any order, from a kingdom to a firm. A founder who steps down without naming anyone has not left a blank. He has made a decision, and the theory lets you say what kind.

## The founder as occupant of the center

Start with the vocabulary. Every institution forms around a **center**: something everyone attends to and orients toward. In an organized human group someone *occupies* it, gives the commands and takes the responsibility. A founder is the clearest modern example of what Katz, following the anthropologists, calls the **Big Man**, the one who seized the center by doing what others couldn't and then took charge of distribution.

Katz has a parable that fits a founder almost exactly. A group escapes a burning building because one person seems to know the way out. Afterward they want to rebuild. If the group elects someone to oversee the rebuilding, a gap opens: "the task of the new leader is not to build the building, but to maintain a majority among those he is serving. Every decision he makes now has a double meaning" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-12)). Then Katz adds: "Of course, all along there was another option: let the guy who got everyone out of the building choose his successor" ([same text](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-16)).

Your founder got everyone out of the building and then declined that option.

## Who is sovereign now?

The sharpest claim comes in *Anthropomorphics*. The occupant of the center choosing his successor is "a foregone conclusion, insofar as we take power to be coherent," because "If some other body, however wide or narrow, chooses the successor, they could presumably choose the time of succession, which is to say, that body could remove the ruler at any time. In that case, that body is the sovereign" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-410)).

Apply that literally. If the founder doesn't name a successor, the board, the major investors or a search firm will. By naming no one, he has shown where the center already was. In a corporation this is less shocking than in a kingdom, since a company is chartered and its owners can remove its head. Katz uses Colin Drumm's terms here. The **outside spread** is whoever can cover the money when no one else can, roughly the lender of last resort. The **outside option** is "whoever within a monarchical order might be leveraged as a possible replacement to the king" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-1)). A founder who names no one hands the outside option to the outside spread: the capital that can wait now picks the next occupant.

Katz also refuses the comforting thought that nothing was chosen. Writing of kings, he says the ruler is "always selecting his successor, even if he doesn’t know that he’s doing so" ([Threading through History](/post/threading-through-history#p-8)). The founder's hires, promotions, sidelinings and who got to learn how he thinks have already shaped the field of candidates. His silence leaves that field unranked and gives the ranking to others.

## What happens inside the firm

The next months follow predictably from the theory. Katz offers a compact formula: "the degree and quality of your fulfillment of imperatives coming from the center (the “pointman”) constitutes a bet on the likelihood of the replacement of the pointman by an outside option" ([Notes on Governance](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics#p-1)). The founder is now the person everyone knows will be replaced, and nobody knows by whom. So every employee's obedience becomes a hedge. Senior people half-follow his last directives while courting the board. Middle managers wait. Projects tied to particular candidates stall or speed up depending on how those candidates' chances are rumored to be moving.

This is the **imperative gap**, the distance between a command issued and a command obeyed, widened across the whole organization. Commands still arrive, but no one can trace them to a center that will still be there next quarter. Katz treats this as the source of factions: when succession is unclear, "everyone obeying him now is simultaneously scrambling around trying to find whom they might be able to recognize as a successor" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-3)).

## Reading the founder's decision

Why would a founder do this? In a related discussion Katz notes that totalitarian leaders almost never publicly choose successors. His reading: "Either they want to maintain the fiction that they are not really in charge or understand that they in an order where it is too dangerous to have someone with a comparable level of legitimacy" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-9)). Both readings carry over. "The board will decide, the culture will carry on" may be the first fiction. Never having let a lieutenant grow strong enough to be named may be the second fear.

Katz's harshest diagnosis applies too. He calls the failure to name a successor a form of **resentment**: "a refusal to see to the naming of your successor—the refusal to acknowledge that the world will continue without you. Socially speaking, it’s a refusal of pedagogy, a refusal of initiation, a refusal to rework precedents" ([Ergodism](/post/ergodism#p-16)). That is strong, but the test it suggests is concrete: whom did this founder teach? A real practice, Katz argues, is one you could "define … in terms of the singularization of the one who will succeed it" ([Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics#p-27)). The best founder picks the person best able to pick their own successor, and so on indefinitely. That is **singularized succession in perpetuity**, Katz's central political concept. Measured against it, a founder with no successor has built a firm, but not yet a practice.

There is a gentler version in his essay on "selving": ideally it should already be obvious "who will be enough like you to be the same under transformed conditions" ([Selving](/post/selving#p-22)). If no one inside the company is obvious, the institution has not yet learned to carry the founder's way of working without him.

## What Center Study suggests doing

It depends where you stand.

**If you advise the founder:** name someone now, and say publicly that the choice can be revised. Katz's model is a ranked and continually updated slate of candidates, publicly displayed, as the way an institution states its own priorities ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). A named successor who is later replaced still tells everyone more than silence does.

**If you're an employee or executive:** Katz's advice has an unusual ethical shape. Don't treat the interregnum as a chance to put your faction in charge. Obey in a way that strengthens orderly succession. He applies this even to the worst occupant: obey "in such a way, drawing upon the discretionary “margin” any imperative allows for, as to increase, even minimally, the likelihood that even that worst president will be in a position to choose his successor" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)). In practice that might mean pressing the founder, while he still holds the center, to designate someone rather than lobbying the board behind his back. Katz calls this **donating your resentment to the center**.

**If you're a partner, supplier or investor:** you will do what Katz calls "controlled usurpation." You test the firm's resilience by sounding out its subordinates and judging who will actually run your link in the supply chain ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-17)). In his model this probing is no scandal; it is how information moves between institutions once markets are understood as the "capillaries" of command.

One larger point from the same essay: Katz thinks capitalism can only be transcended "by forming companies which discount against expected future earnings foundationally, by charter, beyond the life span of anyone running the company" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-24)). A founder who leaves without naming a successor shows the opposite: the company's horizon ends where his own does.

## Read next

- [Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics): the clearest statement of why succession belongs inside any practice, not just inside government. Read paragraphs 25–35.
- [Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession): how outside spread, outside option and succession rankings fit together, with institutions treated as supply chains. This is the closest the archive comes to a theory of the firm.

An exercise to take it further: pick a real founder transition you know of (Jobs to Cook is a well-documented case). Ask whether the founder named the successor himself or the board did, and whether the successor was chosen to continue the founder's practice or to reassure the capital behind it. Then ask whether that successor has named anyone. Most of what Center Study has to say about the company will follow from those three answers.

rows.q: I'm a teacher and my class won't settle. What would Center Study tell me to notice?
rows.a:
Katz doesn't write about classroom management as such. His teaching essays are mostly about college writing courses, not restless rooms. But the core of Center Study is a theory of how a scene settles or fails to, so it gives you a fairly precise set of things to look for. "Won't settle" is, in its idiom, a scene without a center that holds.

## 1. What, if anything, is at the center?

A scene forms around something that holds shared attention. The center "compels in at least the minimal sense that it holds you: while you’re looking at it you’re not looking away" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-5)). So the first thing to notice is not who is misbehaving but what the room is actually attending to, minute by minute.

Usually the answer is not "nothing." It is several rival centers: the phone, the kid who does the voice, a running argument at the back table, you. Prospects of the Hypothesis notes that even in the loosest group "someone takes the initiative, someone sets the tone, someone starts off in a new direction, and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). Map who is occupying center, and when.

## 2. Distraction or fixation?

Katz names two ways shared attention breaks. Distraction "tears us away from the scene of joint attention... and thereby demands a renewed, necessarily risky effort to redirect attention." Fixation "involves tearing oneself away from the scene and, ultimately, turning the other participants into objects of rather than participants in, one’s now singular attention" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-8)).

These call for different responses. The scattered kid and the kid who has locked onto a grievance against a classmate (or against you) are not the same problem. They feed each other, though: "the actuality or fear of distraction favors the formation of fixations, and so the ethical problem consists less in preventing than in recuperating and interrupting distractions and fixations" ([same text](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-9)). *Recuperating*, not preventing: the job is to fold the interruption back into a shared line of attention, not to win a battle against it.

## 3. Is the room going mimetic?

Restlessness spreads by imitation. One student gets up, two more follow. One joke gets topped. Center Study reads this as a slide toward sameness, where everyone becomes interchangeable and so everyone competes for the same few slots. The way out is never a louder version of the same move. It is what Katz calls "imagining a new configuration that would make us other to each other again" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-53)): different roles, different positions, tasks that actually differ.

## 4. Watch where the room's attention converges, including your own

This is the uncomfortable one. A disordered group looks for a single target. In a classroom Katz describes the soft version: "Error is the mark of the scapegoat... The class is organized around the convergence upon error—no one is lynched, but ostracism and exclusion certainly result" ([Originary Grammar and Post-Sacrificial Semiotic Agency](/post/originary-grammar-and-post-sacrificial-semiotic-agency#p-12)).

So notice whether the class settles only when one student becomes the problem everyone looks at. That quiet is borrowed, and it costs you. Notice too that you are always a candidate for the center: "putting someone else at the center implies the possibility of being placed in the center yourself in turn" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-15)). Calling out a disruptor in front of everyone puts both of you on stage.

## 5. Are your imperatives ones they can obey?

Katz's sharpest teaching point is about instructions like "write clearly." Vague standards really mean "become more like me," which is why students keep asking "what you want." They have sensed that you want "a reasonable facsimile, not of who you really are... but of who you imagine yourself to be" ([Paradox, Discipline, Imperative](/post/paradox-discipline-imperative#p-7)). His alternative is imperatives "such that they can participate in creating the shared understanding making it possible to determine when those imperatives have been obeyed" ([same text](/post/paradox-discipline-imperative#p-8)).

Applied to settling, the question is whether the class can *see* what doing the task correctly would look like. "Focus" and "settle down" are like "write clearly." "Everyone write three possible answers, then we compare" is checkable by everyone, including the students. His formula elsewhere is "maximal regulation (very clear rules within a directive assignment that asks students to perform some move that can be publicly examined)" with minimal guessing about what the teacher secretly wants ([review of Farmer](/post/double-helix-v1-farmer-review#p-13)).

## 6. Your own deferral

In Center Study, power comes from deferral, not volume. Some people "will be able to stop and examine a situation while others are rushing in, and they will have the patience to wait and see when the unfolding reality provides an opening" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-46)). So notice when you rush in. And don't expect a single move to fix the room. A good gesture of deferral only makes the crisis "imminently imminent," and "that imminence of imminence gives us a little space within which to work" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4)).

## Putting it together

Center Study wouldn't tell you to suppress the unsettledness. It would tell you to *build a center*: put something in the middle of the room that everyone can point to together and act on in visibly different, checkable ways. In his own words, "we can make sure the class is a dance floor" ([Composition Pedagogy](/post/composition-pedagogy#p-13)). Sometimes the restlessness itself can become that object, if you treat it as something the class looks at rather than something you fight.

**To read next:**
- [Paradox, Discipline, Imperative](/post/paradox-discipline-imperative) is short and directly about why teachers' instructions fail and what to put in their place.
- [Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics) gives the full account of distraction, fixation and joint attention.

**An exercise:** for one lesson, jot down every two minutes what the room's center actually is and who is holding it. Then mark whether each break was a distraction or a fixation. If you tell me the age of your students and what a typical derailment looks like, I can apply this more concretely.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
A pile-on is one of the places where Center Study's basic picture is easiest to see. Katz uses it himself to show what he means by the center:

> "The center is whatever interferes with violent centralization. Think about it this way: have you ever felt (and given into) the temptation to 'pile on' someone who is being criticized, attacked, or ridiculed? There is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple." ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1))

So the first reading is that a pile-on is the originary scene running the wrong way.

## The scene running backwards

On the originary scene, desire converges mimetically on an object. Each participant wants it because the others do. The crisis is deferred when someone converts the grasping movement into a sign that everyone can repeat, and the group draws back to a distance.

In a pile-on the convergence is the same: each reply is provoked by the replies already posted. But nothing turns the grab into a gesture. The target becomes the center as *object* of violence, not as source of deferral. "Violent centralization" is Katz's phrase for this: the community's attention converges on one figure in the mode of appropriation.

## Resentment and the hidden usurper

All resentment is ultimately resentment of the center. A pile-on rarely presents itself as an attack. It presents itself as defending the center against someone who has violated it. The index gives Katz's formulation: "The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes'" ([Bouvard on Scapegoating and Egalitarian Morality](/post/the-egalitarian-vs-hierarchical-model-of-morality#p-1)).

Each participant feels they are restoring order. That is why the pile-on generates so much righteousness and so little restraint.

## A trial without a court

The second reading comes from Katz's media theory. He argues the modern media have always worked by staging trials:

> "All the media does is stage trials and invite the audience to participate vicariously as judges, jurors and, increasingly, enforcers." ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-12))

Social media adds a "call" to participate:

> "The mass media, and now social media, do perpetually position us as judges on events involving some purported transgression, commanding us to 'take a position' and add our little quantum of power to whatever target is being displayed on the Big Scene (and Big Screen)." ([Media as Ritual](/post/media-as-ritual#p-1))

This is where Katz's emphasis on **the juridical** matters. He defines the juridical as the institution that caps the vendetta, the cycle of revenge. Power, for him, is exercised through judgment: "you have power insofar as, and to the degree that, contending parties bring their grievances, counter-grievances and defenses to you rather than resort or revert to the vendetta" ([A New Model of Power](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-3)).

A pile-on borrows the forms of a trial: accusation, evidence, verdict, sentence. It has none of the constraints that make a trial a means of deferral: standing, rules of evidence, an arbiter, a settlement that ends the matter. It is a vendetta in juridical costume.

Katz's practical proposal in [Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-7) follows from this. One should be able to sue someone for calling you a "racist" if they cannot provide "a coherent definition of 'racism'" and show how what you did fits it. The point is to force the accusation back into a form where resentment can be measured and settled.

## Why everyone joins

Katz notes a double desire in the participant: to add "one's own voice in judgment to the crowd directed at the target of the day—but also … the intense desire to be exempt from that judgment" ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-11)).

Joining is a way of not being next. In mimetic terms there is always the possibility "of being utterly silenced, and therefore being taken with the paradoxical necessity of joining the race to silence the other first" ([Talk of the Center](/post/talk-of-the-center-adam-katz#p-30)).

This links to the **Big Scene**: a scene organized not around a center but against the emergence of one. Narratives that treat generalized groups as agents are, Katz says bluntly, "just preparations for lynch mobs, whether the agent in question represents potential perpetrators or victims" ([Hypothesis/Practice Vs. Narrative](/post/hypothesis-practice-vs-narrative-the-iterative-center-gablog#p-18)).

## Not only tribal: the Stack behind the crowd

Here Katz differs from a common reading. It is tempting to say social media "retribalizes" us, returning us to an oral culture of shaming. Katz grants the plausibility of that view but objects: "this leaves the Stack out of account, and the entire order of intelligence, which operates beyond and to some extent through digital orality. It's a consumerist approach to the question" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-1)).

The pile-on is also an output of algorithms, amplification and sometimes bot farms. Looking at an X reply section full of near-identical replies, he wonders whether the whole thread is "a verb or expletive in a much longer sentence including many reply sections, the bot farms and algorithms producing them, resentments amplified by those algorithms" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-9)).

So a center-study reading of a pile-on always asks what Katz asks about any thought: "who wants me to think that?" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-1)).

## What deferral looks like here

Katz does not answer with "be kind" or "don't post." He asks what gesture would defer the convergence. Several are in the texts.

- **Read the virality instead of joining it.** Analysis should work "something like Brecht's 'alienation effect,' which involved breaking down the various gestures and utterances of a character right when the audience is about to get absorbed in some sacrificial drama" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-10)).
- **Design.** Social media can be used "to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger" ([Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14)).
- **Originary satire, aimed at yourself too.** If you do attack, your own investments will show, "so, put them on display in an edifying manner" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-15)). Katz suggests aiming for utterances about half directed at the other and half drawing attention to yourself.
- **For the target: refuse the victim's role.** "Perhaps the hardest thing here is to refrain from entering such spaces with the posture of the exemplary victim in waiting" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-19)). The same goes for retaliation: Katz warns against "the counter-productive reflex of trying to invent some way of calling the accuser the 'real racist'" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-17)).

Behind all of these is a line from [Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-12): "as soon as one takes the worst-case scenario imaginary literally, one is compelled to enact it." A pile-on is the worst case taken literally: this person is the threat, and removing them restores order.

## An application

Picture a mid-level academic whose clumsy tweet is quote-posted by a large account. Within an hour there are 3,000 replies, most variations on three phrases.

A center-study reading notices several things:

- The replies are mimetic. Their sameness is the evidence.
- Each replier claims to defend a center: decency, a vulnerable group, the profession. Each implies the target has usurped it.
- The thread has a juridical shape, with a charge, a verdict and an implied sentence ("this person shouldn't be teaching"). It has no forum where a counter-claim could be heard or the matter closed.
- The quote-poster with the large audience is the "first", the one whose gesture set the scene. But the scene is also shaped by an algorithm that rewards repetition.

The deferring move is not to defend the academic by attacking the quote-poster, which would only restart the convergence with a new target. It is something like asking, publicly and precisely, what the charge is, what would count as evidence, and who could rule on it. That turns the pile-on back toward a case.

## Where to read next

- [Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation) is Katz's fullest account of media as staged trial, with his proposal to replace the spectacle with something else.
- [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center), especially the second half, on the "exemplary victim" and how to enter a hostile space without taking up that posture.
- [Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy) treats scapegoating on social media as a design problem rather than a moral failing.

**An exercise:** pick a recent pile-on you watched. Find the reply that most clearly *set the scene*, the first in Katz's sense. Then write the one reply that would have converted the convergence into a case: a question of what the charge is and who could judge it, rather than another stone. Notice how hard it is to write that reply without it becoming a new attack.

rows.q: Read the rise of prediction markets through Center Study.
rows.a:
A note on sources first. The recent boom in prediction markets is not in the archive: Polymarket and Kalshi, the election-betting surge of 2024, the regulatory fights, the spread from elections to sports and to nearly any headline. That background comes from me. What Katz has done is design a prediction market of his own, Thirdness, and reflect a good deal on what betting on events presupposes. So I'll read the boom through that material. The reading has three layers, and then Katz's counter-proposal.

## 1. A bet is only as good as its closure, and closure comes from the center

Katz begins from a simple constraint. You can only bet on something that will be declared over:

> "The limit, thus far, of betting upon events is that only an event with an official closure can take bets—sporting events are the most obvious example, as the rules for determining winners and losers are transparent and unchanging." ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-11))

Elections are the one public event with comparable closure. That closure depends entirely on trust in the process: if elections came to be seen as fixed, betting on them "would take on a very different character, in which one would be betting, implicitly at least, on whether they will fix it this time" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-11)). From this he draws a diagnostic principle:

> "The range of events that could be bet on can be treated as an index to the, let's say, 'replicability' of existing institutional arrangements." ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-12))

This gives you a first way to read the boom. Every contract names a resolution source and a rule for settling it, and that rule is an occupant of the center. It may be a court, an election board, a newswire, or a crowd of token-holders voting. Anyone betting is betting on that resolver as much as on the world. Katz puts the point most sharply: "maybe it all depends upon whether there are trusted judges, in which case maybe that would be the thing to bet on" ([Presence and Intention in Sampling as Currency](/post/presence-and-intention-in-sampling-as-currency#p-17)).

So the rise of these markets can be read two ways at once. It shows that our institutions can still produce clean closure on a widening range of events. It is also an attempt to manufacture closure where the shared narrative no longer supplies it. My outside observation is that the most revealing moments on these platforms are the resolution disputes, when traders fight over whether something "really" happened. In Katz's terms these are juridical crises in miniature. The bet has exposed a demand for a judge, and the platform has no proper judge to supply.

## 2. Every price was already a bet on succession

The second layer is that prediction markets make explicit what all money already does. Katz writes:

> "Money is a bet on the future... Orderly succession lies in the background of money—if anyone could seize power at any time then it would be impossible to rely on money—it wouldn't work." ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-1))

He goes further, extending this to obedience itself. How fully you carry out the commands of the "pointman" (Katz's term for whoever occupies the center) "constitutes a bet on the likelihood of the replacement of the pointman by an outside option" ([Notes on Governance and Center Study Politics](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics#p-1)). Hence "all bets, i.e., investments, are themselves ultimately bets on the degree of oscillation within succession" ([same, p-5](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics#p-5)).

Two terms here come from Colin Drumm's work, which Katz has absorbed. The *outside option* is a possible replacement for whoever holds power. The *outside spread* is the lender of last resort. Katz's account of the modern Anglo order is that it internalized the outside option as regular rotation between parties and handed the outside spread to the central bank, so that "governments rise and fall depending on how close they are to the middle of that spread" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-2)).

With that in view, it is no accident that elections are the anchor product of the boom. An election market prices the internalized outside option directly and openly. It is the purest instrument of what Katz calls rotation at the center. It is also the exact opposite of the Center Study wager, which is "placing all the bets on a center or prospective or type of pointman so inside" that the outside option disappears ([Notes on Governance](/post/notes-on-governance-and-center-study-politics#p-5)). Polymarket turns turnover into an asset. Katz wants turnover replaced by *singularized succession in perpetuity*: the occupant of the center names a successor, who names a successor, and so on.

The financial lineage matters too. In the essay he co-wrote with Zack Baker, the derivative works by making a future exchange "itself an asset that can be bought or sold: the derivative is the bet on that future exchange" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-79)). They call "the space of the derivative... the true capitalist church." Seen this way, the event contract is the derivative stripped down. It drops the underlying commodity and keeps only the bet on how a scene will close. The "speculative ethos" that essay describes, borrowed from Edward LiPuma, has escaped finance and attached itself to news.

## 3. The danger: forcing the world into win/loss shape

Katz is not simply cheering here. His sharpest warning is in [Trails of Attentionality](/post/trails-of-attentionality#p-12):

> "Reducing the world to predictions means reducing it to predictability and the obvious objection is that you end up screening those events most reducible to prediction: sporting events, elections, deaths, stock market averages"

and further, "insofar as you have to frame less amenable events as predictable you force them to approximate the more amenable events, so things that are not at all like sporting events or elections get framed as such, I.e., in straightforward win-loss terms" ([p-13](/post/trails-of-attentionality#p-13)). That describes the commercial boom quite precisely. Wars, diplomacy and court cases all get re-scened as contests with a finish line. Elsewhere he calls prediction "the modernized version of divination" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-87)).

There is a further twist, and it comes from Peirce: "predictions are really ways of increasing the likelihood that something will or won't happen" ([Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-14)). A prediction is never just a description. It is performative, an intervention in the scene it claims to observe. A very liquid market on an event is therefore part of that event. It pulls attention, resentment and money toward one way the scene could close.

## 4. Katz's counter-design: Thirdness

So what would a market that served deferral rather than divination look like? This is where Katz has the most to say. Thirdness inverts the commercial model in three ways.

**You bet on the judgment, not the event.** Thirdness would make any event bettable "precisely by constituting events as juridical" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-13)). The event becomes a case, with claimants and a tribunal, and "you would really be betting less on the event itself than on the judgment rendered" ([p-14](/post/thirdness#p-14)). The center is no longer hidden in a resolution clause; it becomes the thing traded on. Its premise is that "nothing 'happens' that could not be framed as including potential claimants before some tribunal" ([p-1](/post/thirdness#p-1)).

**Every case is built to be 50/50.** The house acts like a bookie who evens the line. Cases are constructed so that only the inquiry between posting and judgment decides them, and Katz turns this into a whole discipline of thought: "speak only of the 50/50, and continue your discourse by spreading the 50/50 through all the implications of the starting point of your discourse" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-2)). Commercial markets are designed the other way: they look for lopsided, attention-grabbing questions. A 50/50 case cannot be won by inside information or crowd momentum, only by better judgment. As a result, those taking part "are really betting on their own decision processes" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-11)).

**It aims to abolish itself.** The market is meant to make its tacit assumptions explicit until it becomes "something other than a market: a form of ledgering directly interfacing with singularized succession in perpetuity" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-10)). Bets become data exchanged with the center, channeled toward "the horizon of the abolition of the conditions of the terms of the conflict itself" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-17)). All of this depends on "very high levels of integrity and impartiality that would need to be periodically pedagogically renewed" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-23)). Without that juridical temperament, you simply get Polymarket.

Writing in 2023, Katz noted that betting markets "doesn't seem to have had any real influence on those events" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-22)). The boom since then has made that claim at least questionable. In his own terms, that is a sign the markets have become performative and part of the scene, though not yet in a deferring direction.

## An application

Take a typical contract: "Will country X strike country Y before date Z?" Read it through these four layers:

1. **Closure:** who resolves it? A newswire? Then the newswire is the center of this little scene, and its credibility is what is actually being priced.
2. **Succession:** the price measures confidence that current chains of command in X and Y will hold.
3. **Performativity:** large bets on "yes" are signals that can circulate back to the actors involved. My outside observation is that worries about insiders trading on such markets show how directly market and scene are entangled. Katz speculated about using markets exactly this way, to read "correspondences between political activity on the surface and intelligence activity in the depths" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-14)).
4. **The Thirdness alternative:** re-scene the question as a case. One example would be a market "in which even those betting on war would contribute to peace by detecting interference with the conversion of retaliatory tendencies into modes of deferral" ([A Bit More Granularity for a Cybernetics of Judaism and Thirdness](/post/a-bit-more-granularity-for-a-cybernetics-of-judaism-and-thirdness#p-14)).

## What to read next

- [Thirdness](/post/thirdness): the founding proposal. It covers closure, juridical framing, the bookie logic, and the hope that the market becomes "a kind of world brain."
- [Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence): how the 50/50 becomes a way of thinking and writing, and how judgments could turn into data exchanges instead of fines.

An exercise: pick a live contract on one of these platforms. Rewrite it as a Thirdness case. Identify the claimants and the tribunal, and reframe the question at its margins until a well-informed bettor would honestly put it at 50/50. Then notice what you had to learn about the institutions involved in order to get there. By Katz's account, that learning is the real yield of a market.

rows.q: What would Katz make of an organisation that puts every decision to a vote of all its members?
rows.a:
Katz would say the organisation is not doing what it thinks it is doing. In his account a group never really decides collectively. Someone always stands at the center. A vote of everyone on everything hides who that is, and it changes what the person at the center is actually working for.

## There is always a center, even in a meeting

The starting point is what Katz calls centered ordinality: in any shared activity someone goes first, someone second, and so on. Even under the most egalitarian rules, "someone takes the initiative, someone sets the tone, someone starts off in a new direction, and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). In *Power and Paradox* he states it as a general claim: wherever many act together, "we can identify a single leader who makes every decision that counts." He adds that when common action *looks* consensual, this is because shared goals mask the fact that "someone is taking the lead at every point where a disagreement is possible" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-47)).

So the first thing he would do with your organisation is look for that person. Who drafts the motions? Who decides what goes to a vote and in what wording? Who chairs, who counts, and who turns a result into an instruction someone can carry out? In an exchange with the blogger Reactionary Future the point is put sharply: a vote is "never a decision, it's a result," the outcome of a contest between factions ([Bouvard on Ontology, Mimesis, and Sovereign Decision](/post/a-response-to-dark-reformation-on-oligarchy-and-democracy#p-11)). Katz's own reply is that the useful task is learning to see through the forms: "Things that look like oligarchy are in fact monarchy if you know where and how to look" ([same exchange](/post/a-response-to-dark-reformation-on-oligarchy-and-democracy#p-13)).

## What the vote does to whoever leads

Katz works this out in a small parable in *Anthropomorphics*. A group escapes a burning building with one person guiding them, and then has to rebuild. Suppose the leader of the rebuilding holds the post at the assembly's pleasure. Then "the task of the new leader is not to build the building, but to maintain a majority among those he is serving. Every decision he makes now has a double meaning" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-12)). Each choice now has to serve both the work and the next vote.

He describes what follows in stages:

- The more any leader "seems dispensable at the whim of the group, the more this default assumption slides into scapegoating." The group starts imagining committees, rotation, or no leader at all. Yet the need for someone in charge returns "only in a less explicit way, because it is now 'controversial'" ([p-13](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-13)).
- Decisions drift first to "whoever is best able to mobilize a majority," and then to "those who are able to leverage the process of determining majorities" ([p-14](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-14)). In practice this means whoever controls the procedure: the agenda, the quorum, the timing.
- The procedure then needs a justification. "Why a 'majority'? A majority of whom?" To answer, the group has to invent a collective agent, "the members" or "the people," whose wishes everyone then argues about. That agent cannot itself be held to account.

This connects to Katz's insistence that power and responsibility match: "It is immoral to give someone responsibility for doing something without giving them the power to do it; it is immoral to give someone power, or to exercise power, that is not embedded in responsibility" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-61)). When everyone votes on everything, the people who actually carry out a decision have the responsibility but not the power. The majority that made the decision has the power but cannot be called to answer for it. Nobody can.

## Members as proxies

Katz's analysis of universal suffrage carries over to an organisation with only a few dozen members. Under it, "the electorate gets turned into proxies of those who actually exercise power, as they fight their battles with their rivals" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-58)). He also makes a point about knowledge: "All anyone can know authoritatively is the sphere of activity in which he participates." A member who runs the accounts knows the accounts. Asking that member to vote on the hiring policy, the newsletter and the building lease turns their real competence into one undifferentiated vote.

## What he would put in its place

Katz is not against listening to members. In the Reactionary Future exchange he says "there could never be a good reason for voting" and that even a many-member body "should have one person in charge who makes the final decision. But, there will always be deliberation" ([exchange](/post/a-response-to-dark-reformation-on-oligarchy-and-democracy#p-13)). Elections, he argues, do formalise the leader's dependence on those he leads, "but they do so in the worst possible way." That dependence is "far better formalized through modes of consultation through which all members of the community act as eyes and ears" of whoever leads ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-57)).

His preferred mechanism for the question that matters most, who leads next, is that the person in charge chooses a successor, "in consultation with whomever might be able to help him decide," possibly with "a process for providing the group with veto power" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-16)). Members still speak. They speak from their posts and about their posts, to a center that can be identified, and that center answers for the result.

(For comparison from outside the archive: Robert Michels' "iron law of oligarchy" observes that democratic organisations end up run by a small leadership. Katz differs in two ways. He treats this not as a corruption of democracy but as how human groups are always organised. And he wants the arrangement made explicit and accountable rather than lamented.)

## Read next

- [Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center) gives the whole burning-building argument step by step, and is the closest the archive comes to your exact question.
- [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf) is the fuller argument about elections, the transfer of power, and why Katz thinks succession is the central problem for any organisation.

**An exercise:** take an organisation you know that votes on everything. Write down the last three contested decisions and, for each, who framed the question, who set the timing, and who ended up implementing the result. If the same name keeps appearing, you have found the center Katz says was there all along. Then ask whether that person could be held accountable for those decisions, and how.

rows.q: Apply the idea of the idiom to a startup's internal jargon.
rows.a:
Katz never writes about startup jargon as such, but nearly every piece needed is in the archive: his account of the idiom, his distinction (borrowed from Alice Becker-Ho) between jargon and slang, his remarks on how terms of art compress shared attention, and his view of teams and start-ups as small sites of governance. A startup turns out to be an almost ideal place to see an idiom being born and also dying.

## What an idiom is, for Katz

Katz uses "idiom" in place of "theory" or "discourse" because he wants no privileged metalanguage that stands above ordinary speech and rules on it. "There is nothing in language but idioms, so the originary hypothesis is the idiomaticity of idioms" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-7)). An idiom is "a mode of language use constituted through use and therefore more fully available the more embedded in the scenes of its usage" ([Idiomatic Intelligence as Register](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-as-register#p-14)).

Two further features matter for a startup. First, an idiom has a center: it "implies organization around a center such that there are ever new things to point to at the center and that pointing at those things increases interest in the center" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-8)). Second, it is opaque to outsiders by design. The ideal utterance is "utterly unintelligible to those not conversant in your idiom and transparent to those who are" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-7)).

So the question about a startup's jargon is not whether it is clear to outsiders. It cannot be, and shouldn't be. The question is whether it keeps a small group pointing together at the same thing, and keeps generating new things to point at.

## Why a startup produces idiom so fast

A startup is a new scene gathered around a new center: a problem nobody has quite named, and a product that does not yet exist. Katz calls start-ups "proto-empires, and mediators of governance" ([The Political Infrastructure of Judaism](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-21)). In his terms, a new center requires new names, because the inherited vocabulary does not yet let people attend jointly to what matters. Writing about academic and expert terms, he explains why odd words get enforced: "the installation of that expression resulted from the trial and error of realizing that received vocabularies didn’t allow for the shared attention needed to generate new questions" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-8)). Each strange word is a compression. It packs a history of shared noticing into a token that insiders can unpack instantly.

Take a hypothetical case (my illustration, not from the archive). Early on, someone notices that users who invite a colleague in their first week almost never leave. A word appears for this, say "activation," or something odder. In Katz's terms that word is an ostensive. It is a way of saying "*this* is the same thing" across hundreds of user sessions. It also usually starts from an accident or mistake: "All idioms are built upon the cornerstone of mistakenness" ([Originary Mistakenness](/post/anthropoetics-originary-mistakenness#p-35)). Somebody mislabels a chart, someone else picks the label up, and it sticks because it lets people see something together.

## When idiom hardens into jargon

The same word can stop doing that work. Katz names three ways this happens.

**Nominalization.** "Nominalization can freeze discourse into jargon." The cure is "refusing the imperatives the nominalizations start giving you, the imperative exchanges they lure you into (the belief that this terminological tweak with solve the problem)" ([Technology and Magic](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings#p-21)). Anyone who has watched a team rename a failing initiative from "growth" to "momentum" has seen this. The new noun issues commands ("we need more momentum") that lead back to nothing anyone can point to.

**Goodhart's law.** Katz returns to the rule that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being useful as a measure. His remedy is to remember that "any measure is an idiom, a naming, a labeling, a designation that depends on those who can look at that thing and say 'this is the same'" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-4)). Once "activation" becomes a quarterly target, people start manufacturing invites. The word survives, but the joint pointing it once carried is gone.

**Caste.** In his review of Becker-Ho, Katz quotes her account of jargon. As opposed to slang, jargon "serves more to mark out a distance than to set up a real barrier," and it "defends and reinforces a world based on the division of labor by protecting the privileges of a caste" ([Becker-Ho review](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review#p-10)). Startup vocabulary can drift this way. Fluency in the founders' terms becomes a sign of rank rather than a tool for seeing.

A simple test runs through all three, adapted from a criterion Katz uses for claims generally: "the way to approach it must be in terms of respective paths to the ostensive" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-4)). Ask of any term: if I said this word, could two of us walk to a dashboard, a user, a line of code, and agree that *this* is what it names? If the answer is yes, it is still idiom. If the word only produces more words, it has become jargon.

## Two registers inside every startup

Becker-Ho's distinction points to something you can see in any company Slack. There is the official vocabulary of all-hands decks, and there is the team's slang: nicknames for the founder's favourite metric, sardonic labels for recurring failures. Katz suggests that a "slangy pedagogy would be an irreverent exercise in outing the shared, disavowed loyalties and disloyalties inhabiting neutralized concepts" ([Becker-Ho review](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review#p-19)). The slang is often the more live idiom. It records what the team actually sees, including what the official terms are protecting. A founder who listens to it gets intelligence that the deck vocabulary blocks.

## Onboarding and transfer

New hires show you the idiom's condition. Katz's guidance amounts to a theory of onboarding: "All you can do is invite people into a vocabulary... keep speaking it with them, incorporate whenever possible their mistakes as variations on this or that region of the idiom, and use the idiom to name the activities within the group" ([Paradoxes of Self-Referentiality](/post/paradoxes-of-self-referentiality-as-algorithmic-practice#p-9)). A new hire's misuse of a term is not only an error to correct. It is a chance to see whether the term still connects to anything, and sometimes the misuse is a better name.

Katz also wants an idiom that is "both more idiomatic and more transferable" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-15)), and he locates value there. "An idiom marks, commemorates, a scene of learning, and insofar as that scene of learning is transferable it is transmitted to other scenes, infiltrating and converting them" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-4)). The value lies "in the skills, cooperation and devotion of a team" rather than in any patented technique ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-8)). Terms like "MVP" or "product-market fit" (my examples, not Katz's) escaped a handful of firms and spread through the whole economy. This is the transfer he describes, and probably also where they began to flatten.

## An exercise

Take your company's three most-used terms and do what Katz calls translation into the primes ([Compression](/post/compression#p-21)). Rewrite each using only Wierzbicka's universal words: *do, happen, see, want, know, same, other, someone, something*. "Alignment" might become "someone wants us to do the same thing because we see the same thing." Then ask whether that is true in your team right now. Where the translation exposes a gap, you have found the place to rebuild the idiom, either by returning to the scene where the word was born or by letting the slang name what is actually there.

**Read next:** [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) is Katz's fullest statement on idiom versus bureaucratic abstraction, and on how to restart a frozen term. [Compression](/post/compression) explains why specialist vocabularies form in the first place and why that isn't a vice. For the darker side, the [Becker-Ho review](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review) is short and directly about jargon.

One question to take away: who in your company coined its most important term, and would that term survive if they left? This is Katz's succession question applied to a vocabulary.

rows.q: Use Center Study to analyse why a family argues at holiday dinners.
rows.a:
# The holiday table as a ritual scene

Katz has no essay on family holidays as such, but almost everything Center Study needs for one is already in the archive, because the theory begins with a meal. In the originary hypothesis a group converges on a shared object of desire. Someone aborts their grasp and turns it into a gesture: the first sign, a *deferral* of the violence that the convergence threatens. Then everyone eats. The holiday dinner is about the closest thing most modern families have to a ritual reenactment of that scene. A central object (the turkey) sits at the center, everyone is assembled around it, and there is a sign that it is time to begin.

## What deferral looks like at a table

Katz uses the family dinner as an example when he explains deferral. Deferral is not mainly about waiting:

> "sitting and waiting until 7 doesn't make them more civilized or moral than if they get served at 6. What is important is that the meal is properly "framed": everyone is at the table, distractions are eliminated, some kind of sign (like saying grace) that it is time to begin is given, everyone uses their utensils, people don't reach across the table to grab food off others' plates, etc." ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-6))

He also revises Gans's account of the *sparagmos*, the tearing apart of the central object that follows the sign. Katz asks what keeps the shared meal from turning back into a fight among the eaters. His answer is that the sign keeps working during the meal: "the members of the group would "flash" the sign, or in some manner signify a reversion to the restrained and pacific posture modeled on the originary scene" ([p-5](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-5)).

So the first diagnosis is structural. A holiday dinner reproduces the originary configuration: a close group, a center, a shared object of desire. The frame that is supposed to hold it is thin. Grace may not be said anymore, the rules about who speaks and what is off-limits are vague, and nobody has the authority to "flash the sign." The scene is full of mimetic charge, and few practices are there to defer it.

## Why the closest people quarrel most

Center Study starts from mimesis. In the lecture "Mimetic," Katz writes that "the things we would like to think are most "our own" are in fact the most alien to us," and that "imitation leads to rivalry because we learn to desire from our models and must therefore ultimately desire the destruction and our replacement of those models" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-8)). A family is where all of us got our first models. Siblings learned to desire by watching each other and their parents. That is why they fight hardest over things an outsider would find trivial.

Katz describes this in a thought experiment about people trying to say exactly the same thing. Sameness does not bring peace, because "everyone involved would become more expert in noticing ever smaller differences and making ever larger issues of them" ([Talk of the Center](/post/talk-of-the-center-adam-katz#p-22)). A family has shared vocabulary, shared jokes and shared memories, so its members are experts in small differences. The argument about whether the stuffing is "the way Mom made it" is an argument about who repeats the origin correctly, which is the oldest question there is.

## Resentment is aimed at the center

The most useful thing Center Study adds here is its account of resentment. Katz argues that resentment that looks horizontal is really vertical:

> "Even "horizontal" resentments derive from "vertical" ones, because it's the role of the central authority to ensure groups don't come into conflict with each other. If you resent horizontally, it's because you see your object of resentment as the protégé of the "unfair" central power." ([Accessing the Ostensive within the Declarative](/post/accessing-the-ostensive-within-the-declarative#p-11))

In a family, the center is first of all the parents. In "Identities" Katz lists "the parent(s) at the center of the family" as the first center in anyone's life, and calls these "the centers from which imperatives are issued, and which impose a nomos on the scene: the "fair" or "just" division of goods, attention, sympathy, protection amongst siblings" ([Identities](/post/identities#p-1)). The *nomos* is the originary distribution, the original allotment of shares. The holiday table brings the original nomos back. Everyone is a child in that house again, and the old question of who got more attention, protection or sympathy comes back too. When one sibling snipes at another, the target is often the parent who, in the sniper's account, played favorites.

Katz also explains why these grievances never expire. He defines resentment as "your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). The daughter who stayed nearby and took care of her aging father did what was asked. She expects recognition in return, and when the son who flies in once a year gets the warm welcome, that expectation goes unmet. Katz notes that "until they're fulfilled, or the subject is released, imperatives are, strictly speaking, forever" ([p-26](/post/resentment#p-26)). This is why a 1987 slight can come up over the cranberry sauce.

## Succession: who carves?

My next point applies Katz's concepts; he does not discuss families in these terms. He treats *succession* as the central political question and says it describes what everyone is always doing: "trying to "bias" the future so that those loyal to us and those who will continue our projects will be more likely acquire the power to do so" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). Holiday dinners are unacknowledged succession rituals. Someone hosts. Someone carves. Someone decides whether the in-laws come. As parents age, these markers start to move, and in most families nobody names a successor. The center is occupied but not handed on, so the adult children compete over it through proxies: a cooking method, a seating chart, who "really" looks after Mom. A family whose matriarch says plainly, "this year your sister hosts, and here is why," has removed a whole class of rivalry.

## Politics at the table: the Big Scenic Imaginary

Then there is the political fight. Katz's term *the Big Scenic Imaginary* names the habit of treating huge social conflicts as if they were a small group on a single scene ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)). He points out that the groups that supposedly resent each other in such narratives "are almost invariably state-constructed groups designated by law in some way, and therefore representable in familiar media rituals and spectacles" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-16)). In "Identities" he notes that beyond the parents there are "centers backing these with which we are in direct contact: corporations, media, the state," which "support the local ones, or encourage us to resist them" ([p-2](/post/identities#p-2)).

So when Uncle Frank and his niece fight about an election, the Big Scenic Imaginary is being staged at a real small table. Each of them stands in for a giant "we," and the resentment that properly belongs to distant centers is unloaded onto the nearest available body. The fight feels huge and changes nothing, because neither person is anywhere near the center being contested.

## What would help

Center Study does not tell anyone to swallow their feelings. Its idiom for this is *donating your resentment to the center*: turning a grievance into a clearer view of what the center has actually commanded, and what it owes or failed to give. Katz describes treating resentment as a "study of the center," in which you own your resentment "while converting your resentment into greater clarity regarding central imperatives" ([Accessing the Ostensive within the Declarative](/post/accessing-the-ostensive-within-the-declarative#p-12)). In practice, the useful question is less "why is my brother like this?" and more "what did Mom and Dad promise each of us, and what was actually delivered?" That question can be asked together. Forgiveness, on Katz's definition, is letting the imperative you hold over the other person lapse ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-26)).

He also has a compact formula for what the originary sign does: "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)). Family rituals work this way. The toast, the grace and the story told every year are shared sayings that keep everyone from reaching for the same thing at once. Katz notes elsewhere that the indirect politeness of dinner talk is not mere hypocrisy; the same constraints still govern "shared meals today" ([Civilizational Hide and Seek](/post/civilizational-hide-and-seek#p-5)).

Finally, a caution from the third lecture. "No one could know that violence has been deferred, because no one can know what would have happened without the sign of deferral. Maybe it just would have been a harmless little skirmish" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-8)). Even the argument may be a deferral: a contained quarrel standing in for a break that would be far worse. The family that argues every Thanksgiving is, after all, still at the table.

## Where to go next

- [The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral): the short post where the family dinner appears, with Katz's revision of the sparagmos and his claim that deferral is about framing, not waiting.
- [Resentment](/post/resentment): his definition of resentment as an unfulfilled reciprocal imperative, and the definition of forgiveness that comes with it. It is the most useful text for family quarrels.
- [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center): the general theory of how we are held by a center we did not choose.

**An exercise:** at the next family dinner, pick one flare-up and work out three things. Who occupies the center at this table? What imperative is the resentful person claiming to have fulfilled? What reciprocal imperative have they not let lapse? Then ask whether the person being attacked is really the target, or a stand-in for the parent, or for a distant center that nobody at the table can reach.
