rows.q: How does Center Study explain why people resent billionaires?
rows.a:
Center Study does not answer this the way most commentators do, either by calling hostility to billionaires envy or by calling it a just demand for fairness. It asks what center the resentment is addressed to. Once that is clear, the anger turns out to be about governance more than about money.

## Resentment is always aimed at the center

Katz gives resentment a working definition, a structural one rather than a feeling:

"Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse." ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19))

Apply that to the ordinary person angry at Bezos or Musk. They have kept the rules: worked, paid taxes, paid their debts. In return they expected something, perhaps a fair shot, or that the same rules would bind everyone. They believe that return has not come, and they will not let the claim drop.

The structure is triangular. The billionaire looks like the target, but he is not where the resentment is really directed. Katz writes:

"Even “horizontal” resentments derive from “vertical” ones, because it’s the role of the central authority to ensure groups don’t come into conflict with each other. If you resent horizontally, it’s because you see your object of resentment as the protégé of the “unfair” central power." ([Accessing the Ostensive within the Declarative](/post/accessing-the-ostensive-within-the-declarative#p-11))

So resenting a billionaire is resenting a center that has let him get away with something. The billionaire is resented as the center's favourite, the one who seems to be exempt from what binds everyone else. Behind that is a longer history. Resentment "becomes a moral and political factor with the ascension of the Big Man, who occupies the center and thereby becomes a resentment attractor" ([Sovereign Resentments](/post/sovereign-resentments#p-1)). The billionaire draws the attention and the hostility once reserved for whoever stood at the center.

## The Big Scene: society as a pie

The second part of the explanation is the picture of society most people carry without noticing it, which Katz calls the Big Scene. In this picture we all stand around one shared object and divide it among ourselves. Market society, he argues, has not escaped this picture:

"The concept of the free market, contrary to appearances, represents the same kind of primitivism, as if we were all at the same meal exchanging parts of the sacred body with each other: “wealth” and “GDP” are imagined as the beast at the center, even if the beast continues to grow." ([Transposing the Scene](/post/transposing-the-scene#p-4))

Seen this way, a billionaire is simply someone who has taken an enormous piece of the shared meal. Katz says plainly that "Big Scenic thinking can only generate resentment; moreover, it is an indication that we have not transcended sacrificial thinking" ([Stacking Against the Big Scene](/post/stacking-against-the-big-scene#p-3)). The anger is almost built into the picture: if wealth is one pie, every large slice is taken from someone else.

Katz adds a twist. Billionaires share the same picture. He asks why so many of them fund left-wing causes, and answers that they "simply can’t imagine any way of improving society other than giving a bigger piece of the pie to those with the least, because they have no way of imagining society other than on a scene with a shared center rather than a layered order with an occupied and directive center" ([Transposing the Scene](/post/transposing-the-scene#p-11)). The resenter and the resented are caught in the same imaginary, one from below and one from above.

## Why it gets so intense in a liberal order

Every hierarchy produces resentment, but liberal capitalism adds something specific: a gap between the power people are said to have and the power they actually have. Billionaires do not formally rule, yet in Katz's account governance under central banking "primarily serves to maintain a certain “spread,” determined by the financial class, and governments rise and fall depending on how close they are to the middle of that spread" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-2)). In compressed form: "The outside spread is leverage over the outside option" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-69)). The people who control credit have leverage over who can replace those in power.

Where power is real but unacknowledged, people look for who is really in charge. Katz lays out this logic in a related context, the analysis of conspiracy-style suspicion: when an institution "acts in ways that seem to undermine its own foundational purpose, it further makes sense to assume that it is being controlled by some power hostile or indifferent to that purpose" ([Antisemitism and Power](/post/antisemitism-and-power#p-2)). Billionaires are an obvious candidate for that hidden power. His high-low analysis adds a reason why the middle in particular resents them: in a decentered system, rival elites find the middle "an unwelcome hindrance" and ally with the "volatile and manipulable lows and fringes" ([The High-Low Alliance](/post/the-high-low-alliance-toward-a-middlist-absolutist-politics#p-8)).

Katz does not treat this resentment as simply mistaken. Here he departs from Gans, whom he criticises for using firstness only to idealise the market and to tar "its opponents with “resentment”" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-12)). Katz's own critique is close to the resenter's intuition, though put more precisely:

"The real objection to capitalism and central bank rule is precisely that it is always beyond justice because above a certain power level crimes can be committed with impunity because bringing them into a court would threaten the nomos too catastrophically for any orderly disposition to take place." ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-7))

That is the real basis of the resentment. The complaint is less that billionaires are rich than that their wealth puts them above judgment.

## What Center Study does with it

The remedy Katz proposes is neither redistributing the pie nor dismissing the resentment. He suggests three things.

1. **Name agents.** Center Study prefers to "treat only official names as narrativizable agents" ([Stacking Against the Big Scene](/post/stacking-against-the-big-scene#p-4)). "Billionaires" as a class do nothing. Named people, foundations and firms act through specific institutions, and one can trace exactly how.
2. **Turn grievance into cases.** "The juridical provides measures of resentment," Katz writes, and a settlement such as "“$250,000 settles my resentment” gives us an exact measure" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-16), [p-17](/post/nomos-class-action#p-17)). A diffuse rage becomes something a court can weigh, for instance as fraud or defamation.
3. **Donate the resentment to the center.** Resentments become "intelligible and acceptable insofar as they are framed as attempts to improve the system" ([Center Alignment](/post/center-alignment#p-9)). The useful question is not "how do we bring him down?" It is "what would a center look like that could actually hold him to account?"

**To read next:** *[Transposing the Scene](/post/transposing-the-scene)* gives the full account of the Big Scene and why it is so hard to stop thinking in its terms. *[The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment)* takes the "donate your resentment" idea into money and law; it includes the claim that money itself measures "expected future resentments."

**A question to try:** pick one specific billionaire you have seen resented. Using Katz's definition, what imperative do the resenters think they kept, and what reciprocal imperative do they think the center failed to enforce? Is the anger aimed at what he has, or at the impression that no court could ever reach him?

rows.q: I've never heard of any of this. Where do I start?
rows.a:
Welcome. Here is a short version of the whole idea first, then a reading order.

## The one idea everything grows from

Center Study is the body of work of Adam Katz (on Substack he writes as Dennis Bouvard). It starts from what Eric Gans called the **originary hypothesis**: a guess about how language, the human, and the sacred began, in one event.

Katz insists the starting point is simple. The hypothesis "is easily summed up in a couple of paragraphs, at most, and all it really assumes is that human beings are mimetic creatures" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)). *Mimetic* means imitative: we learn what to do, and what to want, by copying others.

The trouble is that if I copy your desire, sooner or later we want the same thing. Then, in Katz's words, the conflict "can only be resolved in one of two ways: one defeats the other; the two share the desired object." The first is what every animal species does. "Only in the second case could something like a 'community' emerge" ([p-3](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-3)).

The hypothesis imagines a group of proto-humans all converging on one desired object, say a kill, closely enough that the usual pecking order breaks down and violence looms. Someone hesitates. The reach toward the object stalls and becomes a gesture that points at the object instead of grabbing it. Others imitate the gesture. That pointing is the first sign, a kind of imitation that "reverses the trajectory of an appropriative gesture by converting that gesture into one of aborted appropriation" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-5)).

Three terms come out of this scene, and you will meet them everywhere:

- **Deferral.** The sign does not abolish the violence. It holds it off for now.
- **The center.** The object everyone attends to while refraining from seizing it. It "holds you: while you're looking at it you're not looking away" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-5)).
- **The scene.** The arrangement of people around a center.

From this follows Katz's definition of the human: "that being who is a greater danger to himself than is posed by any external danger" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-2)).

## Why it isn't just a story about cavemen

Katz's distinctive move is to say we never left that scene: "we have never left and will never leave the originary scene" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-12)). Every word you use carries it. As he notes, for every word, "someone must have been the first to use it in a way that stuck" ([Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin#p-6)).

His compact formula for what language does is: "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)).

You can test this on anything ordinary. Take a meeting or a group chat. Even in the loosest group, "someone takes the initiative, someone sets the tone, someone starts off in a new direction, and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). The scene is already there.

A great deal of Katz's later work, on power, money, law, technology and succession, extends from here. It asks how a community keeps a center, and how it hands that center on, without collapsing into everyone grabbing at once.

## A reading order

1. **The five lectures.** They are short and were built as an introduction. Read them in order:
   - [Origin](/post/origin): why thinking can't avoid origins.
   - [Mimetic](/post/mimetic): imitation as the root of desire and rivalry.
   - [Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence): what "deferral" really means.
   - [The Center](/post/the-center): attention, the center, and power.
   - [The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf): what a sign is, reframed as a "sample."
2. **[The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself).** Katz on why the idea is simple but hard to accept.
3. **[The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis).** What the hypothesis lets you do with politics and institutions.
4. **[Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis).** A chapter of his book *Anthropomorphics*, for the scene told more carefully.

Save the recent Substack essays on money, debt and "Thirdness" for later. They assume the vocabulary.

To aim my next explanations well, it would help to know what brought you here. Was it a tweet, a political question, an interest in language or religion, or something else?

rows.q: Apply the idea of data as currency to supermarket loyalty cards.
rows.a:
# Data as currency, applied to the supermarket loyalty card

Katz never writes about loyalty cards by name. The texts shown here come very close, though, and once the idea is laid out the card turns out to be an almost perfect small-scale version of it. It shows both the present arrangement he criticises and the reversal he proposes.

## The idea in brief

Katz starts from what money originally was. Money "started off as a way of managing distanced distribution from the center—providing tokens of contributions or expected contributions to the center by social participants in sustained cooperative projects" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-1)). Here the *center* means whatever a group's shared attention, authority and distribution converge on. A coin records what you have given toward the common project and lets you draw from it.

His claim is that data already does this work, but only in a subordinate role. We get free social media because its owners sell our data to people who sell us things:

> "So, data is already working as currency here, in a manner subordinated to the currency generated by state-bank interactions, meaning we can pose the question of whether data can function as currency in such a way as to replace money." ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-2))

## The loyalty card as subordinated data-currency

The card is that subordinate arrangement in its plainest form. You hand over your purchase history, a running "sample" of yourself, and in return you get prices in dollars. The data is the real payment, but it only matters because it is converted back into money, both for you and for the chain.

Katz treats this kind of token as currency in its own right: "Reward points from your credit card company or frequent flier miles from an airline are a kind of currency which it's easy to imagine exchanging and speculating on in various ways" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-18)).

His casino image fits the points almost exactly. When he describes AI-run enterprises issuing their own tokens, he says "the center provides you with currency to engage in spheres of activity of interest to the center—kind of like the casino might give you chips to play with albeit in this case not hoping you'll lose—so that those activities will provide data useful to the center" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-20)). Loyalty points are chips issued so that you will keep playing at the table where the data is collected. The question Center Study asks is what the "center" is in this case. Under present conditions it is the chain's balance sheet, and behind that the advertisers and data buyers. Your shopping data becomes an asset valued against expected future earnings, which is exactly the "assetization" Katz wants to undo.

## Why the card exists: loyalty without a relationship

[Constrained Economies](/post/constrained-economies#p-2) explains why the card is needed in the first place. Katz contrasts buying bread for ten years from a baker you know with today's supermarket: "no one thinks the supermarket you go to will miss you, personally, if you start going to its competitor." Even so, the loyalty persists in a changed form, made up of the sales, the specialty items, and the chance of meeting a friend there. "You are 'always already' tied into a certain set of connections, you have a built in 'bias.'" Markets are really networks.

On this reading the card tries to rebuild the baker's personal knowledge of you through data, after the market has removed the personal relationship. It formalizes your built-in bias and gives it a price. The irony is that the store now knows far more about you than the baker ever did, but in a form that cannot "miss" you. It tracks you without belonging with you.

## The reversal: what the card would become

This is where Katz's proposal turns the card inside out. In [Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-25) he imagines a political party, as a nucleus of a new order, issuing its own currency, "modeled, perhaps, on cryptocurrencies, but just as likely on the exclusive 'clubs' promoted by credit card companies." The arrangement he then describes looks like a loyalty scheme:

> "helping secure the majority in some state legislature would entitle one to credits to be used in stores that supply party members in exchange for data regarding shopping habits of party members, which are continually shaped by the new businesses interested in entering an exchange with a guaranteed customer base, extensive legal protections..." ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-26))

The structure is the same as the card: shopping data in exchange for credits at participating stores. The differences are in direction and in who sits at the center:

- **What earns the credit.** You get credits for contributing to a shared project, not for spending money.
- **What the data is for.** The data feeds an "emergent center" that is responsible for its members, not a shareholder or an ad market.
- **What the store gets.** The store receives protection and a guaranteed base, so it is tied into a network of mutual obligation instead of competing for anonymous shoppers.

Katz says plainly that this changes the moral meaning of the same act: currency would be "embedded in a better way of life, including the kinds of data exchanges now considered obnoxious but under different conditions (this is the challenge, at any rate) viewed as a form of reciprocal support" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-26)). The resentment people feel about loyalty-card tracking is, for him, resentment at being sampled for a center that owes them nothing. It is not a reason to reject being sampled as such.

Taken all the way, the card dissolves altogether: "you don't receive a salary and go to the store to buy things—the data you give off attracts and activates others situated within other institutions who are thereby oriented toward meeting your needs and drawing upon your abilities" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-15)). Elsewhere he puts it more bluntly: the more tightly interwoven the organization of data, "the more currency becomes the equivalent of company 'scrip,' certificates and subscriptions privileging specific services and goods" ([Converting Assets to Data](/post/converting-assets-to-data-tributarianism#p-28)). On this view, the points balance is an early form of scrip that has not yet recognized itself as scrip.

## What this asks of you now

You cannot step outside this system by refusing the card. Katz is explicit that "Trying to evade, escape, opt out, withdraw from that technoscene itself just provides more data," and that "we prepare our data in cultivating and assembling ourselves as samples" ([Data as Currency and the Debt to the Center](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-13)). The card makes visible something that is always true, namely that "We are always donating samples, and each and every one of us is a sample" ([Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency#p-4)). The live questions are which center your samples are donated to, and whether you are curating them or simply having them taken.

He is also clear about what the reversal would cost. It depends on "elevated levels of trust" and an "extremely efficient and trustworthy data security arm" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-21)). A loyalty card run by a center you cannot trust is just surveillance with a discount attached.

## Reading next

- [Data as Currency](/post/data-as-currency) is the core essay. Read it in full, especially paragraphs 13–16 on how needs and abilities would be matched without money, and 24–27 on party currency.
- [Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary) places reward points and party coupons inside Katz's larger argument about derivatives and continuity at the center.
- [Constrained Economies](/post/constrained-economies) is a short piece on markets as networks of loyalty, which is the ground the loyalty card stands on.

**An exercise:** look at a recent loyalty-card receipt and list three things the chain now "knows" about you. For each one, ask what institution, if it were genuinely responsible for you, would need that same information in order to meet a need of yours or draw on an ability. The distance between the two answers measures how subordinated your data currently is.

rows.q: What does Center Study suggest about how to write a good prompt for an AI?
rows.a:
Katz never writes a how-to for prompting, but he says a good deal about what prompting is, and that tells you what a good prompt looks like. His starting point in "Techno-Grammar" is that prompt engineering is a new form of something old. It is "essentially the designing of search terms that would elicit results from searches into textual databases (i.e., AI) that will most powerfully suggest the design of a new search term" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-1)). Several practical consequences follow from that.

**1. A prompt is an imperative that has to make it to a declarative.**

Center Study's grammar runs ostensive → imperative → interrogative → declarative. In plain terms: pointing at something, then demanding it, then asking about it, then making a statement. Katz applies this sequence directly to working with an AI:

> "The imperative is the command or demand that some object—which could be a person, a word, an arrangement—be made present."

He adds that "those imperatives that can make the trek through to the declarative will be 'selected for'" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-11)).

So before you write the prompt, ask what you want made present at the end. What would let you and someone else point at the output and say "this is the same" as what you were after? A prompt that never says what would count as fulfilling it is an imperative with no ostensive behind it. It will come back as something answered in general.

**2. A predictable prompt gets the average back.**

Katz learned this the hard way. He asked ChatGPT a stock question about AI and creativity and got an encyclopedia entry. His verdict on that was "perhaps it's my fault for asking such a bland, predictable question—precisely the kind one would open an encyclopedia to answer" ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-8)).

The reason lies in what a language model does. It "provides you with a reading of the text fed in in terms of a kind of 'average' language user." So "the more unpredictable your writing, the more 'interesting' the range of continuations of it you will receive" ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-17)). Elsewhere he predicts that we "will learn to prompt ever more surrealistically" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-2)).

The practical rule is to write the prompt in your own idiom rather than in commonplaces. That means using the specific words, the odd juxtapositions and the particular texts you are working with. His teaching makes a related point: the models so far "can't work with language from a text within another's language in an effective way" ([From Novice to Apprentice](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-54)). So give the model the actual language you care about, not a paraphrase of it.

**3. A prompt carries forward an intention, and you have to decide whose.**

In "Thinking only through Models," Katz says that "the prolongation of some intention that we want to bring to bear on our work is what informs the prompt" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-15)). His example is asking what George Washington would make of today's administrative state. To ask that well, "we'd have to figure out who, exactly, was George Washington (and which texts, of Washington and others, do we draw upon, and how do we weigh them, in determining this)" ([ibid.](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-16)).

A good prompt therefore says which model you are thinking through, and on what evidence. "What would Washington think of X?" is a cheap question. "Drawing on these letters, and allowing for his confusion at the present, what would…" is a real one.

**4. Prompting is iterative, and the selecting is your part.**

Reviewing Dobrin, Katz describes the new skill as "prompting and selecting from among the results of the prompt and then iterating this practice over and over again" ([AI and Writing review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-10)). In good research, you end up with "search terms you keep remaking with each search and the returns of each search, as you learn along with the machine" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-20)).

So the first prompt is a probe, not a finished request. The judgment about which return is "the same thing" you were after stays with you. Katz insists on "the irreducibility of the juridical, of judgment" against AI enthusiasm ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-22)).

He also gives a warning: "Insofar as we come to think in potential 'prompts' … The system is using us as much as we are using it" ([AI and Writing review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-11)).

**5. A prompt can be written against the grain.**

Katz describes prompting as a way to "'solicit' the database, get it to say things it doesn't 'want' to, that deploy their training against their programming" ([Idioms as Operationalized Samples](/post/idioms-as-operationalized-samples#p-19)). A good prompt surfaces what the averaged answer covers over.

**6. A prompt is a kind of petition.**

Katz places prompting in the long line of "imperative exchange" with the center, meaning the give-and-take of commands and requests that began with ritual and prayer. "We're trying to draw out imperatives from the center … whether this is done by more rehearsal of a chant and dance or by revising a prompt or search term eliciting information from the center is the aim" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-20)). The most developed form of that petition is "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)).

Read practically, a strong prompt does not just demand an object. It asks the system to show you how to keep going.

**Applying this**

Take a weak prompt: "Explain resentment in Generative Anthropology."

A stronger one works like this:
- Paste the two passages where Katz defines resentment.
- Ask for the boundary between the two definitions.
- Ask for one case where they come apart.
- Ask for the question you should put next.

The stronger version names the texts, specifies what you would accept as an answer, refuses the average, and builds in the next search.

**What to read next**

- [Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar) is Katz's most direct treatment of prompting as grammar.
- [Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models) explains the "prolonged intention" idea and the Washington example.
- [The Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review) shows him actually prompting, and failing at first.

An exercise: take a prompt you have used recently. Rewrite it so that it names the texts it draws on, states what would count as the "same thing," and asks for its own successor prompt. Then compare the two sets of results.

rows.q: Who is Adam Katz, and who is Dennis Bouvard?
rows.a:
## The short answer

They are the same person. Adam Katz is the author; "Dennis Bouvard" is the pen name he writes under on his Substack and earlier on the GABlog. The Substack's welcome page reads: "Welcome to Center Study Center by me, Dennis Bouvard. Author of Anthropomorphics" ([Originary Hypothesizing](/post/originary-hypothesizing#p-1)). *Anthropomorphics* is Katz's book, so the two names point to one body of work. The archive doesn't say why he chose the pen name, and I won't guess.

## What the archive says about Katz

The author note in the 2019 edition of Eric Gans's *The Origin of Language*, for which Katz wrote the introduction, gives the basic facts. Katz "is the editor of The Originary Hypothesis: A Minimal Proposal for Humanistic Inquiry, and the co-author, with Eric Gans, of The First Shall Be the Last: Rethinking Antisemitism." He has written many essays for *Anthropoetics*, Gans's journal, and "He teaches college writing in Connecticut" ([The Origin of Language](/post/the-origin-of-language#p-482)). His academic essays give his affiliation as the Department of English, Quinnipiac University ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-2)). That background matters for the thinking. Pedagogy, literacy and the teaching of writing keep returning in his work as models for how anything is learned.

## His relation to Gans and Generative Anthropology

For years Katz worked inside Generative Anthropology (GA), the field Gans built on the originary hypothesis: language, the human and the sacred begin together in a single gesture that defers violence around a shared central object. Katz was one of Gans's closest interlocutors. Gans's Chronicle 344 is described as "a continuation of a running dialogue with Adam Katz concerning GA's relationship to politics" ([Chronicle 344](/post/chronicle-344-right-and-left#p-1)).

He eventually broke away. "My longstanding position, while I was working within GA, was that GA (as the disciplinary form of the hypothesis) had to be a transdisciplinary, all-encompassing theory aimed at displacing contenders" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-1)). He names several points of disagreement:

- **Resentment.** One impetus for separating "center studies from generative anthropology was the inadequate and impressionistic discussions of resentment in the latter" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)).
- **Humanism.** He thinks Gans would consider GA a humanism, "and this is part of the broader range of issues on which I left GA and started Center Study" ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-5)).
- **Liberalism.** He describes his own work as "a continuation of the absolutist thinking through which I transitioned out of liberalism back in 2015-6" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). Of Gans's liberal conclusions he writes: "if the conclusion to GA is that we're all free agents on the market, who needs GA?" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-24)).

The name of the field follows from this. Center Study keeps the originary hypothesis but puts **the center** first: whatever holds joint attention and issues imperatives. That starts with the sacred object on the originary scene and runs through the Big Man, kings and states to today's institutions. From there the work moves into power, succession, money and debt, law, and technology. Katz isn't strict about the label: "I won't complain if anyone wants to continue calling what I'm doing 'GA'" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-18)). Where he and Gans differ, though, the positions in this archive are his.

## Where to go next

- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) is Katz's own short account of what the hypothesis is, why people resist it, and his candid view of GA's small community: "Gans, joined more or less regularly by maybe a dozen talented ... academics, and then me" ([p-16](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-16)).
- [Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin) is the gentlest entry into his way of thinking about origins, and leads straight into the other four lectures.

To help me pitch later answers: are you coming to this from Gans and Girard, from the political writing, or completely fresh?

rows.q: What is generative anthropology, in one paragraph?
rows.a:
Generative anthropology is the field Eric Gans founded with *The Origin of Language* (1981), built on a single hypothesis about how the human began. Humans are the most imitative of creatures. Imitation turns models into rivals, so a group of proto-humans converging on one desired object, say a fresh kill, faces a crisis that the animal pecking order can no longer contain. In that crisis someone hesitates, and his grasp becomes a gesture pointing at the object instead of seizing it. The others imitate the gesture, and in that moment language, the human community and the sacred are born together. Gans puts it this way: "It is this aborted gesture of appropriation, designating the object, but no longer directed at appropriating it, that we postulate as the first sign" ([The Origin of Language](/post/the-origin-of-language#p-123)). The object at the center, which seems to hold everyone back, becomes the first god. From then on, representation in every form serves to defer violence. That is why Katz defines the human as "that being who is a greater danger to himself than is posed by any external danger" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-2)). Because everything human is supposed to be traceable back to that scene, GA claims more than to be one theory among others: "it follows that Generative Anthropology must be the human science" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-2)). Katz has taken it further in his own direction, toward power, succession, money and law, under the names "anthropomorphics" and Center Study ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-37)).

**To read next:** [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) is Katz's short case that the hypothesis is simple and hard to deny. The lecture [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center) shows what follows once you start from the center rather than from individual subjects.

rows.q: Is this a religion?
rows.a:
Short answer: no. But Katz himself says the question isn't silly, because the resemblance is real. In his words, the field is "odd in being very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)). The useful thing is to see why both halves of that sentence hold.

## The starting point

Center Study begins from Eric Gans's **originary hypothesis**. Humans are intensely imitative, and imitation breeds rivalry. At some point a group of proto-humans converged on a shared object, most likely a kill, with enough mimetic intensity that the animal pecking order broke down. Someone's grasping hand faltered and became a gesture pointing at the object instead of seizing it. Others imitated that gesture, and the crisis was deferred. That **aborted gesture of appropriation** is hypothesized as the first sign. The language, the human community and the sacred begin together, organized around a **center**: the thing everyone attends to and no one may simply grab.

So the theory puts the sacred at the origin of everything human. That is why it can look like a religion.

## Why it resembles one

**It is an origin story that seems to ask for belief.** Katz acknowledges that "it can feel like one is being asked to 'believe in' something" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)).

**Accepting it is less like adding a theory than like a conversion.** Because the hypothesis is "incommensurable with any other way of thinking about humanity," Katz writes, "Something like a conversion experience may be necessary here: you'd have to be able to abandon and revise all 'priors'" ([p-6](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)). Elsewhere he says it "repels the kind of initiatory revelatory 'download' that is nevertheless the only way of understanding it" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)).

**Its vocabulary is theological all the way down.** The first sign names the center, so the first word is "the Name-of-God." Katz pushes this further: "Language, then, is fundamentally prayer" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-10)). This is why he says the hypothesis "brings secularization to its conclusion and thereby cancels it" ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-1)). If every word names God, a fully secular discourse isn't available.

**It sides with the faiths over the philosophers.** "The implication of the originary hypothesis is that the faiths are truer than philosophy, and it's not even close" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)).

## Why it is the opposite of one

**It is a hypothesis, not a creed.** Katz writes: "I don't see it as a question of 'belief' (which I don't 'believe' in), but it does, perhaps, require a willingness to live or think in a kind of 'suspense'" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)). It "acknowledges it can never be proven, and doesn't promise salvation" ([p-6](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)).

**It explains religions rather than joining them.** It is "the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions." The consequence for believers is pointed. If you take the hypothesis literally, you "can only see your faith tradition as an approximation of a configuration you consider prior and irreducible to that tradition" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)). Its explanation is also deliberately deflationary. It moves "an entire field so far covered by 'theology'" onto "a bunch of not necessarily impressive 'protohumans' who manage to get something 'right'" ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-13)).

**It commits you to no particular theology.** Paganism, monotheism and secularism have all "established centers under particular conditions," and the hypothesis lets you measure each against those conditions ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-3)).

**It has no rite, no founding event and no community of worship.** Katz contrasts this with Girard's followers, who can gather around exposing scapegoating. With the originary hypothesis, "now that we can 'see through' rituals, but without any founding event that enabled us to do so and that we can commemorate and repeat, there's nothing to put in its place" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-10)). He adds, drily: "It's certainly hard to imagine any government demanding generative anthropologists renounce their 'faith' on pain of persecution" ([p-12](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-12)).

Katz holds the two halves together in one phrase. It is "a perfectly materialist refutation of materialism, the one true faith masquerading as subversive heresy" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)). The hypothesis is materialist in its method, but what it shows is that the sacred is irreducible.

## A deeper twist: the word "religion" itself

Katz also distrusts the question's main term. The word is not minimal enough for originary inquiry. Using it to cover Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism, voodoo and tribal rites together is "modeled on Protestantism, with its distinction between 'individual faith,' on the one hand, and either Church or State, on the other" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-32)). Even the religious studies field, he notes, has largely concluded that "there is no single phenomenon called 'religion'" ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-2)). He prefers a plainer word: "We get much closer to minimality with a word like 'commemoration'" ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-3)). Every community commemorates. The question "is this a religion?" therefore partly dissolves. What Center Study studies, and itself practices, is how we commemorate and repeat the scene of deferral.

If you press Katz on what he does believe, he gives a surprising answer: "if pressed on what I 'believe,' my answer will ultimately be 'language,' which seems to me far more miraculous than anything believed in by adherents to other faiths" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-10)). The "faith" in the hypothesis is that "there will always be new things at the center to draw forth further signs and scenes from us" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-14)).

## What this means if you are religious, or not

You don't have to choose between your tradition and the hypothesis, but the hypothesis changes how you hold your tradition. Katz calls historic faiths "discovery procedures whose results can be assessed while being maintained as ongoing inquiries" ([Deferral and Appropriation; Property and the Center](/post/deferral-and-appropriation-property-and-the-center#p-2)). Suppose you learn that a rite came out of a political compromise. That need not empty it. "Congregations can learn to be unscandalized by such inquiries... insofar as any scene must be constructed out of the available materials, which can always be consecrated, regardless of their origins" ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-20)).

If you are secular, the challenge runs the other way. Katz says the hypothesis is hard for both camps: for "the 'secular' (who want causes that can't be provided here because we have a singular event) and the 'religious' (who need a deity to 'legitimate' their miracles)" ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-12)).

## Where to read next

- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) is the most direct and candid treatment of belief, conversion, and why no community has formed around the hypothesis.
- [Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking) works out how the hypothesis both completes and cancels secularization, and what that means for actual faiths.

A question to take with you: think of one ritual or commemoration you take part in, religious or not, such as a holiday, an anthem or a graduation. What does it repeat, and what would it look like to see it, in Katz's terms, as a version of the scene where everyone pointed at the center instead of grabbing it?

rows.q: How is this different from Girard?
rows.a:
The short answer: Center Study accepts Girard's starting point, that humans are mimetic through and through, and then disagrees with him about what happened at the origin. That one disagreement changes what the theory sees, what it is for, and what kind of community can form around it.

## What is kept from Girard

Katz gives Girard real credit. Many thinkers have said humans imitate, but "it's one thing to say humans are mimetic beings, but it's another to say that mimesis makes the human" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-3)). The logic that imitation produces rivalry, because my model shows me what to want and so becomes my obstacle, is taken over whole. So is the idea of a **mimetic crisis**: a group converging on the same object until its existing order breaks down.

## Difference one: the sign, not the murder

For Girard the crisis is resolved when one member of the group is singled out and killed, and the victim afterward becomes the first god ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-2)). Gans's objection, which Katz adopts, is that nothing in this scene would make it remembered or meaningful: "The limit of Girard's account is that there is no reason for the event in question to become meaningful and memorable." Animals kill members of their own species all the time without being changed by it. To call it "murder" already assumes a moral order, and "Girard doesn't account for the emergence of language, which would itself be a prerequisite of a moral order and a community to share it" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-3)).

Gans first tried adding a sign to the end of Girard's scene: everyone points at the body. Then he saw that "if the real point is the pointing, the killing itself is superfluous" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-39)). So the originary hypothesis puts the sign at the height of the crisis. Someone hesitates, and their grab becomes a **gesture of aborted appropriation**: a reach that stops short and so points to the object instead of seizing it. Others imitate the gesture, and the rush is deferred. Katz puts it in one line: "if Girard's scapegoat scene requires the sign, then the generation of the sign no longer requires the scapegoating" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-15)).

This also gives a different account of what imitation can do. Girard's mimesis escalates. Gans finds a "counter-imitation" in the sign that "arrests rather than accelerating mimetic rivalry." The reason is that "a sign or utterance can be different in being the same." We can all repeat a gesture without fighting over it, as we cannot all eat the same piece of meat ([Lecture 2](/post/mimetic#p-12)). Language is mimesis turned against its own destructive tendency.

## Difference two: what sits at the center, and when sacrifice arrives

Because nobody has to die, the thing at the center is most plausibly a food object, an animal kill. That fits the record: "the earliest communities worshipped animals and plants, with human divinity and human sacrifice coming much later, with hierarchical orders" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-41)).

Human sacrifice appears only once a person occupies the center. First comes the **Big Man**, who seizes the ritual center and takes over distribution. Then comes the sacral king, whom Katz calls "the first form of human sacrifice" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-27)). Of the Big Man's usurpation Katz says "this is really the origin of the scapegoating phenomenon studied by Girard" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-15)).

Scapegoating is therefore real but historical, not originary. Katz keeps "a firm place for Girard's scapegoat mechanism": whoever steps into the center "places himself in the position of a potential victim" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-55)). This yields a characteristic Center Study claim: "Scapegoating is also always against the center—even when the occupant of the center leads it. The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes'" ([Bouvard on Scapegoating](/post/the-egalitarian-vs-hierarchical-model-of-morality#p-1)).

## Difference three: what the theory is for

Katz is candid that Girardians have an organizational advantage. "Once you identify scapegoating as the predominant but now discredited way of organizing communities, you can organize intellectual and sub-cultural communities around exposing and resisting scapegoating." That can take the form of a faction within Christianity or a kind of leftism ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-9)). The originary hypothesis "'denies' that the initial … scapegoating ever took place," so it has no founding victim to commemorate ([same, p-10](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-10)).

What Center Study puts in that place is the center itself: who occupies it, how imperatives come from it, how authority passes from one occupant to the next. A Girardian looks at a scene and asks who is being victimized. Katz asks what center the scene is organized around and whether that center is holding.

## Where Katz criticises both

Katz is not simply on Gans's side against Girard. He grants that Girard has something Gans dropped: "for Girard, knowledge of our mimetic desires must be learned and earned." That knowledge requires a kind of ascesis, a disciplined working through of one's own mimetic investments. Katz insists that "there can be no real knowledge without inscription and initiation" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-22)), ([p-24](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-24)). He also names a shared weakness: "the central failure of mimetic theory and GA alike—whatever can't get reduced to the scale of a 19th century French novel can't be thought" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-17)). Neither theory scales up well to states, finance, intelligence agencies and technology, and much of Katz's recent work is an attempt to supply that.

## Trying it on a case

Take an online pile-on against some public figure. A Girardian reading sees a crowd discharging its rivalries onto a victim, and the moral task is to expose the mechanism and side with the victim. A Center Study reading starts from what the scene is centered on. A pile-on usually claims that someone has wrongly taken a central position, that they got away with something the center should have stopped. So the next question is what is wrong with the actual center, whether the platform, the institution or the authority, such that the crowd feels it must do the center's work itself. The victim is still there, but attention moves to the center.

## What to read next

- [Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic) is short and lays out both what Katz takes from Girard and where Gans "transcends" him.
- [Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center), from about paragraph 27 on, sets the two origin stories side by side and follows the consequences into power and the center.

A question to take further: if the first sign defers violence without a victim, what does Katz think deferral looks like now, when nobody can be sacrificed in good faith? His texts on [the Pointman](/post/the-pointman) take this up directly.

rows.q: Is Center Study left-wing or right-wing?
rows.a:
**Neither, in Katz's own terms: he argues the left-right distinction is the thing to get rid of.** That is not a neutral middle, and his conclusions are not neutral. I'll give his argument first, then where his politics actually lands, since the two can seem to pull apart.

## Why the question doesn't fit

Katz treats left and right as a recent product of the end of monarchy, not a permanent feature of politics. He writes that "the Right, in the post-monarchical world (there is no left vs. right in monarchy, as how could the king be either one or the other?), is really just the anti-Left" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-7)). Elsewhere: "The right exists only because of the left—the left is what set “modernity” in motion; the right has always been reactive," so "The Left/Right configuration is parochial and contingent" ([Toward a Unified Field Theory of the Left](/post/toward-a-unified-field-theory-of-the-left#p-13)).

The deeper claim is that both sides share one structure. "Since the fall of monarchy, all of politics, from left to right, have shared the same model of “liberation.”" Every modern position builds its political subject through struggle against an oppressor who has usurped its place ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-12)). In Center Study's vocabulary this is mimetic rivalry: the rival "who has usurped my rightful position at the center." The hardest demand Katz makes of any politics is "deferring the extremely powerful (and propagandistically effective) desire to predicate one’s political aims on one’s own victimization" ([p-13](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-13)). He applies this to the right as well. The standard conservative move of showing that the left are "the “real” racists, misogynists, fascists, etc., is a replication of the same assumption" ([On the Use of the Center-Margin Model](/post/on-the-use-of-the-center-margin-model-to-displace-the-left-right-model#p-7)).

## What replaces it: the center-margin model

Asked what should replace liberation politics, he answers: "With the center" ([Prospects, p-14](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-14)). Every group, from a family to a state, has someone at the center, the one who sets the direction. You can replace that person, but the place remains. So the real political questions are:

- who occupies the center,
- how responsibility is matched to power, and
- how the handoff to a successor happens.

From this angle, left and right are two speeds of one process. Katz uses a model he calls HLvM, "High and Low versus the Middle." (The model comes from the political theorist Bertrand de Jouvenel, not from the archive.) In it, a central power allies with groups below to dissolve the intermediate authorities in between. "So, the Left is the major key of the HL v M accelerated turnover of the officer class; the Right is the minor key, trying to decelerate or, in extremely rare cases (I can’t think of one off-hand), reverse the turnover." Once you ask who will staff a policy and how, rather than which principle it serves, "The whole left-right framing dissipates" ([On the Use of the Center-Margin Model, p-14–15](/post/on-the-use-of-the-center-margin-model-to-displace-the-left-right-model#p-14)).

A worked example. On abortion, "What both sides agree on is that the state should be able do whatever the one making the demand would want: a state incapable of enforcing laws against abortion would also be incapable of enforcing laws allowing abortion" ([The End of Secular Thinking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-end-of-secular-thinking#p-28)). Beneath the partisan dispute, both sides are demanding a capable, coherent center. Katz wants that shared demand to be the starting point.

## Where this lands, honestly

By ordinary standards, the conclusions Katz draws sit on the anti-liberal right, and he says so plainly:

- He describes his core concept as "a continuation of the absolutist thinking through which I transitioned out of liberalism back in 2015-6" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)).
- He calls the left "the cadres of militants levied by those elites interested in furthering the power directly exercised by the state over the individual" ([Some further inquiry into HLvM](/post/some-further-inquiry-into-hlvm-gablog#p-1)).
- In one post he writes, "I work on the assumption that the left is essentially a criminal organization" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-1)).
- He criticises Gans for making Generative Anthropology into "the ideology of liberal democracy" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-8)).

The complications are real too. In theory, he holds that originary thinking itself "it’s not intrinsically committed or opposed to monarchy or democracy, fascism or communism, nationalism or imperialism," and could under some conditions join any of them ([Prospects, p-6](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-6)). He is sharply critical of capitalism. He draws on Bichler and Nitzan's *Capital as Power* and concedes that "absolutists stand with some elements of the contemporary left, those that still have abolishing the capitalist world order on their agenda" ([Debts and Deferences](/post/debts-and-deferences-gablog#p-28)).

The fairest summary: the hypothesis is framed as politically open; Katz's own politics are absolutist, anti-liberal and anti-left; and he refuses the right's reactive, victim-centred style.

## Read next

- [On the Use of the Center-Margin Model to Displace the Left-Right Model](/post/on-the-use-of-the-center-margin-model-to-displace-the-left-right-model) is short and goes straight at your question.
- [The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis) is the clearest case that originary thinking could be taken up across the spectrum, and for what it asks of every political tendency.

**An exercise:** take your own strongest political conviction and imagine the kind of authority that could actually carry it out in a form you'd recognise. Katz's wager is that such an authority would have to be so capable that it would no longer need your demand. Does that hold for your example?

rows.q: What does deferral mean? Explain it like I'm fifteen.
rows.a:
## The short version

To **defer** something means to hold off on it without cancelling it. In Center Study, deferral is the basic human move: when people all want the same thing and are about to fight over it, someone holds back. Holding back turns grabbing into something else, a sign, and the fight is put off. Katz and Gans think this is how language, and humans, began.

## The story it comes from

Center Study starts from an imagined first scene, which it calls the **originary scene**. Picture a group of early hominids around a piece of food. Normally the strongest eats first. This time everyone wants it at once, because each one wants it more when they see the others wanting it. Everyone reaches, and a brawl is seconds away.

Then one of them pauses. His grabbing hand stops halfway and becomes more like pointing. In Katz's retelling, some member of the group "hesitates, presumably out of something like terror (“anxiety” would not be quite right here), is seen by others to hesitate, and is imitated by others" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-5)). Now everyone is pointing at the food instead of grabbing it. That half-grab, half-point is the first sign, the first word. It works because it puts the fight off, and nobody has to win it.

## Why "defer" and not "prevent" or "solve"

Katz insists on this word over its near-synonyms, and the reasons are what make the idea interesting.

1. **You never know what you prevented.** Katz writes that "no one could know that violence has been deferred, because no one can know what would have happened without the sign of deferral. Maybe it just would have been a harmless little skirmish" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-8)). You're always inside the moment, never watching from outside with the answer key.

2. **It doesn't fix the problem forever. It buys room.** "Instead of preventing imminent destruction, we have really done no more than make it 'imminently imminent,' and that imminence of imminence gives us a little space within which to work" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4)). The danger is still there, but now there's time to think, talk, share and build.

3. **It never ends.** Unlike "prevent" or "desist," "'deferral' posits no endpoint. As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). Every generation has to do it again.

4. **It's different from just being scared of each other.** That's deterrence. "When we deter, we just watch each other; when we defer, we allow one another to proceed, to 're-imagine' the shared object of desire in creative ways" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-2)). Deferral lets people share fairly, which is more than a standoff.

## It isn't just "waiting longer"

A common misunderstanding is that more deferral means more self-denial. Katz uses a family dinner: the kids shouldn't grab food out of the oven, but "sitting and waiting until 7 doesn’t make them more civilized or moral than if they get served at 6. What is important is that the meal is properly 'framed'" ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-6)). The frame means everyone at the table, saying grace, not reaching across. Deferral mostly doesn't feel like hunger. "The effect is of a new world opening up" ([same essay](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-1)): a rival turns into someone you're eating with.

## Where you already see it

Small, everyday signs keep the original move going. Saying "excuse me" when you nearly bump into someone puts off a tiny, possible conflict. It also keeps alive a whole habit of politeness that other people built before you ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-10)). That second part matters: "any act of deferral leaves behind it a sign, which can be repeated by someone other than myself" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-6)). Manners, rules of games and courts of law are all stored-up deferral. Katz says outright that "the juridical entails deferring the vendetta" ([Style](/post/style-markers-and-measurements-of-deferral#p-5)). You go to court so you don't have to get revenge yourself.

**Try it on your own life.** Two friends both want the last slice of pizza. One of you says "dibs," or "let's split it," or makes a joke. That's a sign that stops the grab. If "dibs" becomes the rule in your friend group, you've built a small institution of deferral that others can now repeat without inventing it again. And notice that nobody can prove a fight would have happened. That's exactly Katz's point.

(Background, not from the archive: Gans took the word partly from the philosopher Derrida's *différance*, which mixes "differ" and "defer." Katz mentions this in [Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-9).)

## Read next

- **[Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence)**. It's short and spoken, and it's the clearest walk through why this word and not another.
- **[The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral)**. It answers the obvious objection, "can't you defer too much?", and has the dinner-table example.

**A small exercise:** for one day, notice three moments where someone *almost* did the obvious thing (grabbed, snapped back, cut in line) and did something else instead. For each one, ask what sign they used, and whether it was something they made up or something they'd learned from others.

rows.q: Why should I believe a story about the origin of language that nobody witnessed?
rows.a:
## The short answer

You shouldn't *believe* it, at least not in the way you believe a news report or a creed. Katz is blunt about this. GA "can feel like one is being asked to 'believe in' something," he writes, but "I don't see it as a question of 'belief' (which I don't 'believe' in), but it does, perhaps, require a willingness to live or think in a kind of 'suspense'" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)).

What you are offered is a *hypothesis*. The real question is what kind of claim it is and how such a claim gets judged.

## Why nobody could have witnessed it, and why that's not the objection it seems

For the hypothesis, the first sign was not added to an already existing community. The sign, the community and the human come into being together. So there was no one positioned to watch it happen. There is a further point. In the lecture on deferral Katz asks when any scene counts as "closed," and answers that every account of closure is made "as if these events... were witnessed. But from where? Only from upon another scene" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-11)). That holds for every event, not only the first. We never stand outside a scene to certify what happened there. We always reconstruct it from a later scene with signs that the first scene made possible. A "witness" to the origin of language would already need language.

That is also why, as Katz notes, the social sciences have avoided origins since the French Academy banned the topic in 1866. Origin talk "marks one as introducing theology into rational discussions" ([Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin#p-1)). His reply is not that the origin can be proven. It is this: "any positing of an origin must be hypothetical" ([Lecture 1](/post/origin#p-8)). The relevant question is which hypothesis is better.

## How the hypothesis is actually judged

**1. It answers a real question that other accounts dodge.** Human language is not a more complex animal signal. Its signs are conventional. That produces what Katz calls "the properly paradoxical question of how conventions could have been formed without the means of forming conventions" ([Addressing an Objection](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-26)). Rousseau already saw this: you seem to need an agreement in order to make the first agreement. A purely gradual, genetic story never says at what point a signal became something two people can affirm to be *the same* sign. Katz's test case is simple: "If you tell someone you see the same thing as they do, what makes that possible... and, can any of this pertain to anything any other species does?" ([Addressing an Objection](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-27)). If that difference is real, then "the singularity of language means it must have emerged in an event" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)).

**2. It starts from premises you can check today.** The hypothesis assumes almost nothing. Humans are imitative (watch any child). Imitation leads to rivalry over the same object. A rivalry like that can end in only two ways: "one defeats the other; the two share the desired object" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)). Only the second would need to be remembered: "If we've found a way to share something, we need to remind ourselves of it every time we do so; the superior strength of one member of the group over another doesn't need to be commemorated" (ibid., [p-3](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-3)). The same point sets it apart from Girard's version, where a victim is killed at the origin: "Animals kill their own kind without it changing their behavior or form of organization in the slightest" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38)). An event becomes meaningful only if a sign marks it. So the scene is minimal. Some members converge on a desired object, one hesitates, the hesitation is imitated, and the grasping gesture is converted into a pointing one, the "gesture of aborted appropriation."

**3. Minimality is the standard.** "The more minimally, punctually and singularly any hypothesis can account for these successive hypotheses, the better the hypothesis" ([Lecture 1](/post/origin#p-9)). This is not proof. It is the criterion for preferring one origin story to another, and every account of human beginnings is an origin story, including the ones that call themselves gradualist.

**4. It is open to challenge.** Katz invites rivals: "if you have a better account, one that can get us from a hominid that is not yet human, but becomes human," one that transforms the group together and accounts for language, "let's, by all means, hear it" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-9)).

## What Katz concedes

He doesn't pretend the claim is testable in the ordinary sense. It is "an unfalsifiable claim (we could obviously never obtain evidence of the event in which language was invented/discovered)" that is nonetheless "to be taken literally and seriously—but we can also see it as an answer to a very basic, inevitable question—why do words 'mean'?" ([Language, the Deepest and Most Reliable Tradition](/post/language-the-deepest-and-most-reliable-tradition#p-15)). He also takes seriously the objection that a mimetic crisis strong enough to break the animal pecking order would scatter the group before any shared focus could form. His answer is that this makes the scene "highly unlikely, not that it was impossible" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-4)). Gans himself always called the event almost miraculous. On this view the origin is contingent: it may have failed many times and needed to succeed only once. Even after every gap is filled with evolutionary detail, Katz insists, "we need the event" ([Addressing an Objection](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-30)).

## Where the evidence actually lives

There is a sense in which you *can* check the hypothesis, though not by digging. Katz's strongest claim is that the originary scene "has never been 'closed,' only sustained and suspended, and that the very next thing you say will be version of the originary gesture that keeps the event in play or a premature attempt at appropriation that will collapse the scene" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-8)). The hypothesis earns its keep if it lets you see present scenes more clearly.

Take your own question. You asked why you should believe something, and you trusted that "believe" would mean the same thing to me as to you. That sameness wasn't given by your vocal cords or mine. It is a convention we both keep up without either of us having founded it. The hypothesis is an account of how anything could ever be "the same" between two people in this way. If it makes that ordinary fact less mysterious than its rivals do, that is the kind of support it can have. Testimony from a witness could not supply it.

(From outside the archive: physicists accept hypotheses about the early universe that nobody observed, on the strength of what those hypotheses explain about the present. The parallel is loose, since the GA scene can't produce new measurements, but the principle that unwitnessed origins are judged by present explanatory power is not peculiar to GA.)

## What to read next

- [Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin) is the shortest statement of why origin-thinking is unavoidable and how competing origin hypotheses are judged.
- [Addressing an Objection to the Originary Hypothesis](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis) shows Katz answering a serious scientific critique point by point, which is the best way to see how the hypothesis holds up under pressure.

**An exercise:** Think of the last time two people (or two dogs) wanted the same thing at the same moment. List what actually stopped it from becoming a fight. Then ask which of those things a non-human animal could have done, and which required a sign that both parties had to agree was *the same* sign. That boundary is where the hypothesis does its work.

rows.q: What is the center? Everyone here keeps saying it.
rows.a:
## The short answer

The center is whatever holds a group's shared attention. Several people look at it together, know they are looking at it together, and arrange themselves around it. Katz gives the minimal definition in *Anthropomorphics*: "Whatever can invoke and be referenced by an ostensive sign: the center is both cause and product of the sign—as cause it subsists beyond any particular reference, and as product it is continually renewed" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-1)). An "ostensive sign" is simply a pointing: *that*, *look*. The longer answer explains why so much hangs on this.

## Where it comes from: the originary scene

Center Study starts from Eric Gans's hypothesis about the origin of language. Humans are intensely imitative, and imitation turns into rivalry: I want what you want because you want it. Picture a group of proto-humans closing in on a single desirable object, such as a fresh kill. Mimetic desire overrides the old animal pecking order, and everyone moves toward it at once. Someone hesitates. His grasping turns into a gesture that only points. The others imitate the pointing instead of the grab. That aborted grab is the first sign.

What it creates is a center. Each participant now experiences the object as the thing that held everyone back, as if it had issued a command. Katz puts it this way: "The creation of the human is mediated by the creation of the sacred center as the creator of the human" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)). So the center is not a thing people later decided to honour. It comes into being together with the sign and the community, as the point toward which everyone turns.

## What a center does

The lecture on the center makes this concrete through Michael Tomasello's finding that great apes don't point. "Two chimps can't look at something together, and let each other know that they're doing so." An object, in the human sense, is "something we can “let be” and look at together" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-2)). Once there is a center, there is also a margin, the ring of people around it, and each sees the others through it: "the center creates the margin, so you’re looking at others on the margin as held by the center, just as you are" ([#p-5](/post/the-center#p-5)).

This is why Katz says you cannot speak at all without one: "To assume an interlocutor can understand anything I say, to assume he even knows that I’m talking to him, is to assume a shared center" ([Linguistically Constructed Empires within Empires](/post/linguistically-constructed-empires-within-empires#p-13)).

## Two senses: the center and centrality

This distinction is where newcomers usually get lost. Katz uses "center" in two linked ways.

1. **Any momentary center.** "The center" is "always what draws your attention right here and now" ([The Holding and the Held Center](/post/the-holding-and-the-held-center-beyond-disagreement#p-1)): the topic of a conversation, the ball in a game, the speaker at a podium.
2. **The social center.** Behind every passing center there is a lasting one that keeps the whole order together. "So, there’s the center, and there’s centrality, or, as I’ve called it, the occupied center and the signifying center. And the first thing the center tells or commands us is to sustain centrality" ([Lecture 4](/post/the-center#p-6)).

The *occupied* center is the person or office actually sitting there. Historically this began when "some individual “seiz[ed]” the center—what the anthropologists call the Big Man" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-16)), and from him descend chiefs, kings, presidents and bosses. The *signifying* center is what the occupant is answerable to, the meaning and command that outlast any particular occupant. Much of Katz's later work on succession, law and money is about how these two can be kept in line with each other.

This is also where Katz departs from Gans. Of the claim "There’s always a center" he adds "(but I’m not sure whether the founder of GA would agree)" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-10)). Holding that claim firmly, including in politics, is part of what makes Center Study a distinct project.

## Applying it

Take a meeting where everyone insists there is no boss. Katz's point is that a center forms anyway: "someone takes the initiative, someone sets the tone, someone starts off in a new direction, and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). Pretending otherwise doesn't remove the center. It only means nobody is accountable for occupying it. Hence his political reorientation: "discussions of how to clarify our relations to the center are going to be far more promising than discussions over how to liberate ourselves from it" ([#p-19](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-19)).

Your own question is an example. The word "center" has itself become a center for the people around you. It draws everyone's attention, everyone keeps pointing at it, and you have just stepped up to ask what it is. That is a small version of the originary scene.

## What to read next

- [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center): short and spoken, and the best single introduction. It moves from Tomasello to the Big Man to what "the command of the center" means today.
- [The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center), from *Anthropomorphics*. It shows how the center was given a personality, so to speak, before humans were, and how leadership grows out of deferral.

**An exercise:** pick a recent conversation or meeting. What was at its center? Who, if anyone, occupied it? What would have collapsed if no one had?
