rows.q: I read one of the Substack essays and understood almost nothing. Is that normal, and what should I read first?
rows.a:
Yes, that's normal, and it isn't only you. Katz writes the recent Substack essays in a deliberately compressed idiom, and he says so. He keeps "developing a specialized vocabulary, or idiom, for center studies, even if it impedes popularization (never much of a possibility, anyway)—it enhances compressibility" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-9)). Elsewhere he describes the ideal utterance as one "utterly unintelligible to those not conversant in your idiom and transparent to those who are" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-7)). Feeling lost on a first encounter is part of the design.

## Why it happens

Each late essay sits on top of years of earlier posts. A phrase like "the outside spread," "singularized succession in perpetuity," "learncoin," or "the imperative gap" stands in for an argument made somewhere else. In his writing on academic discourse, Katz explains why compressed prose is hard for newcomers: the text works as "an archive of conversations" ([From Novice to Apprentice](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-30)), and if you weren't part of those conversations the phrases look like noise. He also suggests a better response than "this is unclear." It is more useful to recognise that you are looking at "signs here of an unfamiliar disciplinary space" ([The Big Scene…](/post/the-big-scene-is-the-anthropological-basis-of-anarchist-ontology-gablog#p-18)).

The foundation underneath all of it is small. "The originary hypothesis is easily summed up in a couple of paragraphs, at most, and all it really assumes is that human beings are mimetic creatures" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)). In plain terms the argument runs like this:

- We learn to want things by imitating others.
- Imitation therefore drives us toward the same object, which leads to rivalry and the threat of violence.
- In the first human event, a grasping gesture toward a shared object turned into a pointing gesture, an "aborted appropriation." Everyone repeated it, and violence was deferred.
- That gesture was the first sign. The object it pointed to became the center: what holds a group's attention and keeps them apart from one another.

Everything else Katz writes is about what that center becomes over time, from ritual to kings to money, law and technology. In the same essay he admits that his own elaboration of the hypothesis "is 'complex' and poses some difficulties" ([p-11](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-11)). So the difficulty is in the building on top, not in the foundation.

## What to read, in order

1. **The five lectures.** They are short, spoken, and introduce one concept each: [Origin](/post/origin), [Mimetic](/post/mimetic), [Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence), [The Center](/post/the-center), [The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf). If you read only one, read *The Center*, because almost every later term depends on it.
2. **[The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself)** and **[The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis).** These are Katz stepping back to say what the hypothesis is and what it can do, including for politics.
3. **Two chapters from *Anthropomorphics*:** [Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis) gives the scene in full, and [A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social) shows how ostensive, imperative and declarative speech develop from it. That grammar is the engine behind most of the later vocabulary.
4. **Then back to the Substack.** Start with an essay that reflects on the idiom itself, such as [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) or [Compression](/post/compression), before the ones on money, law and governance.

## How to read

Katz gives advice on reading that fits here. You learn more by "entering, even or especially naively, into the 'logic' of a compelling text and taking it on as an identity" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-3)) than by holding it at a critical distance. In practice: don't stop to look up every term. Pick one strange phrase, assume it means something exact, and follow it through the essay.

If you tell me which essay you read, I can take it apart with you and point to where each of its key terms was first worked out. Or try a small exercise after the *Center* lecture: write two sentences that use his phrase "the occupied center and the signifying center" in your own words, and I'll tell you whether you've got it.

rows.q: What does Katz say about climate change?
rows.a:
Katz has no sustained treatment of climate change. It turns up in passing, half a dozen times, usually in scare quotes and always as an example of something else. Those remarks are consistent with each other, though, and they show clearly how Center Study handles a political question like this one: it sets aside the question of who is right about the science and asks what the issue does to power, responsibility and the center.

## 1. He brackets the science and keeps a skeptical distance

Katz never argues the physics. His tone is skeptical: he writes of "the climate changers," of "the supposed problem," of "climate change" in quotation marks. When he reviews a book written for a climate-crisis series, he lets the question drop: "Whatever one's politics and whatever one's views of inequality, social justice, or the question of climate change," the real issue is a global economy run by megacorporations "beholden to no sovereign power" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-32)). Climate is not what he thinks the argument is about.

## 2. The real interest: climate as a pretext for planetary design

His most interesting remark comes in his reading of Benjamin Bratton's *The Stack*. For Bratton, Katz writes, what "most fascinates in ecology is the pretext it provides for design projects that would match the scope of the supposed problem." Katz then turns this around:

> "if, rather than obsessing over trying to minimize (and even shrink) the amount of carbon in the environment, we were to say, 'well, why don't we just accept that all the things the climate changers say is going to happen—melting polar caps, flooded coastlines, super-storms and the rest—will happen and redesign our human habitat in response,' we'd have an 'absolutist' or 'autocratic' project precisely parallel to Bratton's in scope, ambition, and disregard for present political pieties." ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-2))

Katz calls the work of building and arranging the settings people act in *scenic design*, and climate politics is scenic design at the largest scale. Discussing Bratton's "Anthropocene," he agrees: "our stage is now the planet, and we will be designing it, one way or another" ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-29)). What he disputes is who does the designing, and on whose terms.

## 3. The test of power and responsibility

A second remark applies Katz's standard method. He asks what kind of authority could actually do what a political demand asks, in the way the demand imagines it being done. (Elsewhere he calls this the *central imaginary* or *sovereign imaginary*.)

> "The climate changers claim they want to save the planet—what kind of power, social and technological, would have to be composed so as to meet that responsibility? And once it was composed, of course, it might find it has other things to do than pump carbon out of the atmosphere." ([Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user#p-14))

This is the point of the whole move. Take the demand seriously and you are imagining a concentration of power far beyond anything liberal democracy permits. A power of that kind would not simply carry out the demand. It would have its own center and its own priorities. So climate politics turns out to be a disguised argument about sovereignty, carried on by people who claim to reject sovereignty.

## 4. Two warnings

**Handling humans as information.** In the lecture on the sign, Katz warns that once human sign use is treated as just another flow of information, "it much easier to 'handle' and to justify handling humans in any 'Great Reset' one has in mind; for example, vast projects of carbon minimization and extraction, or of social control and immunology" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-9)). His defense is not an appeal to human dignity. It is the claim that human language cannot be reduced to information.

**Enforced orthodoxy.** In an earlier GABlog piece he lists Democratic politicians "looking into suing oil companies and others" for dissenting on climate among the cases where claims "that might be proven more or less true—must be denounced as a priori thought crimes" ([The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies](/post/the-offspring-of-the-progenitor-of-lies#p-7)). Here climate becomes another site of victimary enforcement.

## 5. Climate as one input to the central intelligence

In his later thinking about data and algorithmic governance, he treats climate more calmly. He expects liberals to "keep their fingers on the scale... if they can ever get around to using AI for economic planning around, e.g., 'climate change'" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-81)). His own position is pluralist about inputs: "We want cities to be safer, people to be healthier, children to be more intelligent, air and water to be cleaner," recognizing "there will always be more than one way to approximate these goals" ([#p-83](/post/event-origin-center#p-83)). Then: "The left should be free to input its own obsessions," alongside data on ethnic distribution and family formation ([#p-84](/post/event-origin-center#p-84)). Here climate stops being a moral emergency and becomes one source of data among many for a center that has to weigh them.

## A GA background, marked as Gans's

The archive also reposts a Gans Chronicle (this is Gans's text, not Katz's) that reads the global-warming debate as a Rorschach test. "The victimary thinker would find it painful to believe that if climate change is occurring, we are not significantly to blame," because "to claim all responsibility is to presuppose one's own omnipotence; to affirm one's guilt is to take charge of causality" ([Ending White Guilt](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-3), [#p-4](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-4)). Katz's approach builds on this suspicion of guilt-as-omnipotence. He moves it, though, from psychology to power: what interests him is less what the guilty party feels than what kind of center the demand implies.

## Try it yourself

Take a concrete climate demand, say "net zero by 2050," and run Katz's test. What chain of command would have to exist for it to be achieved in a form its advocates would accept as success? And what else would such a power be likely to decide to do, once it existed?

**Read next:** [The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city), where Katz engages most directly with planetary-scale design and the Anthropocene. Then [Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center), especially its closing sections on feeding data to algorithmic governance and on matching power to responsibility.

rows.q: What does Katz think about China's hukou household registration system?
rows.a:
Katz doesn't write about the hukou system anywhere in the archive I was shown. The closest he comes is China's **social credit system**, which he discusses in one post. So below I first set out what he says there, and then show how his concepts would bear on household registration. That second part is my application, not something he wrote.

## What Katz says about China directly

In [Autocracy Stalks the End of History](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history) (2017), Katz responds to Eric Gans's comparison of Chinese "autocracy" with American "victimocracy." He takes the social credit system as a near-inevitability rather than an aberration: "Pretty much any autocratic (which is pretty much a synonym for “absolutist”) system with access to advanced electronic technology would ultimately end up employing some version of China’s social credit system" ([p-24](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history#p-24)).

He does not treat it as an automatic machine. The decisive point is who sets the terms: "the state, the autocrat, would have to determine what criteria should guide the creation of the algorithms" ([p-28](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history#p-28)). He also treats the system as something that learns. If the state finds its point system "makes a large portion of the population economically unviable (by, say, determining that they can’t use banks or public transportation, or would find it impossible to rent a home or find a mate), clearly the algorithms would have to be recalculated" ([p-29](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history#p-29)). He closes by suggesting that "The Chinese should really find a way to transition from Communism to Confucianism, and maybe we should as well" ([p-30](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history#p-30)).

So his attitude toward Chinese registration and rating apparatus is not liberal alarm. His question is whether such an apparatus is a coherent instrument of a secure center, and whether it is attentive to its own failures.

## What hukou is (from outside the archive)

The following is general background, not Katz. Hukou registers each person to a household and a locality, usually inherited. Access to schooling, health care, housing and pensions has historically depended on where you are registered. The result is a large "floating population": people who work in the cities where they live but who belong, administratively, to villages they may barely know.

## How Katz's concepts would read it

**Registration as naming.** For Katz, the sovereign is the "onomastician-in-chief." Naming is how the center incorporates people and institutions into an order: "Saturating the world with names saturates the world with sovereignty" ([Sovereign as Onomastician-in-Chief, p-14](/post/sovereign-as-onomastician-in-chief#p-14)). He sets absolutism against liberalism on exactly this point: "As opposed to the abstractive process of liberalism, absolutism would involve a concentrative process—placing everyone within orders in which their responsibilities are made clear" ([p-6](/post/sovereign-as-onomastician-in-chief#p-6)). A household register is about as literal a version of naming-into-place as one could find. In his lecture on the sign, Katz contrasts the thin records of an 11th-century parish ("births, deaths, marriages, at most") with modernity, where "each social “particle” has multiple and changing relations to the center" ([Lecture 5: The Sign, p-17](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-17)). Hukou can be read as an attempt to hold the older "gradation of names marking embedded relationships" in place inside a fully modern economy.

**Abstraction and embedment.** This is where the system's internal tension shows up in Katz's terms. Industrialization requires abstracting people from where they are embedded; rural labor has to move to the factories. Katz does not side with the traditionalist here: "the possibility of rejecting abstraction disappeared with the rise of divine kingship a few millennia ago" ([Center and Distribution, p-13](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-13)). But he distinguishes kinds of abstraction. Capitalist abstraction is "pulverizing." The kind "consistent with secure central authority" would "make ever finer distinctions between skills, competencies and forms of authority," so that "abstraction carries with it its own form of re-embedment" ([p-15](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-15)). On that test, the migrant worker is abstracted as labor but re-embedded nowhere: named to one place and working in another.

**Power and responsibility.** Katz's simplest moral test is commensurability: "It is immoral to give someone responsibility for doing something without giving them the power to do it" ([Event, Origin, Center, p-61](/post/event-origin-center#p-61)). A registration regime that assigns people work in a city without the corresponding access there would fail this test, not because it is "unequal," but because it produces a mismatch. In the Thirdness writings he also says that orders must work to "prevent the emergence of “untabernacled” populations outside of the terms of belonging that could be leveraged by other sovereigns" ([Learncoin, p-13](/post/learncoin#p-13)). A large floating population is a plausible candidate for such a group.

**The household as the unit.** The part of hukou Katz might find most congenial is that it treats the household, not the individual, as the basic unit. In [Reconstituting Kinship](/post/reconstituting-kinship) he argues for distributing responsibility back to family networks. He even proposes that admission, employment and marriageability "must be made to depend on whether you have drug addicts, criminals, or even unemployed in your extended family" ([p-6](/post/reconstituting-kinship#p-6)). He imagines this working through voluntary "affinity groups" and better data, which is quite different from an inherited, place-bound administrative status. Still, the instinct points the same way: kinship as a substructure of governance rather than an obstacle to it.

## The likely verdict, held loosely

Katz's frame would not condemn hukou for restricting free movement; that is a liberal objection he rejects. Instead he would ask three questions. Does it tie people to the center through clear names and responsibilities? Does it re-embed those it uproots? Does the state treat its failures, such as the floating population, as data to recalculate on, the way he says a social credit system must? My hunch is that he would see in hukou the right intuition (people should be registered somewhere, through households) attached to a design that leaves a large class with responsibilities but without the matching standing. That remains my extrapolation.

**To read next:** [Autocracy Stalks the End of History](/post/autocracy-stalks-the-end-of-history), his only sustained discussion of Chinese governance. Then [Reconstituting Kinship](/post/reconstituting-kinship), for the household and family as units of responsibility.

**A question to take further:** Katz says a registration or rating system must be "recalculated" when it makes people unviable. What would count as evidence, from inside the system rather than from liberal critics, that hukou has reached that point?

rows.q: What is Center Study's position on abortion?
rows.a:
The short answer is that Katz gives one explicit verdict on abortion, and it cuts against both sides. Most of what the archive says on the subject, though, is not a verdict. It uses the abortion debate to show how political "positions" are built, and what they quietly assume about power.

## The one explicit verdict

The clearest statement is in a 2019 GABlog post:

> "Abortion is wrong, as we can see from the somewhat demonic enthusiasm with which its promoters come to defend it against criticism; but it's not wrong in the way the pro-lifers say." ([From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics#p-17))

Both halves matter. The reason for calling abortion wrong is itself diagnostic. He doesn't argue from fetal personhood or natural law. He points to the *manner* in which its promoters defend it, an enthusiasm that exceeds any reasonable defence of a regrettable necessity. That is a reading of desire and resentment, the kind of reading Center Study does everywhere.

The second half is just as firm. The pro-life framing is also faulty, and he says exactly how.

## Where each side centralizes violently

Katz asks the question he asks of any conflict:

> "Where do we see violent centralizing here: that is, where do the respective sides each imagine its own super-sovereign, the foundation of its discipline of naming, predicated upon sacrificial markings?" ([From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics#p-16))

"Violent centralizing" means converging on someone as a target, the scapegoat structure that every sign exists to defer. A "super-sovereign" is a higher authority, such as Rights, Nature or the People, that one invokes to override whoever actually governs. Each side, Katz argues, has to name its object in a way that marks a victim. The pro-choice side has to reduce the embryo to "a 'set of tissues,' or 'tumor,'" which "even in purely biological terms" it is not. The pro-life side, if it is consistent, has to treat "a pregnant woman who negligently falls down, thereby causing a miscarriage" as guilty of manslaughter. Pro-lifers sense this, and that is why they claim only doctors would be punished, a claim Katz calls "absurd" (same paragraph).

What drives both sides into these markings is the language of rights:

> "Extract 'rights' from the equation and you eliminate the mobilization of the state against one's enemies in the guise of self-protection" ([From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics#p-17))

Every rights claim imagines a state ready to act against specific people. The abortion war is two factions, each trying to aim the state at the other.

## The deeper move: what you're really asking for

The more important part of the archive's treatment is a thought experiment that Katz returns to again and again, the *central imaginary*:

> "One side demands that the state protect the rights of the unborn; the other side demands it protect the rights of women to abort. What both sides agree on is that the state should be able do whatever the one making the demand would want: a state incapable of enforcing laws against abortion would also be incapable of enforcing laws allowing abortion." ([The End of Secular Thinking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-end-of-secular-thinking#p-28))

Being "against abortion" already presupposes a full chain of command: a law, penalties, "an executive who will give orders to law enforcement to, e.g., enter buildings where abortions have been suspected of being performed" ([Sovereignty, Nomos and Parrhesia](/post/sovereignty-nomos-and-parrhesia#p-8)). Put more sharply: "To express an opinion is to fantasize oneself the ventriloquist of central power" ([Ancestries and Meta-Sovereignty](/post/ancestries-and-meta-sovereignty#p-12)).

So Katz redirects attention away from the content of the demand and toward the kind of authority that could actually meet it. Once you imagine that authority concretely, you notice that a power able to do what you want "wouldn't have to and might have something very different in mind." Your demand turns out to be, in effect, a request for a center that answers to no one's demands. This is why the neoabsolutist project he describes is to keep "making demands increasingly subordinate to commands" ([From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics#p-1)).

## Applying it

Suppose you are pro-life and want to think this through Center Study's way. The first step is not to sharpen your arguments about personhood. Ask three questions instead.

- Which actual institutions (courts, medical boards, families, churches) would have to change for abortion to become rare?
- Who would be responsible for that change, and with what powers?
- Can your goal be pursued without naming either the woman or the embryo as the sacrificial target?

Answering these turns a demand ("ban it!") into what Katz calls naming practices "articulated into more systemic practices" ([From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics#p-17)). This is work done inside an order, not a war waged on the other side. The same discipline applies to a pro-choice reader. What would the state have to keep doing, indefinitely and against whom, to guarantee what you're asking for?

## What the archive doesn't say

Katz doesn't take up the details people usually mean by "a position": gestational limits, exceptions, legal regimes. Abortion appears mostly as a worked example of how rights discourse and the central imaginary operate. I won't fill that gap on his behalf. In an older and more playful essay, he even imagines the most extreme factions on each side agreeing on a shared rule for placing their propaganda side by side, "each gambling that being placed next to the extremism of the other will strengthen their own position" ([Oupopo](/post/oupopo-a-preliminary-political-combinatorial#p-9)). That is an exercise in political combinatorics, not a policy.

## Where to read next

- [From Metapolitics to Politics](/post/from-metapolitics-to-politics) is the fullest treatment. Abortion appears here inside the larger argument about demands, commands and naming.
- [The End of Secular Thinking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-end-of-secular-thinking), the chapter of *Anthropomorphics*, develops the central imaginary and why "we'd replace our demands with better ways of following commands."

A question to take further: pick any issue you care about and write out, concretely, the chain of command that would have to exist for your preferred outcome to happen *in the way you want it*. Where does the chain break, and who would have to be marked as the obstacle?

rows.q: What does Center Study say about veganism and animal rights?
rows.a:
Katz never treats veganism or animal rights as a topic of its own. Veganism comes up once in the archive, in passing, and animal rights not at all. Several central parts of the thinking still bear on the question, so here is what the archive supports and where it runs out.

## The one passage: veganism and civilization's "oblivion"

The direct reference is in [Civilization, Violence, Oblivion](/post/civilization-violence-oblivion). Katz's argument there is about civilization, and he uses our relation to animals as his main analogy for how civilization works.

Civilization, he argues, creates "violence free zones" by pushing violence out of sight, and it then depends on our forgetting what makes those zones possible. Eating meat is his model for that forgetting:

> "just as we eat our meals, and can only eat our meals, without giving any thought to millions of penned up, systematically slaughtered, chopped up, chemically preserved, shipped, packaged, etc., animals, we freely interact in our violence free zones on the condition that rather massive forms of violence lie in wait for those who cross certain boundaries" ([Civilization, Violence, Oblivion](/post/civilization-violence-oblivion#p-5))

He calls this state "oblivion," and he treats it as real and as unavoidable. It is not hypocrisy to be exposed. In his account veganism is what happens when that oblivion breaks for a particular person about a particular kind of violence. He uses it as a point of comparison for a much harder renunciation he actually cares about, which is giving up "the invocation of the state on one's side in conflicts with others" ([p-11](/post/civilization-violence-oblivion#p-11)):

> "It would be far more difficult than the veganism that results for many from the shattering of our oblivion regarding our uses of animals." ([p-12](/post/civilization-violence-oblivion#p-12))

In Center Study's terms, then, veganism is an intelligible act of deferral. It refuses one kind of appropriation once the violence behind it has been seen. Katz neither endorses nor rejects it. He treats it as a small, comparatively easy example of what happens when someone stops looking away.

## The animal at the origin

To see why the animal matters to Center Study, go back to the originary scene. The central object around which the first humans gathered, and which they held back from grabbing, was most plausibly a food animal. In the early communities that followed, the center belonged to animals before it belonged to people:

> "The very earliest occupants of the center would be the transfigured forms of the animals placed at the center for ritual purposes and consumption. These beings are the progenitors, guardians, and nemeses of the community." ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-1))

Katz describes the ritual relation as an *imperative exchange*. The community receives from the center and gives back to it:

> "A tribe hunts deer, so their deity is the deer-god—in killing the "token" deer, the group brings the kill to the ritual center, returns some of it to the deer-god (the "type" deer) and, more generally, treats the meal with honor and respect, as the gift that it is." ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-1))

He also suggests that the sign may have spread beyond ritual through hunting and tracking, and that this is how humans "developed forms of kinship with animals, who also follow and leave trails" ([Trails of Liminal Succession](/post/trails-of-liminal-succession#p-3)).

So the originary relation to the animal was neither indifference nor a rights claim. It was sacred indebtedness. The animal is eaten, and the eating is received as a gift and answered with ritual return. Here is my own extrapolation, not something Katz says: modern industrial meat-eating is the extreme case of oblivion, a consumption that no longer marks any debt at all. The modern vegan and the ancient hunter honoring the deer-god are both responding to that debt, though in opposite ways.

## Why "animal rights" is not the Center Study frame

On rights in general Katz is explicit and critical. Rights talk denies that there is a center while depending on one:

> "If rights need to be defended, they need to be defended against someone. When we posit a right, or advocate for one, then, we are imagining a state willing and ready to act against specific people assumed to be potential violators of that right." ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-3))

He does not apply this argument to animals. If you follow it through, though, "animal rights" is a demand that the sovereign act against farmers, labs, and eaters on behalf of beings who cannot themselves claim anything or answer for anything. Center Study would ask the question Katz asks about every right: what kind of sovereign could enforce this in a way you would recognize, and what would it have to become to do so? ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-396) works through this "central imaginary" using abortion as the example.) The animal-rights version of that question is my application.

## The boundary between human and animal

The other thread concerns what separates humans from animals, and here Katz holds firm. Animals signal, but "animals don't have a scene" ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-13)). Only humans take on the debt to the center: "humans will always be the only beings that have taken on this debt" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-11)). He warns that flattening human signification into animal communication is not harmless, because it "would make it much easier to "handle" and to justify handling humans" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-9)).

Arguments for animal rights usually work by shrinking that boundary, and the most influential philosophical versions (Peter Singer, for example, who is outside the archive) argue from shared capacities such as suffering. Center Study moves the other way. Our obligations toward animals, whatever they turn out to be, come from our relation to the center. They do not come from any equivalence between us and the animals.

## What to read next

- [Civilization, Violence, Oblivion](/post/civilization-violence-oblivion): short, and the only direct treatment. Read it with the meat analogy in mind.
- [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf): Katz's fullest critique of rights, which you can test against the animal case yourself.
- [The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center): on the animal ancestors who first occupied the center.

A question to take further: if the vegan's refusal is a deferral, what is it deferring, and toward which center? Is it an imperative exchange with the animal, a donation of resentment against the slaughterhouse to a state that might ban it, or something closer to the ancient acknowledgment of the meal as a gift?

rows.q: What is Katz's view of the energy used by cryptocurrency mining?
rows.a:
## The short answer: Katz doesn't take this up

Nowhere in the archive I was shown does Katz discuss the electricity that proof-of-work mining consumes, or the environmental argument about it. The question about mining as such has nothing in the texts to answer it, and I won't build a position and attribute it to him.

He does write about Bitcoin, and he borrows the word "mining" for his own purposes. Those two threads show how Center Study would reframe your question.

## What Katz says about Bitcoin

His assessments are brief and come from different years, and they don't fully agree with each other.

**Partly sympathetic.** In one essay he says that "if bitcoin and/or related forms of blockchain technology and economy can eliminate capitalist power by removing from state and banks alike debt issuing power, they are to be unequivocally supported" ([Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-10)). The attraction is that it could undercut what he and Colin Drumm call the "outside spread": the central bank as lender of last resort, whose control of credit constrains whoever occupies the political center.

**Skeptical that it is money at all.** In the essay he wrote with Zack Baker, Bitcoin "serves as a store of value, but must rely upon the measure of value established by other currencies (ultimately the dollar) and only very minimally serves as a medium of exchange" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-91)). Later he puts it more bluntly: "Bitcoin is not credit so it's not really money" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-18)).

**The deepest objection.** He takes from Samuel Chambers the view that money is credit, a relation between creditor and debtor, and concludes: "bitcoin is ultimately an attempt to cancel all debt to the center, and therefore will always be limited" ([Universal Translation Machine](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-17)).

This is the core of it. For Center Study, all of us owe a debt to the center from the start: on the originary scene, the shared object was received from the center, and every later exchange carries that obligation forward. A currency built to need no center is trying to escape a debt that, on Katz's account, can't be escaped. That is why he says alternative currencies should be grounded "not in precious metals or the inaccessibility of the blockchain but in sustainable social practices and rituals of succession" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-94)). He also separates Center Study from "contemporary embraces of capitalism, cryptocurrencies and AI technologies" by its "insistence on the irreducibility of the juridical, of judgment" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-22)).

## How he re-uses "mining"

Katz's own version of mining burns no electricity. He calls it **learncoin**, and you mine it when something is learned: "each time you saying 'this is the same' is iterated by others upon a scene that started off the same as itself, you have mined a learncoin" ([On Credit and the Idiom](/post/on-credit-and-the-idiom#p-21)). He calls writing idioms that others take up "protocols and mining—in the sense of authenticating an exchange in such a way as to generate currency for future exchanges" ([Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-4)).

The value is backed by shared attention and by teaching that passes from one generation to the next, not by expended work.

## Applying it: my extrapolation, not Katz's stated view

Here is how the frame might bear on the energy question. Treat this as an application of Katz's ideas, not something he wrote.

Proof of work burns energy to produce trust without a trusted party. Katz notes "contemporary attempts to create technologies that make exchanges trustless" as something his account of technology helps examine ([The Grammar of Technology](/post/the-grammar-of-technology-substack#p-7)). Seen this way, the electricity is the cost of replacing a center with computation. A Center Study critique would then ask less how many kilowatts are used and more what the expenditure is meant to defer, and whether it can defer it. If credit is always ultimately drawn on the center, then no quantity of hashing can stand in for orderly succession and a working system of courts.

I'd also guess Katz would be wary of the usual environmental framing of the debate. In another context he warns that treating humans as mere flows of information makes it easier to justify "vast projects of carbon minimization and extraction, or of social control" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-9)). That passage isn't about crypto, though, so don't treat it as his verdict on mining.

The facts about how much energy mining actually uses come from outside the archive, and Katz doesn't engage them.

## What to read next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf) is the fullest statement of why money is debt to the center, including the passages on Bitcoin and plural currencies.
- [Learncoin](/post/learncoin), read with [On Credit and the Idiom](/post/on-credit-and-the-idiom), shows Katz's alternative: currency backed by teaching and succession.

A question to try: if a proof-of-work network did reliably outlast several governments, would that count, in Katz's terms, as a new kind of center, with its own form of succession? Or would it still only be a store of value parasitic on the dollar?

rows.q: What does Katz say about the causes of the 2008 financial crisis?
rows.a:
Katz addressed 2008 directly once, as it happened, in a 2008 GABlog post, and kept returning to it afterward in a different vocabulary. The two layers are worth separating, because his thinking about money changed a great deal between them.

## The 2008 diagnosis: a "victimary" crisis

In "The Market and Disinterest," written during the meltdown, Katz calls himself "a rank amateur in economics" and says the causes are clear even though the cure is not. His thesis is blunt: "we actually have a victimary financial crisis that, according to some accounts at least, imperils the entire capitalist system" ([The Market and Disinterest](/post/the-market-and-disinterest#p-4)).

"Victimary" is Gans's term, taken up by Katz, for a politics in which claims made on behalf of a designated victim override every other standard. Katz traces a chain:

- activists, including Obama in his community-organizing years, charged banks with "redlining";
- laws then required banks to extend mortgages to minority borrowers;
- those mortgages were bundled into financial instruments;
- when the housing boom peaked and the loans went unpaid, the value built on them vanished, "Not even real money, of course, but promises of future money, which is now worthless because nobody believes the promises" ([p-5](/post/the-market-and-disinterest#p-5)).

His point is that victimary politics, which he had treated mainly as a source of local injustices like admissions or seniority, had now reached the foundations of the market itself.

From outside the archive: this account, which attributes the crisis largely to the Community Reinvestment Act and related mandates, was a common view on the right in 2008. Many economists dispute it and emphasize private-label securitization, leverage, and the ratings agencies. Katz presents it as settled. It isn't.

The post also moves from cause to remedy. Katz first supported the bailout and then reversed himself: "now, I say no" ([p-6](/post/the-market-and-disinterest#p-6)). Where he chooses to stand in defense of the market is "against every law and every employment of governmental power that gives anyone in the government any interest in who wins in the market place" ([p-10](/post/the-market-and-disinterest#p-10)). He reads the whole episode as a choice about the meaning of 9/11: either we refuse "victimary blackmail," or we keep paying it.

A related short post, [Basics](/post/basics#p-4), argues that the real "crisis" is only that lending money one doesn't have to people who can't repay will have to stop. "As far as I'm concerned, that's a blessing, not a crisis."

## 2010: the fear of contagion as the real danger

In "Originary Mistakenness, Defilement and Modernity," Katz reads the bailout through his concept of mistakenness. Every sign, every imitation, carries some error. The modern terror of error is a form of the archaic fear of *defilement*, the fear that one stain pollutes the whole community. In finance that fear becomes the "domino theory": "The real threats to the market system are the desperate attempts to avoid its breakdown." He adds that if the government had stayed out, people would soon have been "buying and selling, lending and borrowing" again, and that "Even if it does [all fall], something will get up again, and we can put our energies into that inevitably risky something" ([Originary Mistakenness](/post/anthropoetics-originary-mistakenness#p-40)).

On this view the cause of the crisis is not only bad loans. It is also a culture that cannot tolerate risk and therefore indemnifies itself, through White Guilt in politics and through bailouts in finance.

## Later: 2008 as a lesson about sovereignty and the "outside spread"

By the 2020s Katz no longer defends the free market in liberal terms, and 2008 shows up in a structural argument instead. Drawing on Colin Drumm, he holds that every market depends on an "outside spread," a lender of last resort who covers dealers when they cannot cover themselves, and that this lender in turn depends on sovereign power: "Markets cannot be sustained without this outside option, an outside option that itself, in the end, is a question of sovereignty, as we saw in 2008. Questions of money are ultimately questions of sovereignty" ([Options on Succession](/post/options-on-succession#p-7)).

On this account 2008 was not a deviation from a healthy market. It revealed what modern money had always been since the founding of the Bank of England: credit backed by the state, organized around the oscillation between the central bank and the state's power to enforce debt. That is the argument of [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf). He also notes that the new thinking about derivatives he draws on "has its origins in the 2008 financial crisis," and that "in times of crisis the entire social order is mobilized by the 'financial'" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-11)).

His objection to bailouts survives this shift, but its grounds change. The problem is no longer interference with markets. It is that the outside spread sits beyond the reach of law: "Larger and larger bailouts (and by whom, exactly?) of financial institutions that can't help but extend their credit lines precisely in expectancy of being bailed out really is unsustainable—we can't just do this every few decades" ([Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-16)). He also warns against "Bernie Sanders style idiocy" about "finance capital" in the same place. The issue is whether credit can be brought under juridical order, not whether bankers should be denounced.

## Putting it together

Read across the years, Katz's answer to "what caused 2008?" deepens:

1. **Proximate cause (2008):** victimary politics distorted lending.
2. **Cultural cause (2010):** a terror of contagion produced the bailout, which entrenched the alliance between regulators and big finance.
3. **Structural cause (later):** a monetary order in which credit hangs on an outside spread that only state power can back, and which therefore can't be held to account. Bailouts follow from that structure.

The third layer doesn't cancel the first two, but it reframes them. The victimary pressure and the bailout reflex both depend on a system in which, as he puts it elsewhere, it is "especially difficult to distinguish genuine innovations in enhancing the circulation of money … from ways of more efficiently implicating the government in matching the funds one has advanced" ([Reflections on Political Economy](/post/reflections-on-political-economy-from-firstness-to-thirdness#p-13)).

## What to read next

- [The Market and Disinterest](/post/the-market-and-disinterest), for the 2008 argument in full and in its original heat.
- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf), co-written with Zack Baker, for the later theory of money, the outside spread and the outside option that turns 2008 into a case study.

A question to take further: in 2008 Katz wanted the government to have no stake in who wins. Later he argues that money is always a product of the center. Can both be true? If not, what would a "disinterested" sovereign look like on the later view?

rows.q: Does Katz write about professional sport?
rows.a:
Not as a subject in its own right. There is no essay on leagues, athletes, fandom or the sports industry. But sport turns up again and again as an *example*, and he reaches for it at several key points in the thinking. Seeing why it keeps serving him is a good way into Center Study.

## A game as a small originary scene

The most basic use is in "The Terror of the Given". He borrows Bernard Suits's definition, that playing a game is "the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles", and reads it back onto the origin:

"playing a game is simulating the originary event, wherein the sign was created as an “unnecessary obstacle” (to simply taking the object) that everyone voluntarily accepts as a necessary mediation." ([The Terror of the Given](/post/the-terror-of-the-given#p-13))

The originary scene is Center Study's founding hypothesis: a group converging on a desired object defers grabbing it, and that held-back gesture becomes the first sign. On this reading, the rules of a game are deferral in miniature. Nothing stops you from picking up the ball in soccer except a sign everyone has agreed to honour.

In the same essay he uses basketball and soccer to explain incommensurability between idioms, meaning ways of speaking that only make sense inside a particular practice. Bouncing the ball downcourt is fine in one game and a violation in the other: "The exact same physical movement has radically opposed meanings in the two settings. That’s all that “incommensurability” means." ([p-10](/post/the-terror-of-the-given#p-10)). His point is that there is "no sport in itself". There are only particular games, just as there are only particular idioms.

## Pegging two sports together

In "Languaging Ordering" he builds a thought experiment, "obnoxiously American (mainly because I don’t get soccer)", around baseball and football ([p-12](/post/languaging-ordering#p-12)). He first finds likenesses between them: the touchdown and the home run both reset the field, and the quarterback and the pitcher both start the play from the center. Then he ties one to the other cybernetically, so that a measurable feature of one season changes the rules of the other. Take an above-average home-run rate early in the baseball season. Under the experiment, "football teams are allowed to throw only a below average number of passes for the first 30% of the season" ([p-13](/post/languaging-ordering#p-13)). Push this far enough and the two sports "would become a single “thing,”". If one town did it with its high-school teams, that town would become strikingly "idiomatic" ([p-14](/post/languaging-ordering#p-14)).

Sport is just the illustration here. The real target is institutions that ought to regulate each other and don't, such as intellectual-property law and actual creativity ([p-15](/post/languaging-ordering#p-15)).

## Closure, betting and the referee

Sport matters most in Katz's later work on Thirdness, his proposed prediction market on judgments. A sporting event is the clearest case of an event with official closure:

"only an event with an official closure can take bets—sporting events are the most obvious example, as the rules for determining winners and losers are transparent and unchanging." ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-11))

He also insists that this closure is constructed. The score is "an arbitrarily restricted representation of the event—an event, moreover, constructed precisely so as to produce a certain outcome in that “aspect.”" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-22)). So Thirdness bets on the judgment rather than the outcome: "betting on the referee’s calls rather than on the game … as long as you keep in mind that the refs are always making calls including all the calls they don’t make" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-14)). The referee is his figure for the juridical, the third party who keeps a dispute from turning into a vendetta.

## Succession, the draft, and the competitive West

- **Relief pitchers.** When he imagines rapid handoffs at the center, he compares them to "a succession of relief pitchers, sometimes each one facing only one batter". He adds that this "need not be seen as an indication of crisis; on the contrary, it can be a sign of deep reserves of trust and experienced cooperation" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4), [p-5](/post/continuum-of-power#p-5)).
- **The draft.** For "pedagogical futures", where institutions invest in the people who will succeed them, his image is a world "as if professional sports teams could draft" players from strong high-school programmes generations ahead ([Trails of Liminal Succession](/post/trails-of-liminal-succession#p-16)). In the same essay "Athletic contests" sit beside moot-court and city-building contests as the substance of education ([p-14](/post/trails-of-liminal-succession#p-14)).
- **Spirit and composure.** His succession rituals call for the kind of composure "we are familiar with from well-run sporting events". He also credits "the sporting and competitive spirit so evident in the West", possibly "a positive result of its hostility to any occupant of the center" ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-18), [p-22](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-22)).

## What this suggests, and what's missing

Taken together, these passages show sport as one of the few places where modern people still live comfortably inside rules, ranked hierarchy, a respected referee and orderly succession, things they resent everywhere else. That is why Katz finds it useful. Notice the questions he would ask of a professional league. Who are its arbiters? How does it handle succession, through drafts, captaincies and coaching trees? How much of the "closure" in a final score is manufactured? Those are the same questions he asks of states.

The archive does not cover sport as a business, the cultural meaning of fandom, or particular players and teams. Anything you build there would be your own extension, not his position.

**Read next:** [The Terror of the Given](/post/the-terror-of-the-given), the fullest treatment of the game as a model of the scene and of idioms. Then [Thirdness](/post/thirdness), to see why the sporting event's "official closure" sits at the center of his juridical project.

**A question to try:** VAR and instant replay have made refereeing far more explicit and contested. Would Katz see that as a perfecting of the juridical, or as a sign that the game's shared deferral is wearing thin?

rows.q: What does Katz say about raising toddlers?
rows.a:
Katz doesn't write about raising toddlers. Nothing in the archive is parenting advice, and the search turned up nothing close to the question. Small children do show up in his work fairly often, though, and always for the same reason: they are where the basic structures of the human are easiest to see. That is the material I can give you.

## Children as the evidence for mimesis

When Katz needs to show that imitation goes all the way down, he points to children. In the lecture on mimesis: "Anyone can see looking briefly at small children can see how deep mimesis goes" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-3)). Elsewhere, defending the starting point of the originary hypothesis, he asks: "How, exactly, do you think you learned to do anything? Can anyone fail to see the logic of imitation leading to rivalry? Again, have you ever watched children, or observed the simplest inter-personal dynamics?" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)).

What he takes from this is that imitation is not a neutral copying of behaviour. "Imitation is ostensive and imperative—you pay very close attention to what another is doing—too close to verbalize it. You take what the other is doing as a tacit command, as if the phrase 'do this' or 'do it like this' was tagged to it" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-5)). For a toddler, every adult gesture works as a command, whether or not the adult means it as one. Imitation also produces rivalry: the child learns to want things from its models, so it wants what the model has.

## Children and the center: pointing

The second place children appear is joint attention. Katz draws on Tomasello's finding that great apes don't point: "This very simple activity, one that very small children can perform very early, is impossible for animals that might be far more intelligent than those children by all kinds of measures. Two chimps can't look at something together, and let each other know that they're doing so" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-2)). For Center Study this is where the object, the subject and the center first appear together. A toddler pointing at a dog and looking back at you to check that you see it too is the human beginning, not an early stage of something more important.

## The child's mistake as the origin of new speech forms

The most interesting passage for your question is about how the imperative was born. Katz, following Gans's *The Origin of Language*, imagines "an inexperienced sign user, perhaps a child, imitating 'blindly' a gesture she has seen others make; another member of the community, perhaps an adult but still unable to conceive of a sign used 'improperly,' 'redeems' the sign by providing its missing referent" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-3)). The child names something that isn't there. The adult, wanting to keep the exchange going (what Center Study calls *linguistic presence*), fetches the thing, and a command now exists that nobody intended to create.

Katz draws a general principle from this. The obvious guess would be that commands start with an adult who "wants" to command a child. In fact, "The reverse is much more likely the case" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-4)). New forms come from mistakes at the margin, and the people at the center take them up and redeem them. Anyone who has lived with a two-year-old will recognise this.

## Teaching as showing

Katz puts pedagogy close to the center of the human. "Showing someone how to do something is the ultimate act of faith... It is also the origin and essence of debt—if someone shows you how to do something, it is inscribed in your practices and you are obliged to maintain and transmit it" ([Trails of Liminal Succession](/post/trails-of-liminal-succession#p-22)). On parental authority specifically, he argues that the law should not reach into the household: "the juridical was not designed to settle disputes between parent and child over curfew times, and parents prohibited from making such decisions will ultimately be useless as reliable witnesses and defenders of everyday norms" ([Reconstituting Kinship](/post/reconstituting-kinship#p-3)).

## Applying it (my extrapolation, not Katz's)

Take two toddlers grabbing the same toy. Each wants it more because the other wants it. In Center Study's terms that is the originary scene in miniature: a mimetic convergence on a central object with no order left to settle who gets it. Read through Katz, the parent's job is less to announce a rule ("we share") than to supply a gesture the children can imitate: holding the toy up between them, pointing, naming it, setting up turns. That converts the grab into shared attention to the thing. Your own restraint, which they are watching and copying anyway, is the lesson. This fits his warning in other places that criteria handed down without a model to imitate ("write clearly", "be good") produce nothing to follow.

## What to read next

- [Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic): the clearest short account of why imitation is everything, and why admitting it feels shameful.
- [A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social): the child's "inappropriate ostensive" and how ostensive, imperative and declarative grow out of one another.

A question to take further: when your toddler says a word for something that isn't in the room, and you go and get it, what exactly have the two of you just taught each other?

rows.q: What does Center Study say about dreams and the unconscious?
rows.a:
## What the archive covers

Dreams barely appear in the archive. There are a few passing remarks, which I gather below, and nothing like a theory of dreaming. The unconscious gets more attention. Katz takes it up in one short essay, and the idea runs underneath much of how Center Study treats the self. The answer below therefore has two parts: a reasonably solid account of the unconscious, then a thin layer on dreams.

## 1. The originary unconscious: the violent imaginary

The main text is "Violent Imaginaries." It starts from a problem with the originary scene. A group of hominids rushing the central object would not actually destroy itself. They would tire out and the pecking order would reassert itself. Katz's answer is that the catastrophe is real as an *imagining*:

> "What is extremely plausible, though, is that such an all-consuming storm of violence is what that breakdown would look like to the members of the proto-human group—and that it would need to look that way in order prompt the invention of the sign." ([Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-3))

He then names that imagining:

> "the intuition or, perhaps, unconscious, constituting the sign is not a reasonable expectation of devastating violence but a violent imaginary." ([Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-3))

On this account the unconscious is not a storehouse of repressed private wishes. It is the scene's own *continuation*, its completion of a partly seen convergence into total catastrophe. Katz borrows Collingwood's point that "imagination must make perception possible in the first place" ([p-4](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-4)). The imaginary is a supplement that has to be in place before you can perceive anything as meaningful. Because the sign answers this imaginary, the claim extends to all of culture: "All signs, and all of culture, then, would have to be constituted by some violent imaginary, one we could read negatively off of the signs of culture themselves" ([p-6](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-6)). Every gesture of deferral carries a negative image of the disaster it holds off. You read the unconscious from the shape of the deferral.

This is why Katz has a qualified respect for psychoanalysis, which he otherwise treats as superseded. He holds that "at least Freud put desire, violence and deferral at the center of his psychology," and that Freud "understood that reality is scenic, and the psychoanalytic session was one more scene or event in a long series of them leading us back to the original scene" ([p-7](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-7), [p-8](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-8)).

The next consequence is that the unconscious cannot be emptied out into consciousness:

> "the violent imaginary can never be made fully conscious—as Freud realized, the patient who came in familiar with his works and proceeded to spill his guts about his passion for his mother and desire to kill his father had simply rearranged the unconscious material under a new repression." ([p-9](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-9))

What can be done instead is to move it onto a shared scene. The imaginary "cannot be represented as such (we can’t paint a picture of it and look at it together) but it can be made the imaginary of the scene of representation itself, rather than of some represented scene" ([p-10](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-10)). In practice this means you don't explain someone's fears to them from outside. You build a space, such as a conversation or a discipline, whose form answers the imagined catastrophe and gives people positions to take up within it.

## 2. "The unconscious" as a figure we borrow from the center

The second move is less sympathetic to psychoanalysis. In Center Study, agency is first attributed to the center and only later borrowed by those on the margin. Katz puts "the unconscious" on the list of modern central beings we borrow from:

> "the modes of central being we now borrow from are now figures called “society,” “ideology,” “the unconscious,” “the media,” and so on." ([The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-2))

Everyone recognizes a residue in our actions that we did not choose, and the disciplines exist to give it a name. Katz deliberately deflates them: "saying that the trauma caused by my parents, or unjust social structures, or unconscious desires, etc., are not all that different from saying I was tempted by the devil" ([p-9](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-9)). These explanations may each be partly true, but they are "black boxes, sites of proxy wars for power", and "To be master of the “unconscious” is to be master of much more" ([p-10](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-10)).

His replacement for "the unconscious made me do it" is a grammar of imperatives. His example is a boy who resents a more popular rival. Asking which hidden drive won does not help. "I think the simplest and most realistic answer is to say he is listening to differing commands" ([p-12](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-12)): hurt him, wait your turn, get stoned, do your homework. These are commands he has heard many times, and many of them have no expiration date. The unchosen part of the self is the crowd of commands one cannot help receiving. In Lecture 4 Katz calls our relation to the center a "hearing" rather than a "reading", "because you hear whether you want to or not" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-6)). In this idiom the unconscious is a hearing that runs ahead of the will.

## 3. What is actually hidden: mimesis, not sex

Following Girard, Katz shifts what is supposed to be repressed. He reports Girard's observation that literature professors "would rather admit they want to have sex with their mothers and kill their fathers than admit that they feel envy" ([Talk of the Center (Adam Katz)](/post/talk-of-the-center-adam-katz#p-15)). What we hide best is how far our desires, gestures and opinions are borrowed. A culture that takes the individual as its basic unit must keep that dependence out of view. Katz adds, provocatively, that belief in the evil eye "demonstrates greater knowledge of social interaction than most of our psychology" ([p-16](/post/talk-of-the-center-adam-katz#p-16)). The archaic belief at least locates the trouble *between* people.

## 4. Dreams: the scattered remarks

- The earliest remark predates the Center Study idiom. In a 2014 post on neuroscience, Katz treats dreams as evidence that the mind does not run deterministically: "Our dreams, for example, are creative and unpredictable" ([Thought Experiment](/post/thought-experiment#p-8)).
- Later he treats dreams as what lies outside a practice: "You can’t control your dreams, but you can prevent your dreams from interfering with your management of your household." He adds, more openly: "And, who knows, maybe such maintenance acts back upon your dreams" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-5)).
- More generally, attention reshapes the unconscious rather than draining it: "The more you know about your “unconscious” the more you produce both greater consciousness and a more generative unconscious as you become attentive and retentive in new ways" ([Inscripto-punctualism](/post/inscripto-punctualism#p-10)).

## Applying it (my extension, not Katz's own)

Katz doesn't interpret dreams, so treat what follows as an attempt to use his tools, not his doctrine. Take a recurring anxiety dream: being chased, a crowd turning on you, a house coming apart. A Freudian reading looks for the hidden wish. A Center Study reading would ask what scene the dream is *completing*. What convergence does it imagine carried through to the end, with no sign issued to stop it? Where does the dreamer stand in that imagined melee: strongest, weakest, a bystander? Then it would ask which competing commands the dreamer is currently hearing in waking life. The dream would be read the way Katz reads culture, as a negative image of a deferral that is under strain. Freud's own wish-fulfilment theory of dreams is outside the archive. Katz cites Freud and Lacan only in passing.

## Where to read next

- [Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries) is short and is the only place Katz sketches an "originary theory of the unconscious." Read it first.
- [The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment) shows how he replaces talk of hidden drives with competing imperatives traced back to a center.

An exercise: pick a choice you made recently that felt "irrational" to you. Instead of asking what unconscious motive drove it, write out three or four commands you were hearing at that moment, and try to say where each came from. Notice whether the "unconscious" part starts to look less like a buried content and more like a crowd.

rows.q: What does Center Study say about string theory?
rows.a:
Katz never takes up string theory directly. The archive has no essay on it and no sustained discussion. What it does have is a general account of what a physical science *is* on Center Study's terms. That account lets us say something about string theory, as long as it's clear that the application is ours and not Katz's.

## The one passing mention

String theory appears once, in a passage defending the originary hypothesis against the charge that it is unscientific because it has no data:

> "No one really 'understands' particle physics or string theory, but these are not things to understand, merely equations to work out." ([Power and Digital Order](/post/power-and-digital-order#p-3))

The passage is complaining that a culture run on algorithms no longer makes room for "imaginary constructs as a mode of truth-seeking." Its voice reads more like Gans than Katz, and I wasn't shown the whole text, so treat it as coming from the GA side of the archive rather than as Katz's position. Either way, string theory is only a foil in it.

## What Katz does say about physics

The substantial material treats science as one kind of **disciplinary space**: a scene built on deferral, like every human scene.

> "The 'subject' of science is the 'community of inquirers,' or the disciplinary space. A group of people is organized around an artificially created scene which has been designed so as to determine what happens if we do this to that." ([Disciplinarity and the Center](/post/disciplinarity-and-the-center#p-4))

The deferral in question is paradoxical: "every truth the inquirers agree upon will only serve as the launchpad for a new inquiry" (same text). Physics doesn't escape the originary scene. It refines the oldest human act, gathering around a center so that everyone can say "this is the same."

Two claims follow that bear directly on string theory.

**1. The declarative has to come home to the ostensive.** In Center Study's grammar, mathematics is the purest form of the declarative, the language of statements. But:

> "However delayed, though, the declarative must come home to the ostensive—even the most complex physics experiment carried out with the most intricate machinery must give the scientist something to see and point to—even if it's just a reading on a meter that is very distantly related to anything we might actually be able to engage with our senses." ([Skewing Toward the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-skewing-toward-the-center#p-11))

He also writes that a discovery has been made "once participants on a disciplinary scene see something that is simultaneously real and a product of the scene of inquiry" ([same text](/post/anthropomorphics-skewing-toward-the-center#p-13)).

**2. Physics is ultimately historical.**

> "science (and I'll suggest this must be true even of mathematics) is always ultimately historical—resolving the most fundamental questions in physics (like the reconciliation of gravity with quantum undecidability) will require situating them within the history of the universe." ([Disciplinarity and the Center](/post/disciplinarity-and-the-center#p-8))

This is the closest the archive comes to string theory's own problem. Reconciling gravity with quantum mechanics is exactly what string theory set out to do.

## Applying this (my extrapolation, not Katz's)

The standard criticism of string theory is that it hasn't produced testable predictions at accessible energies. That criticism comes from physicists such as Smolin and Woit, not from the archive. In Center Study's terms it becomes a question about a scene. String theory is a declarative order that has stayed unusually long without "coming home" to a shared ostensive, a meter reading everyone can point to and agree is the same. Note Katz's "however delayed": delay alone doesn't disqualify an inquiry. What matters is whether the space is still organized around a center that can eventually be pointed to, or whether it has become a scene sustaining itself on its own equations.

Katz's "historical" claim suggests a further angle. If the gravity–quantum problem can only be solved by placing it within the history of the universe, a theory pitched as timeless law, a set of equations to be worked out, may be framing the question wrongly from the start. That is a speculative reading, and it goes beyond anything Katz argues.

## Where to read next

- [Disciplinarity and the Center](/post/disciplinarity-and-the-center) is Katz's fullest account of science as deferral and exchange with the center, and it contains the physics remark.
- [Skewing Toward the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-skewing-toward-the-center) explains why every declarative edifice, mathematics included, rests on ostensives and imperatives.

A question to take further: when you look into a microscope, Katz says your first question is "what am I looking at?" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-15)). What would the equivalent question be for string theory, and who in that disciplinary space is in a position to answer it?

rows.q: Quote the passage from Katz's essay "The Algorithmic Center" where he defines machine deferral.
rows.a:
## That essay isn't in what I was shown

I can't give you that quotation. No essay titled "The Algorithmic Center" appears among the texts I was shown, and I found no passage where Katz defines "machine deferral." I won't reconstruct one, because any wording I produced would be invented.

The passages I do have point the other way. Katz doesn't treat deferral as something machines do. He treats it as what separates us from them.

## What Katz says about deferral and machines

The plainest statement is in a 2024 Substack essay:

> "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation, which is the source of all human creation." ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23))

Deferral is the founding move of the originary scene: a hand reaching for the shared object pulls back, the grasp becomes a gesture, and the gesture becomes the first sign. For Katz, that pulling back is what makes us human. In the same paragraph he grants that AI can take part in reflection and that "what feels can be reduced to the unfeeling." He still locates the human difference in deferral.

He develops the point with a distinction between **tagging and tracking**. Animals follow marks, but "no animal tags in order to track"; humans do, because they can point things out to one another through joint attention. Then he asks the question you seem to be after:

> "If machine intelligence tags in order to track then the human/technical boundary collapses, at least according to the construction I’m proposing here." ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-13))

He admits that machines already do this, for example in surveillance. He still finds "a critical and, accepting the risk of all such claims, irreducible, difference" ([#p-14](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-14)). When humans tag and track human gestures, they open up histories and scenes without end. When an AI turns the same power on itself, it finds only its training data and its algorithm. Nothing in that tells anyone what to do next.

A related claim concerns **linguistic presence**, the ongoing assurance that we are still on the same scene together. Imagining software that could write his essay for him, Katz says a program depending on human input "can’t calculate for “linguistic presence” past a certain point," and concludes:

> "What only humans can contribute to the center, then, is forms of linguistic presence." ([Sampling on the Data Exchange](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange#p-22))

Elsewhere he puts it in terms of **deeming**, which means naming something with authority so that it counts as what it is named: "AIs can’t “deem,” or if they do deem, they have been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human" ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12)).

## Where machines do come in

Machines still matter here. In Katz's terms they can carry and help *measure* deferral even though they don't originate it. He speaks of "tokenizing deferral" through prediction markets ([Universal Translation Machine](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-6)). He also imagines algorithms designed so that people "learn... to think probabilistically, to project probabilities further and further into the future" ([Deferral as Media](/post/deferral-as-media#p-11)). The technology extends human deferral's reach. It does not defer in its own right.

## What to read next

- **[Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human)**. This is his fullest attempt to locate the human/machine boundary and test it.
- **[Sampling on the Data Exchange](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange)**. It shows how he thinks about writing *with* the algorithm instead of against it.

As an exercise, try writing your own definition of "machine deferral." Check it against the originary scene: whose appropriation is being aborted, and who has to recognize the gesture as a sign? The place where your definition starts to strain is likely the boundary Katz is pointing to.
