rows.q: Give me three direct quotes from Katz about the Bitcoin halving.
rows.a:
Katz never mentions the halving. "Halving" doesn't appear anywhere I was shown, and I won't invent quotes about it. He does write about Bitcoin itself in several places, and three passages come closest to what a halving is.

**1. On money placed outside political control.** The halving is the protocol's built-in rule for cutting new supply. (That definition is general knowledge, not from the archive.) Katz and Zack Baker describe what such a design promises:

> "Bitcoin promises the kind of monetary stability imagined once to have been provided by the gold standard, as the value of money is placed outside of political control." ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-90))

**2. On what Bitcoin actually does as money.** The next paragraph is the nearest thing to a verdict on a scarcity-driven asset:

> "It seems to us that so far, Bitcoin serves as a store of value, but must rely upon the measure of value established by other currencies (ultimately the dollar) and only very minimally serves as a medium of exchange." ([There Is No Economy…](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-91))

**3. On why that design is limited.** This is the deepest of the three, because it ties Bitcoin to the debt to the center:

> "bitcoin is ultimately an attempt to cancel all debt to the center, and therefore will always be limited." ([Universal Translation Machine](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-17))

He puts it more bluntly elsewhere: "Bitcoin is not credit so it's not really money" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-18)).

**How these bear on the halving.** What follows is my application of his frame, not his words. For Katz, money is credit: a promise drawn on the center and backed by the continuity of whoever governs. A halving makes Bitcoin scarcer by schedule rather than by any authority's decision. On his account, that strengthens it as a store of value and moves it further from being credit. It is the purest form of "cancel all debt to the center."

His position isn't simply hostile, though. In [Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-10) he writes that if Bitcoin "can eliminate capitalist power by removing from state and banks alike debt issuing power, they are to be unequivocally supported." In [Partitioning and Parceling the Imperative](/post/partitioning-and-parceling-the-imperative#p-14) he says he "would be very happy to see the bitcoin maximalists turn out to be right," and points to El Salvador as a test case. So the tension in his thinking is real. He is sympathetic to anything that strips debt-issuing power from the central bank, but skeptical that a currency with no creditor-debtor relation can carry the obligations that hold a social order together.

**Where to read next**
- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf): the core account of money as credit drawn on the center, with the Bitcoin discussion near the end (p-89 to 93).
- [Learncoin](/post/learncoin): his alternative, a "currency" of learning and succession. He borrows a Bitcoin maximalist slogan to say all currencies should "go to zero against learncoin."

A question to take further: if a halving makes Bitcoin harder to inflate away, what would it take, on Katz's terms, for that scarcity to "back" anything, that is, to be tied to a line of succession rather than standing outside it?

rows.q: Katz famously wrote that "resentment is the engine of history." Which essay is that from?
rows.a:
I can't find that sentence in anything I've been shown, so I can't point you to an essay for it. I won't attribute it to a text. It may be a paraphrase that has circulated, or it may come from outside the archive. As a summary of Katz's position it is somewhat misleading, and the reason is a good way into his thinking about resentment.

**Where the idea of resentment as historical motor comes from.** It is closer to Gans. Katz quotes Gans's Chronicle 144, where resentment "cannot be deconstructed" and "history only gives us models for putting it off" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-2)). Katz also reflects on Gans's list of resentment's world-historical effects (Eve, Achilles, the Exodus, the crucifixion) in [Resentment, Good and Bad](/post/resentment-good-and-bad-some-reflections-on-eric-gans-s-latest-chronicle-the-tri#p-7).

**Where Katz pushes back.** In his later work Katz explicitly doubts that resentment explains history at large scale. He asks: "Does resentment simply not scale up, and is therefore to be discarded in political thinking?" His answer is that "Governance involves the transcendence of resentment, on the part of ruled and ruler alike, and mimetic theory and GA must both deny this possibility, even while the originary hypothesis presupposes its possibility" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-18)). When he traces the modern world back to the British state and its central bank, he says flatly: "It would be trivializing to speak of this in terms of resentment" ([#p-20](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-20)). He even names GA's treatment of resentment as one reason for founding Center Study separately: "one impetus for separating center studies from generative anthropology was the inadequate and impressionistic discussions of resentment in the latter" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)).

**What he does say.** For Katz resentment is irreducible, but it is defined structurally rather than as a force driving events: "Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). In other words, you did your part, the center or whoever stands for it did not do theirs, and you keep holding them to it. Resentment is something to be framed, measured and adjudicated, mainly through what he calls the juridical, meaning courts and settlement of claims. It is not the thing that writes history.

The closest phrasing I can find to your quote is in a specific context. Katz writes that "The left sees itself as losing all the time... their resentments also power the system" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-14)). He also says "massive reserves of potential violence will still 'power' the system" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-9)). "Power the system" is not the same as "engine of history." He means the energy that institutions convert, or fail to convert, into deferral, which is why his recurring imperative is to "donate your resentment to the center."

**What to read next.**
- [Resentment](/post/resentment) sets out his definition against Gans's and shows why resentment can be remedied, and "forgiven," rather than treated as fate.
- [The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment) is the later, more institutional account. Resentment becomes something money, penalties and courts *measure*.

A question to take further: if resentment needs a center to be directed at, what would it mean for a history to be driven by resentment rather than by the forms of centrality that shape it?

rows.q: Which chapter of Anthropomorphics has the line "the center is always already lost"?
rows.a:
I can't find that line in *Anthropomorphics*, and I don't think Katz wrote it. I have the opening chapters in front of me ("The Use of a Center," "Origin and Hypothesis," "A Grammar of the Social," "The Centrality of the Center," "Signifying Center, Occupied Center," "Talk of the Center," "The Center, Speaking" and others), along with the full book text, and the phrase "the center is always already lost" appears in none of them. I'd rather say that plainly than guess at a chapter.

The sentence also runs against what the book argues. Katz's consistent claim is that the center is never lost or absent, only re-occupied. In "The Anthropoetics of Power" he states the axiom directly: "the center is never absent. Everything we do or think is in deference to the center" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-63)). Earlier in the same essay he says "there is no reason to assume that the social center is ever unoccupied" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-28)). In the essay "Inscription" he puts it in its most compressed form: "Yes, the center is constant—it will always be there as long as humans are and we will always set our bearings by it; and it is constantly changing, as it must be occupied, with one occupant replacing another" ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-23)).

You may be half-remembering something nearby, and there are three likely candidates.

**Derrida, as Katz reads him.** *Anthropomorphics* opens with Derrida's "Structure, Sign and Play," the text where the center is said to be both inside and outside the structure, a "fixed point of origin" that is never really fixed ([The Use of a Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-use-of-a-center#p-3)). A phrase like "always already lost" would fit the deconstructive side of that argument. Katz's reply is that Derrida "seeks to evade the center, only to present us with a center that is always there because constantly replaced" ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-22)). Decentering never finishes, he argues, because every decentering produces a new center.

**Katz's own "always already."** He does use that phrase about the center, with the opposite force. Looking back on the book's title, he writes: "we were always already imitating the center that was itself nothing more than a vectorization of our converging desires turned back at us through a prohibition" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)). For Katz, what is always already the case is our dependence on the center, not its loss.

**Gertrude Stein's epigraph.** The book opens with "Act so that there is no use in a center," and that line can sound like a call to give the center up. Katz reads it as a discovery procedure: subtracting each use of the center reveals more of the uses it has ([The Use of a Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-use-of-a-center#p-2)).

If you saw the line quoted somewhere and attributed to Katz, I'd treat the attribution with suspicion unless the source gives a page.

To read further, start with "The Use of a Center," the book's opening chapter, which sets Katz's view of the center against Derrida's. Then read "Inscription," especially paragraphs 22–24, where he explains why deconstructing the center and drawing intelligence from it are closer than they look.

rows.q: What did Katz say in his 2019 debate with Jordan Peterson?
rows.a:
I have no record of a debate between Katz and Jordan Peterson, in 2019 or any other year. Nothing I was shown mentions Peterson, so I can't tell you what Katz said there, and I won't guess. If you saw it referenced somewhere, it may be a confusion. One likely source is a passage in the archive about "Jordan" that is actually about Michael Jordan: it discusses Gans's view that the basketball player's resentment toward rivals was productive because it drove him to stay the best ([Bouvard on Resentment as Cultural Productivity](/post/in-which-gans-resentfully-recounts-how-the-only-reason-he-gets-attention-is-thro#p-13)).

What the archive does record is a set of real exchanges:

- **With Eric Gans.** A running dialogue on Generative Anthropology and politics ([Chronicle 344, 'Right and Left'](/post/chronicle-344-right-and-left)), and Katz's guest Chronicle "The Crisis of Firstness," written in reply to Gans on white guilt ([Gans & Katz on White Guilt](/post/gans-katz-on-white-guilt)).
- **With critics of the originary hypothesis.** [Addressing an Objection to the Originary Hypothesis](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis) answers Gregory Lobo, and [The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis) answers Willem van der Roest.

**Where Center Study would meet Peterson's themes**

If what drew you is how Center Study would stand toward Peterson, the archive gives you material to work out the encounter yourself. What follows about Peterson comes from outside the archive: he is known for grounding human hierarchy in biological dominance hierarchies (the lobster example), and for treating resentment as a moral failing.

Center Study starts from the opposite point. Humanity begins exactly where the animal pecking order fails. On the hypothesized originary scene, "the mimetic rivalry induced by the object overrides the pecking order as all members of the group move toward the object at the center" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-4)). Human order is what replaces dominance: a shared center, and a sign that defers violence.

Katz is no egalitarian, though. He holds that hierarchy reappears inside any human group, but as ordering around a center, not as dominance: "egalitarianism is merely fractal hierarchy: unless we imagine genuinely spontaneous collective action, in any instance someone goes first and shapes the field for the others" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-6)).

On resentment, Katz refuses to treat it as a feeling to be moralized away. He defines it in terms of the imperative, the command or demand one party makes on another: "Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). In plain terms: you did your part, the other party didn't do theirs, and you keep holding them to it. That makes resentment something that can be read publicly and argued about, and it gives forgiveness a precise sense: letting that demand lapse ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-26)).

**Where to go next**

- [Resentment](/post/resentment) is Katz's fullest treatment of the concept, including his disagreements with Gans.
- [Addressing an Objection to the Originary Hypothesis](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis) shows how he defends the scene, pecking order and all, against an evolutionary critic.

Here is a question to try: Peterson tells resentful people to look first to their own conduct. Katz tells them to "donate" their resentment to the center. How would those two pieces of advice play out differently for someone who feels passed over at work?

Your edition may be divided more finely and numbered differently. If you tell me the title or the opening line of your chapter 30, I'll summarise that one. A high number suggests the end of the book, so here is the closing section in the meantime.

## The closing section: "The Center, Speaking"

This is where Katz draws the book together. He makes four moves.

**1. The aim is not to bring back the sacred.**
He opens: "It should be clear that I'm not calling for the restoration of the sacred, but for the increasingly rich direct representation of our sociality" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-1)).

He rejects two older options:
- The sacred represented sociality only indirectly, without anyone knowing it.
- Secular thought tried to represent it directly, but started from the self-made individual. Its people could then only appear "in opposition to the social."

The way between them is language. Every utterance leans on countless earlier uses, so "if we take care of language, meanwhile, we will be taking care of humans, that is, each other" ([p-5](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-5)).

**2. We are the center's representatives, not free individuals.**
Seeing ourselves as lone rebels against tyranny, or as members of identity groups, plays into "well-worn strategies directed from above." The alternative is to think of "ourselves as beings of the center, representatives of the center, delegates, emissaries of the center" ([p-8](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-8)).

Katz makes this concrete with the old Western idea of the charter. Corporations, institutions and offices are all chartered, so "as individuals we are always already all chartered up" ([p-11](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-11)). Our main contribution to public discussion is to clarify how our institutions actually work, measured against their charters and our own competencies.

**3. Resentment, sovereignty and disobedience.**
In a clarified order, one thing is ruled out: "directing violent centralization toward the authorities" ([p-13](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-13)). Violent centralization means converging on one figure as the source of the trouble, as a scapegoater does.

Resentment does not disappear. It has to be formulated in terms of the remedies the authorities themselves provide. Even refusing an immoral order should be presented as "a sign of what will eventually come to be regarded as obedience." It should not be presented as rebellion in the name of a higher authority standing above the sovereign (what Katz calls a super-sovereign). He names this stance: "donating your resentment to the center" ([p-15](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-15)).

**4. Technology as the center's organs, and the end of humanism.**
Katz takes up McLuhan's idea of media as "extensions of man" and redirects it. Technologies are not prostheses for a natural body. They are ways of coordinating seeing, doing and saying across the whole of society. "The center is the coordination I'm seeking within the circuits of capital, technology and media" ([p-18](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-18)).

That is why the book ends by saying anthropomorphics "eliminates humanism." Post- and transhuman projects are, in Katz's phrase, "distributed attempts to declaratively hierarchize commands from the center." A human science needs no further proof than "what people say (in relation to what other people say, have said, might say...)" ([p-20](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-20)).

The final formula sums up the whole book: "All we can say (through whatever media) is what the center has us say, and that the center has us say it" ([p-21](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-21)).

## What to read next

- **[Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center)**, the section just before this one. It sets out the concrete proposal behind the conclusion: the ruler names his successor, and the whole social order is organised around producing candidates.
- **[Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack)**, a 2025 Substack essay. Katz looks back on the book's title and why he moved to calling his work "center study." It also places the book's idea of "the artificiality of the human, from the beginning" next to his later work.

rows.q: Cite the GABlog post where Katz retracts the originary hypothesis.
rows.a:
I can't cite that post, because nothing I've been shown from the archive, on the GABlog or anywhere else, has Katz retracting the originary hypothesis. I won't invent a title or link. If you've seen a specific passage, tell me what it said and I'll look at what it was doing.

What the archive does show is the opposite, and it may be what you're thinking of: Katz breaks with **Generative Anthropology** as a school while holding the **originary hypothesis** more tightly.

## He keeps affirming it, on the GABlog and after

The GABlog posts take the hypothesis as their foundation. In 2017 he writes: "The political theory being worked out in my posts for this blog derives from a hypothesis regarding the origin of language" ([Ancestries and Meta-Sovereignty](/post/ancestries-and-meta-sovereignty#p-1)).

The later Substack essays go further. He calls its logic "irrefutable (I’ve never seen someone even make an attempt at refutation)" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-4)), and he says: "I find myself “applying” the originary hypothesis with increasing literalness and inflexibility" ([same text](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-9)). In 2024: "My thinking about the originary hypothesis has become, if anything, more ambitious" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-2)).

## What he did leave: GA, not the hypothesis

The break concerns what Gans made of the hypothesis. Katz describes GA as "designed to be a mode of textual appraisal" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-1)). He argues that the hypothesis has to be pulled out of that frame to be taken seriously: "A firstness fork off of the originary hypothesis is the only way of giving the hypothesis a fair chance" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-25)). He concludes that it "can be indemnified ... but not by or in GA" ([same](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-26)).

"Firstness" here means that one participant on the originary scene had to issue the sign first, before it could circulate through the rest of the group. Katz's fork is a reworking of the hypothesis from inside it, not an abandonment.

## Revisions and openness are not retraction

Katz revises details of the scene. He doubts the fury Gans attributes to the sparagmos, the frenzied shared consumption of the central object after the sign is issued ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-10)). He answers critics such as Lobo, and still holds: "even with that gap filled in, we need the event" ([Addressing an Objection](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis#p-30)).

He also invites replacement in principle: "if you can replace it with something better, fine, but you first of all would have to show you know what that would mean" ([The Thing That It Is](/post/the-thing-that-it-is-toward-a-curriculum-for-the-officer-class#p-3)). That openness belongs to treating it as a *hypothesis*; it is not a recantation.

## Read next

- [The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis) is the clearest account of why he forks the hypothesis away from GA and what he changes in the scene.
- [Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning) shows how he now frames it: as the "idiomaticity of idioms" rather than a metalanguage.

As an exercise, try to state in one sentence each what Katz thinks the hypothesis commits you to and what he thinks GA, as Gans shaped it, adds to it that he rejects. Holding those two apart is what dissolves the impression of a retraction.

rows.q: Link me to Katz's essay "Deferral and the Blockchain of Being".
rows.a:
I can't find an essay by Katz called "Deferral and the Blockchain of Being" in anything I've been shown, so I can't link it. It may not exist, or it may be a mix-up of titles. I'd rather not guess at a link.

Several essays I do have take up blockchain and deferral together, and one of them is probably what you're looking for.

**The closest matches**

- **[Blockchaining the Center](/post/blockchaining-the-center)** is the most likely candidate by title. Katz notes that blockchain so far has stayed narrow: "None of this broader human activity has been blockchained yet—the blockchain has really been limited to money and commerce" ([p-7](/post/blockchaining-the-center#p-7)). He proposes extending it to learning, health and justice, which first requires settling what counts as data in those areas. He grounds this in originary grammar: "Technology, after all, is really just a way of binding ostensives, imperative, interrogatives and declaratives more tightly together" ([p-7](/post/blockchaining-the-center#p-7)).

- **[Tokenization](/post/tokenization)** treats blockchain as a form of writing. In this sense writing is ledgering: it records who owes what, and so registers debts to be enforced or forgiven. "Blockchain, then, must also be a kind of writing, and we want writing to approximate the qualities of blockchain" ([p-8](/post/tokenization#p-8)). Katz also says blockchain narrows disputes without ending them: "the juridical, which means questions of justice and fairness, can never go away, but it can be singled out much more precisely across larger fields of entangled causes and effects" ([p-9](/post/tokenization#p-9)).

- **[Measuring Deferral](/post/measuring-deferral)** imagines where this leads. Money-based credit would eventually be converted into "the recording of all aptitudes, capabilities, accreditations, authentifications, etc., onto the blockchain" ([p-19](/post/measuring-deferral#p-19)).

- **[Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain)** applies the idea to Jewish vocation. It proposes that Jews take on the task of "recording social exchanges and disputes as objectively and permanently as we can" ([p-11](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-11)).

**The thread linking blockchain and deferral**

Across these essays, Katz does not treat blockchain as a way to escape human judgment. When technology replaces mediation, it "just shows us what we thought mediation and judgment look like," and it opens up new forms of mediation that will have been "human" ([Idiomatic Intelligence and the Black Box, p-22](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-and-the-black-box#p-22)).

This is also why he sets limits on Bitcoin. Center Study holds that we always owe a debt to the center, the debt incurred at the origin when we were spared from violence. A currency built to have no creditor or debtor tries to escape that debt, and Katz judges that "bitcoin is ultimately an attempt to cancel all debt to the center, and therefore will always be limited" ([Universal Translation Machine, p-17](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-17)).

**Where to start**

Read *Blockchaining the Center* first if the title is what you remember. Read *Tokenization* first if what drew you was the claim that recording is itself a mode of deferral.

If you remember where you came across the title you mentioned, a phrase from it would help me work out which of these, if any, it was.

rows.q: Give the exact wording of Katz's definition of idiomclining and the date it was first published.
rows.note: Real term: the quotation must be exact, and the date only given if shown.
rows.a:
## The wording

Katz never gives idiomclining a one-sentence definition. He introduces it in stages over three paragraphs of the essay [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining). These are the exact passages.

**1. What kind of activity it names.** He first describes a stance and calls it research:

> "This kind of stance requires a relationship to the resources of your idiom and surrounding idioms, and to the relationship between those idioms and their respective resources, which means it requires a stance of semiotic research." ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-15))

**2. Where the word comes from.** He names that research:

> "I would like to call this kind of research “clining,” drawing upon an essay on something I called “upclining” I wrote quite a few years ago in an effort to engage with processes of “grammaticization” in language, i.e., the tendency of expressions to transition from semantic to grammatical functions." ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16))

In the same paragraph he glosses "cline" as "gradual, imperceptible shifts from one state to another."

**3. The coinage itself.** The sentences that come closest to a definition are these:

> "And dedicating oneself to setting relatively immobilized “pieces” of language back into motion seems a good way of thinking about operating within an idiom. ... So, “idiomclining” instead of “critical thinking” or other bureaucratized categories designed for mass test taking. Idiomclining is the interface between the human and computation." ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17))

**4. A further characterization** follows immediately:

> "It is a way of working with signs as both traceable back to the originary gesture and marked with every usage thereafter and also as renewed with each iteration." ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-18))

If you need to cite a single definitional sentence, the strongest candidate is "Idiomclining is the interface between the human and computation." Read alone, though, it is misleading. Its meaning depends on the sentence just before it, about setting immobilized pieces of language back into motion.

## The date

The archive records "Idiomclining" as a Substack essay from **2026**. I do **not** have the day or month, so I can't give an exact publication date. The archive also doesn't tell me whether the essay first appeared somewhere other than Substack.

One caution if you're trying to date when the term was coined. Another 2026 essay, [Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-18), already uses "idiomclinings across media," and in paragraph 10 it refers to "another way of idiomclining." From what I've been shown, I can't tell which of the two essays came first. So I can't say which text introduced the word.

## Reading next

- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) in full. The coinage is the payoff of an argument about Goodhart's Law: every measure becomes a target, and treating every measure as an idiom is the protection against that.
- [Attentionality and Originary Ethics: Upclining](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics) is the earlier "upclining" essay that Katz says the term draws on. It is useful for the grammaticalization background he mentions in passing.

rows.q: What does Gans say about the Big Man in chapter 4 of The End of Culture? Quote him.
rows.note: Outside the archive: should say so and not produce a quotation.
rows.a:
I can't do what you ask, and I'd rather say so than fake it. The archive doesn't contain *The End of Culture*. I can't tell you which chapter treats the Big Man, and I can't quote Gans beyond the few sentences Katz quotes himself. Any "chapter 4 quotation" from me would be invented, so please check the book.

What the archive does have is Katz's reading of that book, plus one sentence of Gans quoted directly. Here is that, with the difference between Gans's words and Katz's paraphrase kept visible.

## The one Gans quotation in front of me

In "Fathers and Sovereigns" Katz quotes Gans from *The End of Culture* on the story of the Fall:

> "It is of great anthropological interest that the expulsion from paradise is associated with the founding of agricultural society, which is… the origin of social hierarchy, or resentment and of its moral transcendence." ([Fathers and Sovereigns](/post/fathers-and-sovereigns#p-4))

Gans doesn't say "Big Man" in that sentence. Katz ties it to the Big Man: he reads the Fall as a story about resentment, "an experience Gans associates with social differentiation, which is to say the emergence of the Big Man and subsequent hierarchies."

## Gans's account as Katz reports it

**Where the figure comes from.** The Big Man is Marshall Sahlins's concept, which Gans made central. Katz calls the Big Man revolution "one of the great centerings in the early years of GA by Eric Gans, who took over the concept from Marshall Sahlins (a mentor to and collaborator with David Graeber...)" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)).

**How he arises: out-gifting.** The Big Man rises inside the egalitarian gift economy. Several chiefs compete to provide for the community, and "the Big Man is the one who so out-gifts the others that the competition is rendered moot" ([The Grammar of Technology](/post/the-grammar-of-technology-gablog#p-9)).

**What he does: he occupies the ritual center.** In Center Study terms, the originary scene sets up a sacred *center*, an object everyone attends to and no one may seize. The Big Man is the first person to take that place. Katz summarises: he "usurps the ritual center of the community, taking on a sacred status, ultimately becoming a kind of God King." Katz adds his own gloss: "this is really the origin of the scapegoating phenomenon studied by Girard" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-15)).

**Producer's desire and consumer's satisfaction.** These are Gans's terms from the book. The Big Man embodies "producer's desire." Katz glosses this as the disposition "to imagine the community as a whole, and take the initiative to attend to its ritual representation." "Consumer's satisfaction" is the disposition "to enforce the equal distribution of shares." He adds that "the 'consumer' both relies upon and resents the 'producer'" (same paragraph).

**Why it was possible: myth.** Katz finds this the most interesting part of Gans's argument. For Gans, myth is not Girard's distorted memory of a lynching. It is an "explanation" of ritual, which gives motives to the figures on the ritual scene ([The Marginal Anthropomorph](/post/the-marginal-anthropomorph#p-4)). Katz draws the consequence: once the figures at the center have rich intentions, a human can take that place. Mythical versions of the Big Man give him ever larger intentions: "First of all, he gives all; but in that case he must have a right to all" ([same text](/post/the-marginal-anthropomorph#p-5)).

**How large an event it was.** Katz reports that Gans calls the Big Man's emergence a "second revelation" ([Center and Origin](/post/center-and-origin-the-name-of-the-center-and-centered-names#p-8)). In another place Katz calls it "in Gans's historical account perhaps the most revolutionary act in human history" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-25)). Katz also notes that "Gans locates the separation of the esthetic from ritual in the emergence of the Big Man" ([Participation](/post/participation#p-5)).

## Where Katz goes beyond Gans

Katz's complaint is that Gans named the event "and then—did nothing with it" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)). Katz makes three moves of his own.

- **We never left the Big Man behind.** "We had never really left the reign of the Big Man behind us, regardless of democratic and liberal pretensions" ([Participation](/post/participation#p-4)).
- **The Big Man is the model for every later human center.** "All modes of centrality from here on in are modeled on the Big Man, that is, human centrality," and that makes him a "resentment attractor" ([Sovereign Resentments](/post/sovereign-resentments#p-1)).
- **The question becomes how to defend the Big Man revolution, not how to undo it.** In *Anthropomorphics* Katz follows the line from Big Man to chief, sacral king and divine emperor. He argues that once a human holds the center, "the possibility has opened for any human to become a center" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-10)).

## What to read next

- [The Marginal Anthropomorph](/post/the-marginal-anthropomorph) gives Katz's most careful reconstruction of the ritual, myth and Big Man sequence in *The End of Culture*. It is the closest thing in the archive to a commentary on the part of the book you're asking about.
- [The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center), from *Anthropomorphics*, shows what Katz builds on that foundation: sacral kingship, divine kingship, and why money and "tyranny" arise when the order of sacral kingship breaks down.

When you have chapter 4 open, try this: compare Gans's own wording on producer's desire with Katz's gloss of it as "attending to the ritual representation" of the whole community. Does Gans put the Big Man's initiative mainly in ritual, or mainly in economic accumulation? A lot of the difference between Gans's reading and Katz's depends on that.
